options: Bright, because of increased tissue water
Dark, since pathology shortens T2 relaxation
Invisible unless contrast has been given
The same low signal as cortical bone
body.explain: Oedema, inflammation and many tumours add water, which is bright on T2, making T2 and FLAIR the workhorses for detecting disease.

body.prompt: A double inversion-recovery black-blood sequence is used to:
options: Null flowing blood to show the vessel wall or myocardium
Brighten flowing blood to reveal patent vessels
Suppress signal from cortical bone
Increase the specific absorption rate
body.explain: Two inversion pulses null inflowing blood, producing a black-blood image that highlights the vessel wall or myocardial edge.

body.prompt: Signal averaging (increasing NEX) improves SNR by a factor of:
options: The square root of the number of averages
Directly with the number of averages
Twice the number of averages acquired
It has no effect on the signal
body.explain: Averaging reduces random noise as the square root of the count, so quadrupling NEX doubles SNR at four times the scan time.

body.prompt: At a fixed scan time, pushing spatial resolution higher usually costs:
options: SNR
Contrast weighting
Slice count only
Nothing
body.explain: Smaller voxels hold fewer spins, so at fixed time and averages higher resolution comes at the expense of signal-to-noise.

body.prompt: Gibbs (truncation) ringing is reduced by:
options: Increasing the matrix to sample more k-space
Lowering the acquisition matrix instead
Raising the receiver bandwidth setting
Adding a fat suppression technique
body.explain: Ringing comes from truncating k-space at sharp edges; sampling more high-frequency data with a larger matrix narrows and reduces it.

body.prompt: The best way to improve lesion conspicuity is often to:
options: Raise contrast to noise, not just SNR
Maximise raw signal to noise alone
Increase the field of view broadly
Lower the acquisition matrix size
body.explain: A lesion is seen because its signal differs from the background; maximising CNR (through sequence and contrast choice) matters more than raw SNR.

body.prompt: FLAIR is fundamentally which class of sequence?
options: Inversion recovery with a long TI
A spoiled gradient echo technique
A balanced steady-state sequence
A conventional single spin echo
body.explain: FLAIR is inversion recovery; the long TI nulls CSF while the readout keeps T2 weighting, unmasking periventricular disease.

body.prompt: Setting a gradient-echo flip angle at the Ernst angle:
options: Maximises signal for the given TR and T1
Nulls the fat signal completely
Removes motion artefact from images
Doubles the in-plane resolution
body.explain: The Ernst angle is the flip that yields peak steady-state signal for a chosen TR and T1, optimising SNR in fast gradient-echo imaging.

body.prompt: Single-shot fast spin echo (HASTE / SSFSE) is especially useful for:
options: Motion-prone T2 imaging like MRCP or fetal scans
High-resolution T1-weighted brain imaging
Diffusion tensor imaging of white matter
Dynamic perfusion-weighted imaging studies
body.explain: Acquiring a whole slice after one excitation freezes motion, so single-shot FSE suits uncooperative patients and bright-fluid T2 studies.

body.prompt: Image blurring in fast spin echo increases with:
options: A longer echo train with higher ETL
A shorter echo train length used
A larger prescribed field of view
A lower static field strength
body.explain: Later echoes in a long train have decayed and are recorded with different T2 weighting, which blurs fine detail as ETL grows.

body.prompt: Chemical shift of the second kind (the India-ink boundary) is seen on:
options: Opposed-phase gradient echo images
Spin echo T1-weighted images only
Diffusion-weighted echo planar images
Time-of-flight angiography images
body.explain: When fat and water share a voxel and are out of phase, their signals cancel at fat-water borders, drawing a dark outline.

body.prompt: Dielectric (standing-wave) artifact, causing central signal loss, is more common:
options: At 3 T in large body parts, eased with pads
At low field strengths such as 0.5 T
When imaging small peripheral joints
Only with spin echo sequences used
body.explain: Short RF wavelengths at high field can form standing waves in large or ascitic abdomens; dielectric cushions even out the B1 field.

body.prompt: A flow void (dark rapidly flowing blood) on spin echo occurs because:
options: Fast spins exit the slice before the 180 pulse
Flowing blood has a very short T1
Gadolinium contrast is present in blood
The readout gradients momentarily fail
body.explain: Spins that exit the slice between the 90 and 180 pulses are not refocused, so patent fast-flow vessels appear as signal voids.

body.prompt: The entry-slice (flow-related enhancement) phenomenon brightens:
options: The first slices as unsaturated blood enters
The central slices of the imaging slab
Stationary fat within the imaging slab
Dense cortical bone in the region
body.explain: Unsaturated inflowing spins are fully magnetised, so the entry slices of a stack show bright vessels, the basis of time-of-flight MRA.

body.prompt: Cross-excitation (slice cross-talk) is minimised by:
options: Interslice gaps or interleaved acquisition
Delivering a higher SAR to the patient
Using a larger acquisition matrix
Acquiring more signal averages
body.explain: Imperfect slice profiles let adjacent slices partly saturate each other; a gap or interleaved ordering keeps their excitations apart.

body.prompt: Truncation (Gibbs) artifact tends to be worst when:
options: The matrix is low at a high-contrast edge
The phase matrix is set very high
The static field strength is low
Chemical fat suppression is applied
body.explain: Fewer sampled k-space lines cannot represent a sharp edge, so ringing is most visible at high-contrast borders on low-matrix images.

body.prompt: Pulsation ghosts from an artery overlying the anatomy can be shifted off the region by:
options: Swapping the phase and frequency axes or a sat band
Raising the repetition time to reduce them
Lowering the receiver bandwidth to reduce them
Increasing the field of view to reduce them
body.explain: Ghosts propagate along the phase axis, so swapping encode directions moves them elsewhere, and a sat band removes the pulsating source signal.

body.prompt: Central restricted diffusion within a ring-enhancing lesion favours:
options: A pyogenic abscess over necrotic tumour
A simple non-enhancing fluid cyst
A benign fat-containing lipoma
Normal unaffected brain tissue
body.explain: Viscous pus restricts diffusion (bright DWI, dark ADC) in the cavity, whereas necrotic tumour usually does not, aiding the distinction.

body.prompt: Multiple tiny foci of blooming on SWI after head trauma suggest:
options: Diffuse axonal injury, microhaemorrhages
An acute ischaemic territory infarct
Fatty change within the brain tissue
Normal age-related change only
body.explain: Shearing injury tears small vessels, leaving microhaemorrhages that bloom on susceptibility imaging at grey-white junctions and the corpus callosum.

body.prompt: A marrow-replacing lesion in a vertebra characteristically appears:
options: Dark on T1, replacing bright fatty marrow
Brighter than normal marrow on T1
Invisible across all pulse sequences
Bright only on time-of-flight images
body.explain: Normal adult marrow is fatty and bright on T1; tumour or infiltration replaces that fat and stands out as low T1 signal.

body.prompt: A T1-bright lesion whose signal drops on fat-suppressed images contains:
options: Fat, as in a lipoma or dermoid
Subacute methaemoglobin blood
A focus of dense calcification
Slowly flowing venous blood
body.explain: Loss of the bright T1 signal with fat suppression proves the source is fat, separating a lipoma or dermoid from haemorrhage or melanin.

body.prompt: Increasing the number of phase-encode steps at a fixed FOV:
options: Improves phase resolution but adds scan time
Shortens the overall acquisition time
Lowers the phase-encode resolution
Has no effect on acquisition time
body.explain: Each extra phase-encode line is another TR of acquisition, so finer phase resolution directly costs scan time.

body.prompt: Frequency (readout) oversampling is used to:
options: Prevent aliasing along the frequency direction
Raise the specific absorption rate delivered
Suppress the chemical shift fat signal
Shorten the repetition time TR used
body.explain: Sampling more points during readout is essentially free and prevents wraparound along the frequency axis, so scanners often do it automatically.

body.prompt: Receiver bandwidth is best described as:
options: The range of frequencies sampled during readout
The strength of the static magnetic field
The maximum gradient slew rate value
The transmitted radiofrequency power
body.explain: Bandwidth sets how fast the echo is digitised; higher bandwidth samples faster (shorter TE, less chemical shift) but admits more noise.

body.prompt: Reducing the phase FOV without phase oversampling risks:
options: Aliasing, with anatomy wrapping in the phase direction
Chemical-shift misregistration along the frequency axis
A magnet quench that dumps the cryogen suddenly
Gradient coil failure during the phase encode step
body.explain: If the phase FOV is smaller than the object, out-of-FOV tissue folds back; phase oversampling or a larger FOV prevents the wrap.

body.prompt: The menisci of the knee are best evaluated on:
options: Short-TE proton-density sagittal and coronal images
Maximum-intensity-projection MRA of the popliteal vessels
Time-of-flight angiography of the knee arteries
A single-shot heavily T2-weighted acquisition only
body.explain: Menisci are low-signal fibrocartilage; short-TE proton-density sequences give the detail needed to detect tears within them.

body.prompt: Multiparametric prostate MRI relies most heavily on:
options: High-resolution T2 and diffusion with dynamic contrast
Time-of-flight MRA of the pelvic arteries
STIR fat-suppressed imaging of the gland only
A single non-contrast T1-weighted sequence
body.explain: Prostate cancer detection uses T2 anatomy plus restricted diffusion and dynamic enhancement, combined in the PI-RADS assessment.

body.prompt: Breast MRI for cancer detection depends on:
options: Dynamic post-gadolinium T1 with fat suppression and subtraction
Non-contrast T2-weighted imaging of both breasts only
Time-of-flight angiography of the internal mammary vessels
Diffusion-weighted imaging used entirely on its own
body.explain: Malignant enhancement kinetics are the key finding, so fat-suppressed dynamic T1 with subtraction is the core breast MRI technique.

body.prompt: Gadolinium-based contrast agents work by:
options: Being paramagnetic and shortening the T1 of nearby tissue
Emitting their own radiofrequency signal directly
Physically blocking incoming RF excitation pulses
Absorbing the switching gradient magnetic fields
body.explain: Gadolinium is paramagnetic; it shortens local T1 so tissue it reaches brightens on T1-weighted images, marking vascularity or barrier breakdown.

body.prompt: Compared with linear agents, macrocyclic gadolinium agents are:
options: More kinetically stable, with a lower risk of ion release
Less kinetically stable, releasing free ions more readily
Not approved for any routine clinical use in patients
Built from iron oxide rather than a gadolinium chelate
body.explain: The macrocyclic cage holds gadolinium more tightly, reducing free-ion release and the associated risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

body.prompt: Standard extracellular gadolinium agents are cleared primarily by:
options: Renal excretion
The biliary system
Exhalation
The skin
body.explain: Most gadolinium chelates are filtered by the kidneys, which is why impaired renal function prolongs exposure and raises NSF risk.

body.prompt: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is most associated with:
options: Less-stable linear agents given in severe renal failure
Iron-based agents given to otherwise healthy patients
Oral contrast agents used for bowel opacification
Imaging at very high static magnetic field strength
body.explain: NSF has been linked to gadolinium release from less-stable agents in patients with severe renal impairment, so screening and agent choice matter.

body.prompt: Gadolinium enhances a brain lesion only where:
options: The blood-brain barrier has broken down
Fatty tissue is present within the lesion
Dense calcification is present in the lesion
Blood flow through the lesion is fast
body.explain: An intact blood-brain barrier excludes gadolinium; enhancement therefore indicates a lesion that has broken the barrier or lies outside it.

body.prompt: The first-line treatment for true gadolinium-induced anaphylaxis is:
options: Epinephrine
An antihistamine alone
A diuretic
Oral steroids alone
body.explain: Anaphylaxis is rare with gadolinium but, when it occurs, is treated first with epinephrine plus airway, breathing and circulation support.

body.prompt: A negative oral contrast agent for MRCP (e.g. a manganese-rich juice) is used to:
options: Darken stomach and bowel fluid so ducts stand out
Brighten overlying stomach and bowel fluid instead
Enhance the liver parenchyma on delayed imaging
Suppress fat signal across the upper abdomen
body.explain: Nulling bright gastric and duodenal fluid removes signal that would overlap the biliary tree on heavily T2-weighted MRCP images.

body.prompt: One tesla equals how many gauss?
options: 10,000 gauss
100 gauss
1,000 gauss
body.explain: 1 T = 10,000 G, which is why a 1.5 T magnet's controlled boundary is drawn at the 5-gauss (0.0005 T) line.

body.prompt: Phase-contrast MRA has the unique ability to:
options: Quantify flow velocity and its direction
Suppress fat signal without an inversion pulse
Directly image cortical bone with high signal
Substantially shorten the minimum echo time
body.explain: By encoding velocity as phase, PC not only depicts vessels but measures flow rate and direction, useful in shunts and CSF studies.

body.prompt: The carotid arteries are commonly imaged with:
options: Contrast-enhanced MRA or time-of-flight
MR cholangiopancreatography of the ducts
STIR fat-suppressed neck imaging only
Diffusion-weighted imaging of the neck
body.explain: Neck vessels are shown with CE-MRA for speed and coverage or with TOF when contrast is contraindicated.

body.prompt: Peripheral (run-off) CE-MRA of the legs typically uses:
options: A moving-table bolus-chase acquisition
A single static slab covering the pelvis
Time-of-flight imaging used on its own
Diffusion-weighted imaging of the legs
body.explain: A bolus-chase follows the contrast down the legs by stepping the table, capturing the arterial tree from pelvis to feet in one injection.

body.prompt: Time-resolved MRA (e.g. TWIST or TRICKS) trades:
options: Some spatial resolution for temporal resolution and flow timing
Signal-to-noise ratio for reduced radiofrequency SAR
Slice thickness in exchange for a larger field of view
Contrast weighting in exchange for faster scanning
body.explain: Sampling the k-space centre frequently yields many time frames, revealing arterial-to-venous transit at the cost of some spatial detail.

body.prompt: Non-contrast MRA options for patients who cannot receive gadolinium include:
options: Time-of-flight, phase contrast, and gated fast-spin-echo
Only CT angiography with an iodinated contrast bolus
Only invasive catheter angiography of the vessels
No non-contrast angiographic options really exist
body.explain: Flow-based TOF and PC, plus fresh-blood or quiescent-interval techniques, provide angiograms without any contrast agent.

body.prompt: MR venography of the dural sinuses can be performed with:
options: 2D time-of-flight, phase contrast or post-contrast
MR cholangiopancreatography of the biliary tree
STIR imaging of the skull-base bone marrow
Diffusion tensor imaging of white-matter tracts
body.explain: Venous sinus patency is assessed with flow-based TOF or PC venography, or with post-contrast venography, to detect thrombosis.

body.prompt: Myocardial viability after infarction is assessed with:
options: Late (delayed) gadolinium enhancement imaging
Time-of-flight MRA of the coronary arteries
MR cholangiopancreatography of the ducts
Diffusion tensor imaging of the myocardium
body.explain: Scar takes up and retains gadolinium, so bright signal on delayed inversion-recovery images maps non-viable myocardium.

body.prompt: MR enterography distends and images the small bowel using:
options: Oral contrast to distend the bowel with post-gadolinium imaging
A single low-resolution localiser through the abdomen
Time-of-flight angiography of the mesenteric vessels
STIR fat-suppressed imaging of the entire skull base
body.explain: Luminal distension with oral contrast plus fat-suppressed dynamic post-gadolinium sequences shows bowel-wall inflammation in Crohn disease.

body.prompt: A shoulder MR arthrogram improves detection of labral tears by:
options: Injecting dilute intra-articular gadolinium, then fat-suppressed T1
Giving intravenous contrast through a peripheral vein only
Using time-of-flight angiography around the shoulder joint
Using MR cholangiopancreatography around the joint space
body.explain: Distending the joint with dilute gadolinium outlines the labrum and cuff, and fat-suppressed T1 makes contrast-filled tears conspicuous.

body.prompt: Female pelvic (uterine) MRI relies chiefly on:
options: High-resolution T2 in orthogonal planes
Time-of-flight MRA of the pelvic arteries
Diffusion-weighted imaging used on its own
STIR fat-suppressed imaging of the skull
body.explain: Zonal uterine and cervical anatomy is best shown on high-resolution T2, with diffusion and contrast added for characterisation.

body.prompt: Suspected cervical cord injury with neurological signs is best evaluated with:
options: Sagittal T2 and STIR of the cervical spine
Time-of-flight MRA of the neck vessels
MR cholangiopancreatography of the ducts
Cardiac cine imaging of the heart chambers
body.explain: T2 and STIR reveal cord signal change, ligamentous injury and marrow oedema after trauma, complementing CT of the bones.

body.prompt: Perfusion imaging is commonly added to a brain-tumour protocol to:
options: Estimate tumour vascularity and help grade it
Suppress fat signal surrounding the tumour
Shorten the overall length of the scan
Screen the patient for retained metal implants
body.explain: Dynamic susceptibility-contrast perfusion measures relative cerebral blood volume, which rises in high-grade tumours and guides biopsy.

body.prompt: The SI unit of magnetic flux density (field strength) is the:
options: Tesla
Gauss
Hertz
Sievert
body.explain: Field strength is quoted in tesla in SI units; the older gauss (1 T = 10,000 G) survives in the 5-gauss safety line.

body.prompt: The gradient slew-rate limit exists mainly to prevent:
options: Peripheral nerve stimulation
Radiofrequency heating and burns
Ferromagnetic projectile accidents
Sudden magnet quench events
body.explain: Very fast gradient switching can stimulate peripheral nerves, so slew rate is capped to keep dB/dt below the stimulation threshold.

body.prompt: A patient with a standard (non-MR-conditional) cochlear implant is generally:
options: Kept out of the magnet unless documented MR-conditional
Always safe to scan regardless of field strength
Safe to scan at 3 T but unsafe at 1.5 T
Safe to scan without any prior device screening
body.explain: Many cochlear implants contain an internal magnet and are unsafe or only conditionally safe, so they require documentation before scanning.

body.prompt: Medication patches with a metallic backing should be:
options: Removed before scanning to avoid skin burns
Left in place for the full examination
Covered with a metal shield before imaging
Ignored, since patches pose no heating risk
body.explain: The conductive foil in some transdermal patches can heat under RF, so such patches are removed (and replaced afterward) to prevent burns.

body.prompt: An external insulin pump worn by a patient should be:
options: Removed and kept outside the magnet room, not MR-safe
Left on the patient for the entire examination
Placed inside the bore beside the imaging coil
Taped securely onto the receiver coil housing
body.explain: External insulin pumps are electronic and not MR-safe, so they are removed before the patient enters the scanner room.

body.prompt: Caution with gadolinium is commonly triggered when the eGFR falls below about:
options: About 30 mL/min/1.73m2
About 90 mL/min/1.73m2
About 120 mL/min/1.73m2
About 60 mL/min/1.73m2 always
body.explain: Severe impairment, often defined as an eGFR under 30, raises NSF risk and prompts avoiding or minimising gadolinium and preferring stable agents.

body.prompt: The MRI safety screening questionnaire must be:
options: Completed and reviewed before every examination
Filled out only once every calendar year
Optional for routine outpatient exams
Skipped for familiar repeat patients
body.explain: Screening is repeated and reviewed each time because implants, surgeries and pregnancy status can change between visits.

body.prompt: When positioning a patient, padding between the skin and the bore or cables serves to:
options: Prevent RF burns by breaking conductive contact
Improve the overall signal to noise ratio
Shorten the repetition time between echoes
Suppress the bright signal from fat
body.explain: Insulating pads stop skin-to-skin or skin-to-bore contact that could form a current loop, which is a key step in preventing RF burns.

body.prompt: Cortical ribbon and basal-ganglia restricted diffusion, with rapid dementia, suggests:
options: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or encephalitis
A benign simple fluid-filled arachnoid cyst
A fatty benign intracranial lipoma lesion
Ordinary age-related brain volume changes
body.explain: Cortical ribboning on DWI is a classic clue to prion disease or encephalitis, prompting correlation with clinical and CSF findings.

body.prompt: A wedge-shaped T2/FLAIR hyperintensity following an arterial territory indicates:
options: A subacute infarct
A lipoma
Normal flow
A calcified nodule
body.explain: Infarcts respect vascular territories and become bright on T2/FLAIR as vasogenic oedema develops over hours to days.

body.prompt: A homogeneously enhancing mass with markedly restricted diffusion (very low ADC) suggests a:
options: Hypercellular tumour such as lymphoma
A benign simple fluid-filled cyst
A fatty intracranial lipoma
An old chronic gliotic infarct
body.explain: Dense cellularity packs nuclei and restricts water, so lymphoma and other hypercellular tumours show low ADC and avid enhancement.

body.prompt: An open (incomplete) enhancing ring facing the cortex is a clue to:
options: Tumefactive demyelination over tumour or abscess
An acute ischaemic territorial infarct
A benign fatty intracranial lipoma
Dense dystrophic parenchymal calcification
body.explain: Demyelinating lesions often enhance in a horseshoe pattern with the open edge toward grey matter, helping distinguish them from tumour.

body.prompt: An actively shielded magnet is designed to:
options: Reduce the external fringe (stray) field
Increase the specific absorption rate
Cool the interior of the magnet bore
Encode spatial position of signal
body.explain: Extra shield coils confine the fringe field closer to the magnet, shrinking the 5-gauss footprint and easing siting requirements.

body.prompt: Open or permanent-magnet low-field scanners are particularly useful for:
options: Claustrophobic or bariatric patients, lower field
Achieving the highest possible image SNR
Delivering the fastest gradient performance
Cardiac perfusion imaging exclusively
body.explain: Open designs trade field strength (and SNR) for patient access, helping claustrophobic, bariatric or paediatric patients tolerate the exam.

body.prompt: Higher gradient amplitude and slew rate primarily enable:
options: Thinner slices and faster higher-res imaging
A stronger main static magnetic field
Delivering greater RF transmit power
Consistently lower SAR to the patient
body.explain: Stronger, faster gradients sharpen spatial encoding and shorten echo spacing, supporting high-resolution and fast sequences like EPI.

body.prompt: The component that detects the returning MR signal is the:
options: Receive coil
Gradient coil
Shim coil
Cryostat
body.explain: Receive coils (often phased arrays) pick up the small RF signal from precessing spins; gradients and shims serve encoding and homogeneity.

body.prompt: Compressed sensing accelerates acquisition by exploiting:
options: Image sparsity with incoherent undersampling
A much stronger static magnetic field
A higher RF energy deposition rate
A substantially longer repetition time
body.explain: If an image is sparse in some domain, it can be reconstructed from far fewer, pseudo-randomly sampled k-space points, shortening the scan.

body.prompt: PROPELLER (BLADE) radial-like acquisition is valued for being:
options: Motion-robust from oversampled central k-space
Delivering the highest possible resolution
Completely free of every imaging artifact
Inherently fat-suppressing on all sequences
body.explain: Rotating blades repeatedly sample the k-space centre, letting the reconstruction detect and correct bulk motion between blades.

body.prompt: Partial-echo (fractional-echo) readout is used to:
options: Shorten the minimum echo time TE achievable
Lengthen the overall repetition time TR
Increase the deposited RF energy SAR
Suppress the surrounding fat signal
body.explain: Sampling one side of the echo and synthesising the rest lets the sequence reach a shorter minimum TE, useful for bright-blood and short-T2 imaging.

body.prompt: In echo-planar imaging, shorter echo spacing reduces:
options: Geometric distortion from off-resonance
The overall signal to noise ratio
The prescribed imaging field of view
The excitation radiofrequency flip angle
body.explain: Distortion in EPI accumulates with the time between lines, so tighter echo spacing (or parallel imaging) reduces the geometric warping.

body.title: Fat suppression: STIR, spectral, Dixon and water excitation
body.html:
Fat is bright on most sequences and can hide pathology, so suppressing it raises the conspicuity of edema, enhancement and marrow disease. Four methods dominate:

  • STIR (short-TI inversion recovery) nulls fat by its T1. Because it acts on T1 and not frequency, it is uniform even in a poor field (off-isocenter, near metal), but it is not fat-specific and will null anything with fat's short T1, including gadolinium-enhancing tissue, so it is not combined with contrast.
  • Spectral (chemical-shift) saturation uses a frequency-selective pulse to saturate fat before readout. It is fat-specific and contrast-compatible but fails where the field is inhomogeneous, and it is harder at lower field where the fat-water frequency gap is smaller.
  • Dixon acquires in-phase and opposed-phase echoes and computes separate water-only and fat-only images, robustly and quantitatively.
  • Water excitation tips only the water protons, used in high-resolution cartilage imaging.

Choosing among them trades uniformity (STIR) against specificity and contrast compatibility (spectral, Dixon) and speed.
keypoints: STIR nulls fat by T1: uniform in a poor field, but not contrast-compatible.
Spectral fat-sat is fat-specific and contrast-compatible but needs a homogeneous field.
Dixon uses in-phase and opposed-phase echoes for robust water-only and fat-only images.
Water excitation tips only water, used in high-resolution cartilage imaging.
Suppressing bright fat raises conspicuity of enhancement, edema and marrow disease.
body.worked_example: You are protocoling a shoulder MRI and the coil placement puts the joint off isocenter, near the edge of the magnet's homogeneous volume, close to surgical hardware. You want fat suppression so labral fluid and marrow edema stand out. A frequency-selective spectral fat-sat pulse depends on a clean, uniform separation between the fat and water resonance peaks; off isocenter, and worse near metal, the local field varies enough that the pulse partly saturates water in some spots and misses fat in others, giving patchy, unreliable suppression. Switching to STIR solves the uniformity problem because it nulls tissue by T1 relaxation rather than by resonance frequency, so it does not care how homogeneous the local field is. The trade-off shows up later in the same exam: if a contrast-enhanced sequence is planned, STIR cannot be used for that part, because gadolinium shortens the T1 of enhancing tissue down near fat's T1, and STIR would null the enhancement right along with the fat. For that portion of the exam, spectral fat-sat closer to isocenter, or Dixon, is used instead.
memory_hooks: STIR nulls by T1, so it is field-uniform but not contrast-safe. Spectral fat-sat is frequency-selective, so it is contrast-safe but field-sensitive.
Off isocenter, near metal, or at low field where the fat-water frequency gap is small: reach for STIR, not spectral fat-sat.
Dixon separates water and fat by acquiring in-phase and opposed-phase echoes and solving for both signals, which keeps it reliable and quantitative where a single saturation pulse would fail.
exam_traps: STIR contrast is not purely a fat-null overlay. TE still contributes T2 weighting underneath, so fluid can be bright from T2 on a STIR image, which is easy to misread as pure T1 behavior.

Spectral fat-sat depends on field strength: the fat-water chemical shift is a fixed 3.5 ppm, but that translates to a wider frequency gap at higher field, so it is easier at 3T and harder at 1.5T or below, especially over a large FOV.

Water excitation is not the same technique as fat saturation. It selectively excites water protons at the outset rather than suppressing fat afterward, which is why it suits very short TR, high-resolution cartilage sequences.

body.title: Data acquisition: k-space, encoding and the Fourier transform
body.html:
MRI does not measure the image directly; it fills k-space, a grid of spatial-frequency data, and the Fourier transform converts that into the picture. Two gradients encode position within a slice: frequency encoding is applied during readout, mapping position to signal frequency, and phase encoding is stepped once per TR to fill successive k-space lines. Because each line needs its own TR, the phase matrix (not the frequency matrix) drives scan time.

The center of k-space carries bulk signal and contrast; the periphery carries edges and fine detail (resolution). This explains many techniques: partial Fourier samples just over half of k-space using its symmetry; centric ordering fills the center first to capture contrast at a chosen instant (dynamic MRA); parallel imaging skips lines and uses coil sensitivities to unfold the result; and zero-filling interpolates to a finer display matrix without adding true resolution. A true 3D acquisition adds a second phase-encode (partition) gradient through the slab.
keypoints: MRI fills k-space; the Fourier transform makes the image.
Frequency encoding is during readout; phase encoding steps once per TR.
The phase matrix drives scan time; the frequency matrix is essentially free.
k-space center = contrast and signal; periphery = resolution and edges.
Partial Fourier, parallel imaging and centric ordering all manipulate how k-space is filled.
body.worked_example: You are running a 2D sequence with a TR of 500 ms, a phase matrix of 192, and 1 excitation (NEX). Scan time is TR multiplied by the number of phase encoding steps multiplied by NEX, so 500 ms times 192 times 1 comes out to about 96 seconds. If you drop the phase matrix to 128 and keep TR and NEX the same, scan time falls to about 64 seconds because you are now filling fewer k-space lines. If instead you had reduced the frequency matrix from 256 to 192, scan time would not change at all, since frequency encoding is sampled entirely within a single readout window during each TR. This is exactly why the phase matrix, not the frequency matrix, is the lever technologists pull to cut acquisition time.
memory_hooks: Frequency encoding is essentially free: it all happens inside one readout window per TR. Phase encoding is the expensive one: every step needs its own TR.
The center of k-space carries signal and contrast, the edges carry resolution and fine detail, so losing central lines hurts contrast and losing peripheral lines hurts sharpness.
k-space is a map of spatial frequencies, not a map of anatomy. The Fourier transform is what turns that spatial frequency data into the picture you actually read.
exam_traps: Do not confuse which encoding drives scan time. It is the phase encoding matrix, not the frequency encoding matrix, because phase encoding needs a fresh TR for every step while frequency encoding is captured entirely within a single readout.

Zero filling, sometimes called a zip, interpolates the image onto a finer display matrix and can look sharper, but it adds no true spatial resolution because no new spatial frequencies were actually acquired.

Partial Fourier uses k-space's conjugate symmetry to skip roughly half the phase encoding steps, saving time or shortening TE, but it comes at some SNR cost since fewer real lines are averaged into the final image.

body.title: MRI instrumentation: magnet, gradients, RF and coils
body.html:
An MRI scanner is four subsystems working together. The main magnet provides the strong static field, usually a superconducting magnet cooled by liquid helium; its homogeneity is fine-tuned by shim coils, and its fringe field extends beyond the bore, bounded by the 5-gauss line. Gradient coils (x, y, z) superimpose linear field variations for slice selection and spatial encoding; their fast switching makes the acoustic noise and can cause peripheral nerve stimulation. The RF system uses a transmit coil to excite spins (the B1 field) and receive coils (often phased arrays) to detect the tiny returning signal and enable parallel imaging.

Supporting these, the RF (Faraday) shield around the room blocks external radio interference, and higher field strength (for example 3 T versus 1.5 T) raises SNR but also raises SAR, chemical shift and susceptibility. A quench is the sudden loss of superconductivity that boils off helium, which is why the room has an oxygen monitor and a vent.
keypoints: Superconducting magnets are cooled by liquid helium; shims optimize homogeneity.
Gradient coils encode position and cause the acoustic noise and PNS.
The RF transmit coil excites spins; receive (phased-array) coils detect signal.
The Faraday shield blocks external RF (zipper); the 5-gauss line bounds the fringe field.
Higher field raises SNR but also SAR, chemical shift and susceptibility.
body.worked_example: During a scan the technologist sees a bright, repeating linear band of noise crossing the image that has nothing to do with the patient's anatomy, and traces the cause to the scan room door being left open. The room's copper Faraday shield only blocks stray radiofrequency energy from entering or leaving the room when the enclosure is completely sealed. With the door ajar, ambient radiofrequency signals leak in and beat against the scanner's own frequency, producing the classic zipper artifact. Once the door is closed the shield is intact again and the artifact disappears, which confirms the room shielding, not the scanner hardware, was the cause.
memory_hooks: Superconducting magnets stay at field with liquid helium cooling, because once resistance drops to zero the current keeps circulating without any power input.
Gradient coils do the spatial encoding and make the loud switching noise. RF coils do the exciting (transmit) and the listening (receive).
Higher field strength buys more SNR, but it also raises SAR and widens the chemical shift artifact. Nothing about going up in tesla is free.
exam_traps: Do not confuse the transmit coil's job, exciting spins with the B1 field, with the receive coil's job, detecting the tiny returning signal. Phased array coils are about receive sensitivity and enabling parallel imaging, not about excitation.
A quench is a sudden, uncontrolled loss of superconductivity that rapidly boils off the helium, not a routine event. It is why the magnet room has an oxygen monitor and a quench pipe vented outside.

Do not confuse the 5 gauss line, the fringe field safety boundary around the magnet, with the Faraday shield, the room enclosure that blocks external radiofrequency interference. One concerns the static magnetic field, the other concerns RF noise.

body.title: 3D imaging and reconstruction: volumes, MIP and reformats
body.html:
A 2D acquisition excites one slice at a time; a 3D volumetric acquisition excites a whole slab and phase-encodes through it, yielding thin, contiguous (gapless) partitions with high SNR. When the voxels are isotropic (equal in all directions), the volume can be reformatted (MPR) into any plane without loss of resolution, so one acquisition serves every viewing angle.

Volumes are also shown as projections: a maximum-intensity projection (MIP) keeps the brightest voxel along each ray to show bright vessels in MR angiography, while a minimum-intensity projection (MinIP) keeps the darkest voxel to show veins on susceptibility imaging or air. The trade-offs to remember: 3D gives thin slices and high SNR but is more motion-sensitive and can take longer, while thick 2D slices are fast but suffer partial-volume averaging. Adjacent 2D slices can also cross-talk through imperfect slice profiles, reduced by an interslice gap or interleaving.
keypoints: 3D excites a slab and partition-encodes it: thin gapless slices, high SNR.
Isotropic voxels allow multiplanar reformatting in any plane.
MIP displays bright vessels; MinIP displays dark veins or air.
Thick 2D slices are fast but blur small findings (partial volume).
Slice cross-talk is reduced with an interslice gap or interleaving.
body.worked_example: A 3D time-of-flight MR angiogram of the circle of Willis is acquired as a thin slab with isotropic voxels, and a maximum-intensity projection is generated by casting rays through the volume and keeping only the brightest voxel along each ray, producing a single angiogram-like image. Because a MIP collapses a 3D volume into a 2D projection, an overlapping vessel or an adjacent bright structure such as fat or a draining vein can project onto the artery of interest and mimic a stenosis or obscure a real one, so the thin source partitions must always be reviewed to confirm any narrowing seen only on the MIP. Because the acquisition used isotropic voxels, the same volume can also be reformatted with MPR into a coronal or oblique plane that follows the vessel's course, without reacquiring any data.
memory_hooks: MIP keeps the brightest voxel along each ray, and MinIP keeps the darkest. MIP shows arteries, MinIP shows veins or air.
Isotropic voxels are the ticket to free reformats: one acquisition, any plane, no loss of resolution.
A finding seen only on the MIP is not confirmed until it is checked against the thin source images.
exam_traps: A MIP can hide a true stenosis or mimic a false one, because overlapping vessels and venous contamination project onto the same pixels. Always correlate with the source images before calling a stenosis.

Time-of-flight MRA signal is contaminated by anything with a short T1 or fast in-plane inflow, such as fat, subacute blood, or slow venous flow, which can masquerade as vessel signal on the MIP. Fat suppression or saturation bands help control this.

Thin contiguous 3D slices give high SNR per unit volume, but at the cost of longer scan time and greater motion sensitivity than thick 2D slices, so 3D is not automatically the better choice for every exam.

body.title: Regional anatomy: planes and sequences by body part
body.html:
Each body part has a preferred plane and sequence chosen to display its key structures. A few high-yield examples:

  • Neuro: the internal auditory canals are screened with thin heavily T2-weighted images (CISS/FIESTA) for the vestibulocochlear nerve; the pituitary with thin dynamic post-contrast coronal T1; the temporal lobes with thin oblique coronals through the hippocampi.
  • Musculoskeletal: the rotator cuff (supraspinatus) on oblique coronal; the ACL on sagittal oblique; the menisci on short-TE (proton-density) sagittal and coronal.
  • Body: MRCP uses heavily T2-weighted sequences so static bile and pancreatic fluid are bright; the liver is characterized with multiphase dynamic post-gadolinium T1; the prostate with high-resolution T2 plus diffusion and dynamic contrast; the breast with fat-suppressed dynamic T1 and subtraction.

The recurring logic: pick the plane that lies along or across the structure of interest, and the contrast that makes its pathology stand out (fluid-sensitive, fat-suppressed, or dynamic enhancement).
keypoints: Choose the plane along or across the structure of interest.
Neuro: thin T2 for cranial nerves; dynamic coronal T1 for the pituitary.
MSK: oblique coronal for the cuff, sagittal for the ACL, short-TE for menisci.
Body: MRCP is heavily T2; liver, prostate and breast rely on dynamic contrast.
Match the contrast (fluid-sensitive, fat-sat, dynamic) to the pathology sought.
body.worked_example: A referral requests MRI of the shoulder to evaluate a suspected rotator cuff tear. The technologist plans oblique coronal images angled parallel to the supraspinatus tendon rather than a true anatomic coronal, because a plane that cuts across the tendon obliquely can create the illusion of a tear or underestimate a real one. Oblique sagittal images, angled perpendicular to the cuff, are added to assess tendon retraction and muscle atrophy. A fat-saturated proton-density or T2 sequence is chosen over plain T1, because fluid within a tear needs to appear bright against suppressed fat, so a full-thickness tear shows as a fluid-bright gap through the tendon. The same logic explains why the knee is imaged with short-TE sequences angled along the meniscal anatomy, rather than a single generic axial scan.
memory_hooks: Plane follows the structure: oblique coronal for the cuff, oblique sagittal for the ACL. A plain anatomic plane will not do.
Fat-saturated fluid-sensitive sequences catch the tear because fluid is bright and fat is dark; plain T1 alone can hide it.
MRCP is heavily T2-weighted because static fluid such as bile and pancreatic juice stays bright while everything else fades.
exam_traps: An anatomic, non-oblique coronal through the shoulder can mimic or obscure a cuff tear. The oblique plane parallel to the supraspinatus is required for accurate assessment.

Dynamic post-contrast timing matters as much as plane for the pituitary. A microadenoma enhances less avidly and later than the normal gland, so it shows up as a relatively dark focus against the brightly enhancing gland only on the early dynamic images.

Tendons and menisci oriented near 55 degrees to the main field can show artifactual increased signal on short-TE sequences, the magic angle effect, which can mimic tendinosis or a tear. A longer-TE sequence helps confirm whether the finding is real.

body.title: Building a protocol: why each sequence is there
body.html:
A protocol is a deliberate sequence of acquisitions, each present for a reason. A routine brain study typically includes T1 (anatomy), T2 and FLAIR (fluid-sensitive pathology, with FLAIR nulling CSF), and DWI (acute ischemia), with post-gadolinium T1 added when enhancement is relevant. Disease-specific protocols tune this base: acute stroke leans on DWI/ADC; multiple sclerosis emphasizes FLAIR plus post-contrast T1; a brain tumor adds perfusion to grade vascularity; the temporal lobes get thin hippocampal coronals for epilepsy.

Body and vascular protocols follow the same logic: cardiac viability uses late gadolinium enhancement, enterography distends bowel and images dynamically, and non-contrast angiography uses time-of-flight or phase contrast. The technologist also builds in artifact control: flow compensation, gating and saturation bands for pulsatile flow, and metal-artifact-reduction choices (spin echo over gradient echo, high bandwidth) around hardware.
keypoints: Routine brain: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, plus post-gadolinium T1 when needed.
Each sequence answers a specific question; disease tunes the base protocol.
Stroke leans on DWI; MS on FLAIR; tumor adds perfusion.
Angiography uses TOF, phase contrast or timed contrast.
Protocols build in artifact control (gating, sat bands, metal-reduction).
body.worked_example: Ordering a routine brain protocol for suspected multiple sclerosis, the technologist starts with a three-plane localizer to plan slice angles, then sagittal FLAIR to screen the corpus callosum, where MS plaques classically radiate outward from the ventricles. Axial FLAIR and T2 survey the rest of the brain, since plaques are bright on both, and post-gadolinium T1 separates active demyelination, which enhances, from old inactive plaques, which do not. DWI is included as a routine safety net for a silent acute infarct, even though MS plaques themselves do not typically restrict diffusion. Each sequence answers one question: T1 for anatomy, T2 and FLAIR for the fluid-sensitive lesion burden, and post-contrast T1 for activity, so no sequence is present without a reason and none of the reasons duplicate each other.
memory_hooks: Every sequence in a protocol answers a different question. If two sequences answer the same question, one of them may not be needed.
Localizer sets the angles, T1 shows anatomy, T2 and FLAIR show fluid-sensitive pathology, and post-contrast T1 shows activity or blood-brain-barrier breakdown.
Disease tunes the base protocol: stroke leans on DWI, MS leans on FLAIR plus post-contrast T1, and tumor adds perfusion.
exam_traps: Adding a post-contrast sequence does not remove the need for a pre-contrast T1. Without it, intrinsically T1-bright material such as fat, blood, or melanin cannot be told apart from true enhancement.

Flow compensation, gating, and saturation bands are artifact-control choices added to existing sequences, not sequences of their own, and they are built in specifically to suppress pulsatility and flow artifact.
Metal-artifact-reduction choices favor spin echo over gradient echo and a higher receiver bandwidth, since gradient echo and low bandwidth both increase susceptibility artifact around hardware.

body.title: MR angiography and venography: TOF, PC and contrast methods
body.html:
MR angiography shows vessels three ways. Time-of-flight (TOF) saturates stationary tissue so fresh inflowing blood is bright (flow-related enhancement); it needs thin slabs perpendicular to flow and fails for in-plane flow. Phase contrast (PC) encodes velocity as phase, so it not only depicts vessels but quantifies flow velocity and direction; its VENC must exceed the true velocity or the phase aliases. Contrast-enhanced MRA shortens blood T1 with gadolinium for a fast, flow-independent angiogram, where bolus timing to the arterial phase is everything (peripheral run-off uses a moving-table bolus chase, and time-resolved methods trade spatial for temporal resolution).

MR venography assesses the dural sinuses or deep veins with 2D TOF, PC or post-contrast venography. For patients who cannot receive gadolinium, non-contrast techniques (TOF, PC, and ECG-gated fresh-blood or quiescent-interval methods) provide angiograms with no contrast at all.
keypoints: TOF: inflowing unsaturated blood is bright; it fails for in-plane flow.
Phase contrast quantifies velocity and direction; VENC must exceed peak flow.
CE-MRA is fast and flow-independent but depends on arterial bolus timing.
MR venography uses TOF, PC or post-contrast to assess sinuses and deep veins.
Non-contrast MRA (TOF, PC, fresh-blood) serves patients who cannot have gadolinium.
body.worked_example: You are planning a phase-contrast MRA of the carotids and need to pick a VENC. Peak systolic velocity in a normal carotid is roughly 60 to 100 cm per second. If you set VENC at 20 cm per second, velocities above that wrap around and alias, showing as artifactually reversed or wrong-magnitude flow in the vessel center. If you set VENC at 150 cm per second to be safe, you avoid aliasing but the phase signal for the actual flow is now a small fraction of the encode range, so the velocity measurement is noisy and less sensitive. The right move is to set VENC just above the expected peak velocity for that vessel, around 80 to 100 cm per second here, so you get maximum phase sensitivity without wrapping.
memory_hooks: VENC is a ceiling: set it just above the expected peak velocity. Too low wraps (aliases), too high wastes sensitivity.
TOF is qualitative and anatomic; PC is quantitative, giving both velocity and direction because it literally encodes phase to speed.
CE-MRA trades flow-dependence for T1-shortening: it is fast and not affected by in-plane flow or saturation, but only as good as bolus timing.
exam_traps: TOF fails for slow or in-plane flow because those spins sit in the slab long enough to become saturated like stationary tissue; thinner slabs, or multiple overlapping thin slabs (MOTSA), limit this saturation.

For patients who cannot receive gadolinium (severe renal impairment, prior reaction), non-contrast options exist: TOF, PC, and ECG-gated fresh-blood or quiescent-interval single-shot techniques for venography and lower-extremity angiography.

Time-resolved contrast-enhanced MRA trades spatial resolution for temporal resolution to catch the arterial phase before venous contamination; a single mistimed acquisition can overlap arterial and venous signal.

body.title: MRI contrast agents: gadolinium, safety and special agents
body.html:
The workhorse MRI contrast agents are gadolinium chelates. Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens the T1 of nearby tissue, so where it accumulates the tissue brightens on T1-weighted images. In the brain it reaches tissue only where the blood-brain barrier is broken, so enhancement flags tumor, active demyelination or infection. Agents are excreted by the kidneys, which is why renal function (eGFR) is checked first: in severe impairment, less-stable linear agents are linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF), so more stable macrocyclic agents at the lowest effective dose are preferred, or contrast is avoided.

Reactions range from mild (hives, treated with antihistamines and observation) to rare anaphylaxis, whose first-line treatment is epinephrine. Gadolinium is avoided in pregnancy unless essential. Beyond standard extracellular agents, hepatobiliary agents aid liver characterization, iron-based agents can act as blood-pool agents, and negative oral agents darken bowel fluid for MRCP.
keypoints: Gadolinium is paramagnetic, shortens T1, and brightens tissue on T1 images.
Brain enhancement marks blood-brain-barrier breakdown.
Check eGFR: NSF links less-stable linear agents to severe renal failure.
Prefer stable macrocyclic agents at the lowest effective dose; avoid in pregnancy unless essential.
Mild reactions get antihistamines; anaphylaxis is treated first with epinephrine.
body.worked_example: A patient is scheduled for a contrast-enhanced brain MRI and the eGFR comes back at 25 mL per minute per 1.73 square meters, in the range associated with nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk from gadolinium exposure. Gadolinium itself is the toxic part once it is released from its chelate, so agents are engineered to hold it tightly. Linear chelates bind gadolinium less securely than macrocyclic chelates, so more free gadolinium can be released and deposited in tissue, including skin, and in patients with poor renal clearance this is the mechanism behind NSF. Because gadolinium is cleared through the kidneys, poor renal function means the agent, and any gadolinium it releases, stays in the body far longer, raising both exposure and risk. The response is not to skip a clinically indicated scan but to use a stable macrocyclic agent at the lowest dose that answers the clinical question, with the decision documented. If the goal instead were biliary imaging to look for a bile leak, a hepatobiliary agent, partly excreted through the liver into bile rather than only through the kidneys, would be chosen over a standard extracellular agent.
memory_hooks: Gadolinium is the toxic part; the chelate is what makes it safe to inject. Macrocyclic chelates cage it more tightly than linear ones, which is why NSF risk concentrates in linear agents.
Renal clearance is why eGFR is checked before contrast: poor kidney function means gadolinium lingers longer, raising both tissue retention and NSF risk.
Special-purpose agents to keep straight: hepatobiliary agents for liver and bile, iron-based agents for blood-pool vascular imaging, negative oral agents to darken bowel fluid for MRCP.
exam_traps: NSF risk depends on chelate stability and renal function together. Group II macrocyclic agents are very low risk, and current ACR guidance no longer requires routine eGFR screening before them, though many facilities still confirm renal function before any gadolinium and no agent is truly risk-free.

A prior allergic-type reaction to iodinated CT contrast or a shellfish allergy does not predict a gadolinium reaction; that cross-reactivity belief is a myth even for iodinated contrast, though any prior contrast reaction of any kind raises general risk.
Anaphylaxis is treated first with epinephrine, not antihistamines or steroids. Antihistamines are for milder urticarial reactions, not the airway and cardiovascular compromise of true anaphylaxis.

body.title: Flip angle: the Ernst angle and the SAR trade-off
body.html:
The flip angle is the angle by which the RF pulse tips the net magnetization away from the main field. It is one of the most useful contrast knobs in MRI, and what it does depends on the sequence family.

  • 90 degrees puts all the magnetization into the transverse plane, giving the maximum signal from a single excitation. This is the classic spin-echo excitation.
  • Gradient echo does not use 90 degrees. With short TRs there is no time for full longitudinal recovery, so a smaller flip angle yields more steady-state signal.
  • The Ernst angle is the flip that maximizes signal for a given TR and tissue T1, following cos(Ernst angle) = exp(-TR / T1); a shorter TR or shorter T1 means a smaller Ernst angle.

In gradient echo the flip angle also steers contrast: a larger flip leans toward T1 weighting, while a smaller flip leans toward proton density and T2*. The catch is SAR: flip angle scales with RF power, so a bigger flip deposits more heat, which is why fast, high-flip, short-TR sequences can reach SAR limits, especially at higher field strength.
keypoints: The flip angle is how far the RF pulse tips the magnetization from the main field.
90 degrees gives maximum single-shot signal (classic spin echo).
Gradient echo uses a smaller flip; the Ernst angle maximizes signal for a given TR and T1.
Larger flip leans to T1 weighting; smaller flip leans to proton density and T2*.
Flip angle scales with RF power, so a larger flip raises SAR.
body.worked_example: You are running a T1-weighted spoiled gradient echo of the brain with a short TR of 8 ms. At a 90 degree flip the longitudinal magnetization barely recovers between pulses, so the signal is weak. Lowering the flip toward the Ernst angle for white matter, roughly 12 to 15 degrees at that TR, restores signal. The Ernst angle is the flip that maximizes steady-state signal for a given TR and T1, where cos(Ernst) equals exp(-TR/T1). A short TR pushes the Ernst angle small, which is why fast gradient echo uses low flip angles.
memory_hooks: Short TR wants a small flip. As TR drops, the Ernst angle drops with it.
cos of the Ernst angle equals E1, and E1 is exp(-TR over T1).
exam_traps: SAR scales with the square of the flip angle and with the square of field strength, so trimming the flip angle is the fastest way to cut SAR.
The Ernst angle maximizes signal, not contrast. A higher flip can give stronger T1 weighting even though total signal is lower.

body.title: What makes an image T1 weighted?
body.html:
T1 weighting comes from a short TR and a short TE. A short TR does not give tissues time to fully recover along the main field, so tissues with a short T1 such as fat recover more signal and look bright, while tissues with a long T1 such as fluid stay dark. The short TE keeps T2 differences from having much say.

T1 weighted images show anatomy well: fat is bright, water and CSF are dark, and gadolinium enhancement stands out because it shortens T1.
keypoints: Short TR and short TE produce T1 weighting.
Fat is bright and fluid is dark on T1.
Gadolinium shortens T1, so enhancing tissue looks bright.

body.title: Why is fluid bright on a T2 weighted image?
body.html:
T2 weighting uses a long TR and a long TE. The long TE lets transverse magnetisation decay before the echo is read, so tissues with a long T2 like water and CSF keep their signal and stay bright, while short T2 tissues lose signal and go darker.

Because many diseases raise local water content, they become bright on T2 and are easy to spot, which is why T2 is often called the sensitive sequence for pathology.
keypoints: Long TR and long TE produce T2 weighting.
Water and CSF are bright on T2.
Most pathology raises water content, so it lights up on T2.

body.title: How does spin echo differ from gradient echo?
body.html:
Spin echo uses a 90 degree excitation and a 180 degree refocusing pulse. The 180 degree pulse cancels fixed field inhomogeneity, so contrast reflects true T2. The images are clean but the scan is longer.

Gradient echo refocuses with a gradient reversal instead of a 180 degree pulse, usually with a small flip angle. It is fast and suits 3D and breath hold work, but it does not correct field inhomogeneity, so its contrast reflects T2 star and it is more prone to susceptibility artifact.
keypoints: Spin echo refocuses with a 180 degree pulse and reflects true T2.
Gradient echo refocuses with a gradient and reflects T2 star.
Gradient echo is faster but more sensitive to susceptibility.

body.title: What does an inversion recovery sequence do?
body.html:
Inversion recovery begins with a 180 degree inverting pulse that flips magnetisation to the negative direction. As tissues recover through zero, a chosen inversion time (TI) decides which tissue sits at its null point when the readout starts. A tissue at its null gives no signal and is suppressed.

Two common uses are STIR, with a short TI to null fat, and FLAIR, with a long TI to null CSF so periventricular lesions stand out.
keypoints: A 180 degree pulse inverts magnetisation, then TI selects what is nulled.
STIR uses a short TI to null fat.
FLAIR uses a long TI to null CSF.

body.title: What is k-space?
body.html:
k-space is the raw data matrix where the scanner stores the spatial frequency information of an image before reconstruction. Each point contributes to the whole image, not to a single pixel, and a Fourier transform converts filled k-space into the final image.

The layout matters: the center of k-space holds low spatial frequencies that carry contrast and overall shape, while the edges hold high spatial frequencies that carry fine detail.
keypoints: k-space stores spatial frequencies, not pixels.
A Fourier transform turns k-space into the image.
Center gives contrast, periphery gives detail.

body.title: Why does the center of k-space matter most?
body.html:
The central lines of k-space hold the low spatial frequencies that set overall brightness and contrast. Sequences can exploit this: centric ordering in contrast enhanced angiography captures the center while gadolinium is at peak.

Because the center dominates contrast, motion or error in the central lines degrades the whole image, whereas error at the periphery mostly softens fine detail.
keypoints: Central k-space sets contrast and brightness.
Centric ordering captures the center at peak enhancement.
Motion in central lines harms the whole image.

body.title: What is signal to noise ratio and what raises it?
body.html:
Signal to noise ratio (SNR) weighs the wanted signal against background noise, and a higher value gives a cleaner image. SNR rises with a larger voxel (thicker slice, larger field of view, or coarser matrix), a higher field strength, more signal averages (NEX), and a narrower receive bandwidth.

Every gain has a cost: bigger voxels lose resolution, more averages take time, and a narrow bandwidth can worsen chemical shift. A protocol is always a trade among SNR, resolution, and scan time.
keypoints: SNR is wanted signal versus noise.
Bigger voxels, higher field, more NEX, and narrow bandwidth raise SNR.
Each SNR gain trades against resolution or time.

body.title: How do slice thickness and matrix affect the image?
body.html:
Slice thickness and matrix size together set voxel size. A thicker slice or coarser matrix means larger voxels, more signal, and better SNR, but lower spatial resolution and more partial volume averaging. A thinner slice or finer matrix sharpens resolution but lowers SNR.

Partial volume averaging happens when one voxel spans more than one tissue and reports a blended value, which can hide small structures.
keypoints: Slice thickness and matrix set voxel size.
Bigger voxels raise SNR but lower resolution.
Thick slices increase partial volume averaging.

body.title: STIR versus chemical fat saturation: when do you use each?
body.html:
STIR nulls fat by its T1 using an inversion time near 150 to 170 ms at 1.5 T. Because it works on T1, it is robust where the field is uneven, such as the extremities or off center anatomy. Its drawback is that it also suppresses anything with a similar T1, including some gadolinium enhancement, so STIR is avoided after contrast.

Chemical fat saturation applies a frequency selective pulse at the fat peak. It is fat specific and works with contrast, but it needs a very uniform field and can fail near metal or at the edge of a large field of view.
keypoints: STIR nulls fat by T1 and is robust in an uneven field.
STIR can also null enhancement, so avoid it after gadolinium.
Chemical fat sat is fat specific but needs a uniform field.

body.title: What is the Dixon method?
body.html:
The Dixon technique separates fat and water using the fact that their signals drift in and out of phase as TE changes, because fat and water precess at slightly different frequencies. By acquiring in phase and out of phase echoes, the scanner computes separate water only and fat only images alongside the standard sets.

Dixon gives uniform fat suppression even across a large field of view and tolerates field imperfection better than a single fat saturation pulse.
keypoints: Dixon uses in phase and out of phase echoes to separate fat and water.
It yields water only and fat only images.
It gives uniform fat suppression over a large field of view.

body.title: What causes chemical shift artifact?
body.html:
Fat and water protons resonate at slightly different frequencies. Because the scanner uses frequency to encode position, this offset places fat and water signals at slightly different pixels along the frequency direction, giving a bright or dark border where fat and water meet, seen at kidney and vertebral margins.

Chemical shift grows with higher field strength and with narrower receive bandwidth, so widening the bandwidth reduces it.
keypoints: Fat and water resonate differently and shift along the frequency axis.
It shows as a bright or dark edge at fat water borders.
Wider bandwidth and lower field reduce it.

body.title: How is patient motion artifact reduced?
body.html:
Motion smears signal along the phase encode direction because phase encoding is spread across the whole scan. Useful steps include a shorter scan, breath holding or respiratory gating, cardiac gating, and saturation bands over moving tissue such as the anterior abdominal wall.

Swapping the phase and frequency directions can move the artifact off the region of interest, while averaging tends to blur rather than remove motion.
keypoints: Motion smears along the phase encode direction.
Gating, breath holding, and saturation bands reduce it.
Swapping phase and frequency can move the artifact off the anatomy.

body.title: When is a 3D acquisition preferred over 2D?
body.html:
A 2D acquisition excites one slice at a time. A 3D acquisition excites a whole slab and phase encodes along the slice direction as well, producing a stack of thin contiguous slices with high SNR that can be reformatted in any plane.

3D is preferred when you need thin isotropic voxels, multiplanar reformats, or the best SNR, for example in brain, MR angiography, and joint imaging. The cost is a longer scan and more sensitivity to motion.
keypoints: 2D excites one slice; 3D excites a slab and phase encodes through it.
3D gives thin isotropic voxels and multiplanar reformats.
3D takes longer and is more motion sensitive.

body.title: What are the three magnetic field systems in an MRI scanner?
body.html:
An MRI system uses three fields. The main magnet (B0) is the strong static field, usually superconducting, that aligns the protons. The gradient coils add small switchable fields that vary with position to encode space and select slices. The radiofrequency (RF) coils transmit the excitation pulse and receive the returning signal.

The loud knocking of a scan is the gradient coils rapidly switching against the main field.
keypoints: B0 is the strong static field that aligns protons.
Gradients encode position and select slices.
RF coils transmit excitation and receive signal.

body.title: What are the four MRI safety zones?
body.html:
The American College of Radiology defines four zones of increasing control. Zone I is freely accessible public space. Zone II is the interface where patients are screened and interviewed under supervision. Zone III is a restricted area such as the control room, where unscreened people and equipment are kept out. Zone IV is the magnet room itself, where the strong static field is always on.

Access tightens from Zone I to Zone IV, and only screened people enter Zone IV.
keypoints: Zone I is public, Zone II is patient screening.
Zone III is restricted control space, Zone IV is the magnet room.
The magnet in Zone IV is always on.

body.title: What is the difference between projectile risk and implant risk?
body.html:
Projectile or missile risk is the danger that a ferromagnetic object outside the body, such as scissors, an oxygen cylinder, or a wheelchair, is pulled violently into the bore. This is why loose metal is banned from Zone IV.

Implant risk concerns devices inside the patient that can heat, move, or malfunction in the field. Each implant must be checked against its labeling, since a device may be MR safe, MR conditional, or MR unsafe.
keypoints: Projectile risk is external ferromagnetic objects pulled into the bore.
Implant risk is heating, movement, or malfunction of internal devices.
Implants are labeled MR safe, MR conditional, or MR unsafe.

body.title: How is a patient screened before an MRI?
body.html:
Screening asks about anything dangerous in the magnet: cardiac pacemakers and other electronic implants, aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, and metal fragments, especially in the eye. Pregnancy, kidney function for contrast studies, and claustrophobia are also reviewed.

Screening is repeated and documented, and any uncertain implant is verified before the patient enters Zone IV. A careful interview and a ferromagnetic detector both play a part.
keypoints: Ask about pacemakers, aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, and metal fragments.
Review pregnancy, kidney function, and claustrophobia.
Verify any uncertain implant before entering the magnet room.

body.title: How does gadolinium change the MRI signal?
body.html:
Gadolinium based agents are paramagnetic. They create no signal themselves; instead they shorten the T1 of nearby water protons, which makes those tissues brighter on T1 weighted images. That is why enhancement looks bright.

At high concentration gadolinium also shortens T2 and can cause signal loss, but at clinical doses the T1 effect dominates. Enhancement marks where the agent reaches, such as vascular tissue and areas of blood brain barrier breakdown.
keypoints: Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens T1 of nearby water.
Shortened T1 makes enhancing tissue bright on T1.
Enhancement marks vascularity and blood brain barrier breakdown.

body.title: What is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis?
body.html:
Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) is a rare but serious condition linked to gadolinium exposure in patients with severe kidney impairment. It thickens and hardens skin and connective tissue and can be disabling.

Risk is highest with poor renal function and with older, less stable agents. Practice lowers risk by checking kidney function (often eGFR) before contrast, using the lowest effective dose, and preferring more stable macrocyclic agents in at risk patients.
keypoints: NSF links gadolinium to severe renal impairment.
It hardens skin and connective tissue.
Check eGFR and use stable agents at the lowest dose in at risk patients.

body.title: How does restricted diffusion appear on DWI and ADC?
body.html:
Diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) measures how freely water moves. Where diffusion is restricted, as in acute stroke or a very cellular tumor, water cannot move, so signal stays high and the area looks bright on DWI.

The ADC map is calculated from the diffusion data and shows the opposite: truly restricted tissue is dark on ADC. Reading both together avoids T2 shine through, where a bright DWI is really just long T2 rather than true restriction.
keypoints: Restricted diffusion is bright on DWI and dark on ADC.
Acute stroke and cellular tumors restrict diffusion.
Read DWI with ADC to exclude T2 shine through.

body.prompt: This axial brain image was acquired with TR 500 ms and TE 12 ms. What weighting is shown?
options: T1-weighted
T2-weighted
Proton density
FLAIR
body.explain: Short TR with short TE gives T1 weighting: CSF is dark and fat and white matter are relatively bright. A long TR with a long TE would be T2 (bright CSF), a long TR with a short TE would be proton density, and FLAIR is an inversion-recovery sequence that specifically nulls CSF.

body.prompt: The axial brain scan shown used a long TR of 3500 ms and a long TE of 110 ms. What weighting does this image show?
options: T1-weighted
T2-weighted
Proton density
Diffusion weighted
body.explain: A long TR combined with a long TE produces T2 weighting, seen here as bright CSF. Proton density uses a long TR but a short TE, and T1 weighting uses a short TR. Diffusion weighting requires diffusion gradients, not simply a long TE.

body.prompt: This axial brain image was obtained with TR 3500 ms and TE 15 ms. Based on the appearance, which contrast weighting is this?
options: T1-weighted
T2-weighted
Proton density
STIR
body.explain: A long TR minimizes T1 contrast and a short TE minimizes T2 contrast, leaving an image dominated by tissue proton density with high overall signal and modest gray-white differentiation. STIR is a fat-suppression inversion recovery technique, not what is used here.

body.prompt: This axial brain image uses an inversion recovery sequence with TR 9000 ms, TE 100 ms, and TI 2548 ms. What is notable about the CSF signal, and what sequence is this?
options: CSF is nulled (dark) on a FLAIR sequence
CSF is bright on a standard T2 sequence
CSF is nulled on a STIR sequence
CSF is bright on a proton density sequence
body.explain: The long TI of about 2548 ms at 1.5T nulls the signal from CSF while preserving T2-weighted contrast elsewhere, which is the defining feature of FLAIR. STIR uses a much shorter TI to null fat, not CSF.

body.prompt: On a spin echo sequence acquired with TR 500 ms and TE 12 ms, which statement about this technique is correct compared to a susceptibility-weighted gradient echo scan?
options: Spin echo uses a 180 degree refocusing pulse, which compensates for static field inhomogeneities that a gradient echo scan would show as signal loss
Spin echo is more sensitive to susceptibility artifact than gradient echo because its refocusing pulse amplifies local field distortions from blood products
Spin echo cannot produce T1-weighted contrast
Spin echo requires diffusion gradients to form an image
body.explain: The 180 degree refocusing pulse in spin echo corrects for fixed field inhomogeneities and susceptibility dephasing, so spin echo images show relatively little susceptibility artifact. Gradient echo and SWI sequences lack this refocusing pulse and are far more sensitive to susceptibility effects such as hemorrhage or calcification.

body.prompt: This axial brain image was acquired with a susceptibility-weighted sequence (TR 28 ms, TE 20 ms, flip angle 15 degrees). Why does this technique reveal small amounts of blood products or calcium that a routine spin echo scan may miss?
options: It uses a very long TE with no refocusing pulse, so local field distortions from paramagnetic substances cause pronounced signal loss
It uses a 180 degree refocusing pulse that amplifies susceptibility effects
It relies on diffusion gradients to detect iron
It suppresses fat signal, which unmasks hemorrhage
body.explain: SWI is a gradient echo technique with a relatively long TE and no refocusing pulse, so it is highly sensitive to local magnetic field distortions caused by paramagnetic or ferromagnetic substances like deoxyhemoglobin, hemosiderin, and calcium. This produces pronounced signal loss (blooming) at sites of susceptibility change that spin echo sequences, with their refocusing pulse, largely mask.

body.prompt: The axial brain image shown was acquired as a diffusion-weighted scan with a b-value of 1000 s/mm2. What does the b-value control in this sequence?
options: The strength and duration of the diffusion-sensitizing gradients, which determines how strongly restricted water diffusion attenuates signal
The flip angle used for excitation
The inversion time used to null a tissue
The number of slices acquired in the scan
body.explain: The b-value reflects the strength, duration, and spacing of the diffusion gradients. A higher b-value makes the sequence more sensitive to water diffusion, so tissue with restricted diffusion loses less signal and appears relatively bright compared to freely diffusing water.

body.prompt: This axial brain image was acquired with periodic bulk motion during the scan. What image-quality problem is demonstrated?
options: Motion artifact, seen as ghosting and blurring propagated along the phase-encoding direction
Aliasing caused by too small a field of view relative to the anatomy
Chemical shift artifact at fat-water boundaries
Zipper artifact from RF leakage into the scan room
body.explain: Periodic patient motion during data acquisition produces discrete ghost copies of moving structures and blurring, characteristically spread along the phase-encoding direction because motion is encoded there over the course of the scan. Aliasing, chemical shift, and zipper artifacts have distinct causes and appearances.

body.prompt: This axial T1-weighted brain image was acquired without patient motion. Which statement best describes why a motion-free acquisition like this one is diagnostically preferable to a motion-degraded scan?
options: It shows sharp anatomic borders without ghosting, so subtle structures are not obscured
It has a shorter TE, which always eliminates motion artifact
It uses a larger flip angle, which prevents any patient movement
It was acquired without phase encoding, so motion cannot appear
body.explain: Without patient motion during acquisition, tissue borders remain sharp and there is no ghosting or blurring superimposed on the anatomy, which is what makes an image diagnostically reliable. TE, flip angle, and phase encoding do not by themselves prevent motion artifact; only patient stillness (or motion mitigation techniques) does.

body.prompt: This image was acquired with a time-of-flight MR angiography sequence. Why do the vessels appear bright against a dark background?
options: Unsaturated blood flowing into the imaging slice produces high signal (flow-related enhancement) while stationary tissue becomes saturated and suppressed
The vessels were injected with an iodinated contrast agent that is inherently bright on MRI
Fat suppression was applied, which selectively brightens blood vessels
The long TR nulls all stationary tissue signal by inversion recovery
body.explain: TOF MRA relies on flow-related enhancement: rapid repeated RF pulses saturate stationary tissue in the slice, but fresh, unsaturated blood flowing into the slice gives strong signal, making vessels appear bright against a suppressed dark background. No contrast agent is required for standard TOF technique.

body.prompt: A routine brain exam shows discrete repeating ghost bands spread across the phase-encoding direction. What is the most likely source of this artifact?
options: Patient bulk motion or physiologic motion occurring periodically during data acquisition
Susceptibility from a dental implant located far outside the field of view
Gradient nonlinearity at the edge of the bore
RF coil malfunction causing signal dropout
body.explain: Periodic bulk or physiologic motion (such as swallowing, pulsatile flow, or patient movement) during phase encoding creates discrete ghost copies displaced along the phase-encoding axis. Susceptibility, gradient nonlinearity, and coil malfunction produce different, non-periodic artifact patterns.

body.prompt: On a susceptibility-weighted sequence, what causes the pronounced signal loss (blooming) seen at sites of blood products?
options: Local magnetic field distortion from paramagnetic blood breakdown products causes rapid dephasing that is not refocused, since this sequence uses no 180 degree pulse
The long TR of this sequence fully recovers longitudinal magnetization, which brightens hemorrhage and increases the visible signal loss at the site
Fat suppression pulses selectively darken blood products
The short TE prevents any susceptibility effect from being visible
body.explain: SWI is a gradient echo technique without a refocusing pulse, so local field distortion from paramagnetic substances like deoxyhemoglobin or hemosiderin causes uncompensated dephasing and pronounced signal loss, exaggerated further by phase processing. This blooming effect is a hallmark of susceptibility-sensitive gradient echo imaging.

body.prompt: On a T1-weighted spin echo image acquired without any fat-suppression pulse, what is the expected appearance of subcutaneous fat?
options: Fat remains bright since no fat-suppression technique was used
Fat is dark because a fat-saturation pulse was applied
Fat cannot be seen without contrast administration
Fat appears bright only if TE is very long
body.explain: Without a fat-saturation or other fat-suppression technique, fat retains its inherently short T1 relaxation time and appears bright on a T1-weighted spin echo image. Applying a fat-sat pulse is what would darken it.

body.prompt: On a T1-weighted spin echo image acquired with a fat-saturation pulse enabled, what is the expected appearance of subcutaneous fat?
options: The subcutaneous fat signal is suppressed and appears dark
The subcutaneous fat becomes brighter than before
CSF becomes bright due to fat saturation
There is no visible change since fat-sat only affects the liver
