body.explain: A fat-saturation pulse selectively excites and dephases the resonant frequency of fat protons before the imaging sequence, suppressing fat signal so it appears dark. This helps distinguish fat from enhancing tissue or hemorrhage that might otherwise be similarly bright.

body.prompt: A diffusion-weighted scan (b-value 1000) in a patient with acute onset neurologic symptoms shows a focal area of markedly high signal. What does this finding most likely represent?
options: Acute ischemic stroke, where restricted diffusion from cytotoxic edema produces high DWI signal
A chronic old infarct, which typically shows equally high DWI signal because established gliosis restricts water diffusion in the same way
Normal brain parenchyma with no abnormality
A simple arachnoid cyst
body.explain: In acute ischemic stroke, cellular energy failure causes cytotoxic edema and restricted water diffusion, which produces markedly high signal on DWI within minutes to hours of onset, before changes are visible on conventional T1 or T2 sequences. Chronic infarcts typically show diffusion pseudonormalization or facilitated diffusion rather than restriction, and cysts follow free water signal, not restricted diffusion.

body.prompt: A susceptibility-weighted scan shows a focal area of pronounced signal dropout (blooming). In the correct clinical context, what does this finding most likely represent?
options: Hemorrhage, since paramagnetic blood breakdown products cause local susceptibility artifact and signal loss
A simple fluid-filled cyst, which shows the same blooming pattern because the fluid it contains also distorts the local magnetic field
Normal calcified choroid plexus with no clinical significance
A fat-containing lesion such as a lipoma
body.explain: Blood breakdown products such as deoxyhemoglobin and hemosiderin are paramagnetic and create local magnetic field distortion, producing pronounced signal loss on susceptibility-weighted imaging. This blooming effect is characteristic of hemorrhage and is used clinically to detect even small amounts of blood that other sequences may miss. Simple cysts and fat do not create this susceptibility effect.

body.prompt: On a post-contrast T1-weighted spin echo scan, a focal area of abnormal enhancement is seen in a mass lesion. What does contrast enhancement typically indicate?
options: Breakdown of the blood-brain barrier or increased vascularity, allowing gadolinium to accumulate and shorten T1, as seen in many tumors
The lesion is definitely benign and requires no follow-up
The patient received an iodinated contrast agent that is directly visualized on MRI in the same way that it is seen on a CT examination
Enhancement only occurs in old, chronic infarcts and never in tumors
body.explain: Gadolinium-based contrast agents shorten T1 relaxation time in tissue where they accumulate. Areas of blood-brain barrier breakdown or abnormal, leaky vascularity, common in many primary and metastatic brain tumors, allow gadolinium to accumulate and appear bright on post-contrast T1-weighted images. Enhancement pattern helps characterize a lesion but does not by itself prove it is benign, and MRI does not directly visualize iodinated CT contrast agents.

body.title: Contrast reactions: recognition and management
body.html:
How common, and what is not a reaction. Adverse reactions to a gadolinium-based contrast agent occur in roughly 0.07 to 2.4 percent of patients, and the vast majority are mild. True anaphylaxis is rare, on the order of 0.001 to 0.01 percent, and fatal reactions are rarer still. A transient feeling of warmth or flushing during injection is not a true reaction; reassurance is usually all it needs, and calming an anxious patient before the injection can prevent symptoms from escalating.

The three severity tiers. Reactions are graded in three tiers:

  • Mild: nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, itching, and limited hives. The radiologist evaluates the patient, vitals are taken, and the patient is observed for up to 30 minutes.
  • Moderate: diffuse erythema, bronchospasm, wheezing, hypotension, or a vasovagal episode. Not immediately life threatening but can progress, so medical treatment and monitoring until resolution are required.
  • Severe: laryngeal edema, unresponsiveness, seizures, arrhythmia, and anaphylaxis. These demand immediate treatment.

Telling the two low blood pressure pictures apart. A vasovagal reaction, often triggered by anxiety around IV placement, produces hypotension with bradycardia, pallor, nausea, and sweating; the first maneuver is to elevate the legs or use the Trendelenburg position to restore blood flow to the brain, then recheck vitals until the patient improves. Anaphylaxis produces hypotension with tachycardia, typically alongside hives, facial or laryngeal swelling, or wheezing, and it is the clear indication for epinephrine.

Extravasation. A separate problem is extravasation, where contrast enters the soft tissue instead of the vein, causing swelling, redness, burning, and pain. A warm compress promotes reabsorption and circulation, a cold compress relieves pain, and a radiologist should assess the site before the patient leaves.

The rapid response sequence. When a reaction occurs: remove the patient from the scanner and assess breathing, pulse, and consciousness; alert the covering radiologist and, if needed, the emergency response team; prepare the emergency equipment and medication box in a safe zone outside the magnetic field; inform responders of the study type, the agent given, and when the reaction began; then deliver medications exactly as the physician directs.

The medication box. Each drug pairs with an indication:

  • Albuterol for wheezing
  • Atropine for bradycardia
  • Diphenhydramine for mild urticaria
  • Dextrose for hypoglycemia
  • Furosemide for pulmonary edema
  • Epinephrine for anaphylaxis

Epinephrine and disposition. Per department protocol, the epinephrine auto-injector is the one drug a technologist may give decisively: 0.3 mg for patients 30 kg and over, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg, pressed firmly against the lateral thigh until it clicks and held for several seconds. Every patient who receives an auto-injector goes to the emergency department for monitoring.

Premedication and monitoring reference points. Patients with a prior severe reaction are premedicated, commonly prednisone 50 mg by mouth 13, 7, and 1 hour before contrast plus diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before. While monitoring: SpO2 above 95 percent is normal and 92 percent or less suggests hypoxemia; normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and 80 diastolic.
keypoints: Reactions to gadolinium-based agents are uncommon and mostly mild; anaphylaxis occurs in roughly 0.001 to 0.01 percent of patients.
Vasovagal means hypotension with bradycardia, pallor, and sweating; anaphylaxis means hypotension with tachycardia plus hives or airway involvement.
For extravasation, a warm compress promotes reabsorption, a cold compress relieves pain, and a radiologist assesses the site before discharge.
In an emergency: remove the patient from the scanner, alert the radiologist and response team, prepare equipment and the med box outside the field, inform responders, and deliver drugs as directed.

The epinephrine auto-injector is the one drug a technologist may give per department protocol: 0.3 mg at 30 kg and above, 0.15 mg for 15 to 30 kg, and every recipient goes to the emergency department.
body.worked_example: Five minutes after a gadolinium-based contrast injection, a patient develops spreading hives and begins to wheeze, with a heart rate of 118. Skin and airway involvement together meet anaphylaxis criteria, so this is treated as a severe reaction rather than a mild one. The technologist removes the patient from the scanner, checks breathing and pulse, alerts the covering radiologist, and moves the patient to a safe zone outside the magnetic field with the medication box and emergency equipment ready. Because both skin and airway are involved, the radiologist directs intramuscular epinephrine into the lateral thigh without delay, with albuterol as an adjunct for the wheeze, and the patient is monitored and sent to the emergency department.
memory_hooks: Slow and pale points vagal, fast with hives points anaphylaxis.
Compresses for extravasation: warm to clear it, cold to calm it.
The response flow spells RAPID: Remove, Alert, Prepare, Inform, Deliver.
exam_traps: Both vasovagal reactions and anaphylaxis drop the blood pressure; the heart rate separates them, slow for vasovagal and fast for anaphylaxis.
Warmth or flushing during injection is an expected sensation, not a true reaction, so the answer is reassurance rather than medication.
Diphenhydramine treats mild urticaria only; epinephrine, not an antihistamine, is the drug for anaphylaxis, and premedication reduces but does not eliminate repeat risk.

body.prompt: A patient develops scattered hives and itching a few minutes after a gadolinium-based contrast injection. Vital signs are normal. How is this reaction classified?
options: Mild, observe and notify the radiologist
Moderate, needing bronchodilator therapy
Severe, needing immediate epinephrine
Not a reaction, so no observation needed
body.explain: Urticaria with stable vitals is a mild reaction. The radiologist should still evaluate the patient, and observation for up to 30 minutes is appropriate because hives can progress.

body.prompt: During a contrast injection a patient develops stridor, facial swelling, and worsening difficulty breathing. Which severity category is this?
options: A mild reaction that resolves with reassurance
A moderate reaction managed with observation
A severe reaction requiring immediate treatment
A vasovagal episode managed with leg elevation
body.explain: Laryngeal edema signals a severe, potentially life threatening reaction. The emergency response sequence starts at once and epinephrine is prepared without delay.

body.prompt: Both a vasovagal reaction and anaphylaxis can drop the blood pressure. Which finding points to a vasovagal cause?
options: Bradycardia with pallor and sweating
Tachycardia with spreading urticaria
Wheezing with new facial swelling
Stridor with a rising heart rate
body.explain: Vasovagal reactions cause hypotension with a slow heart rate, pallor, and diaphoresis. Anaphylaxis typically pairs hypotension with tachycardia plus hives or airway symptoms.

body.prompt: A patient becomes pale, sweaty, and faint right after IV placement, with a slow pulse. What is the best first maneuver?
options: Elevate the legs to restore brain blood flow
Give an epinephrine auto-injector in the thigh
Apply a warm compress at the injection site
Administer an oral antihistamine right away
body.explain: This is a vasovagal reaction. Raising the legs or using Trendelenburg position returns blood to the brain while help is called and vitals are rechecked until the patient improves.

body.prompt: Contrast extravasates into the soft tissue of the forearm. What is the purpose of applying a warm compress?
options: It promotes reabsorption and circulation
It numbs the site and relieves the pain
It prevents infection at the puncture site
It constricts vessels to limit the swelling
body.explain: Warm compresses aid reabsorption of extravasated contrast by improving local circulation, while cold compresses are the choice for pain relief. A radiologist should assess the site before the patient leaves.

body.prompt: Which contrast reaction is the clearest indication for giving epinephrine?
options: Anaphylaxis with airway compromise
Nausea shortly after the injection
Isolated hives with stable vital signs
Warm flushed feeling during injection
body.explain: Epinephrine is the first line drug for anaphylaxis and severe bronchospasm. Nausea, isolated hives, or flushing do not call for it.

body.prompt: An anaphylactic reaction occurs in a child who weighs 20 kg. Which epinephrine auto-injector dose is correct?
options: 0.15 mg, the junior auto-injector dose
0.3 mg, the standard adult device dose
0.5 mg, repeated every three minutes
1 mg given slowly by intravenous push
body.explain: Children weighing 15 to 30 kg receive the 0.15 mg junior device. Patients at or above 30 kg, about 66 pounds, receive the 0.3 mg adult dose.

body.prompt: Per department protocol, which emergency drug may an MRI technologist administer on their own initiative during anaphylaxis?
options: Epinephrine by auto-injector
Diphenhydramine by IV push
Atropine from the med box
Nitroglycerin under the tongue
body.explain: The epinephrine auto-injector is typically the one medication a technologist may give decisively in an emergency. Every other drug in the box requires a physician to order and direct it.

body.prompt: After a technologist gives an epinephrine auto-injector for a contrast reaction, what must happen next?
options: The patient goes to the emergency department
The patient leaves once the hives have faded
The exam resumes when breathing feels normal
A second dose is always given ten minutes on
body.explain: Vital signs are watched closely and every patient who receives epinephrine goes to the emergency department, because symptoms can rebound and repeat dosing may be needed.

body.prompt: A patient with a prior severe reaction to gadolinium-based contrast is scheduled for a contrast MRI. What is a standard pre-medication schedule?
options: Prednisone 50 mg at 13, 7, and 1 hour before, plus diphenhydramine 1 hour before
Prednisone 50 mg as a single dose about 30 minutes before entering the scanner
Diphenhydramine 50 mg nightly for three days with no corticosteroid given at all
One epinephrine injection administered immediately before the contrast is dosed
body.explain: A common regimen is prednisone 50 mg by mouth 13, 7, and 1 hour before contrast, with diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before. It lowers but does not eliminate the risk of a repeat reaction.

body.prompt: A patient begins wheezing after contrast administration. Which emergency medication box drug treats this symptom?
options: Albuterol, an inhaled bronchodilator
Atropine, which raises the heart rate
Furosemide, which clears excess fluid
Dextrose, which corrects low glucose
body.explain: Albuterol relieves bronchospasm and wheezing. Atropine treats bradycardia, furosemide treats pulmonary edema, and dextrose treats hypoglycemia.

body.prompt: During a contrast reaction the heart rate falls to 38 beats per minute. Which medication box drug addresses this finding?
options: Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia
Albuterol for airway smooth muscle
Aspirin for suspected cardiac ischemia
Nitroglycerin for severe anginal pain
body.explain: Atropine is the medication box drug for bradycardia. The physician directs its use; the technologist prepares the box but does not administer it.

body.prompt: The radiologist evaluates mild hives after contrast and requests treatment. Which drug matches this indication?
options: Oral diphenhydramine, an antihistamine
Intramuscular epinephrine at 0.3 mg dose
Nebulized albuterol to treat the rash
Sublingual nitroglycerin for comfort
body.explain: Mild urticaria is treated with 25 to 50 mg of oral diphenhydramine when the physician requests it. Epinephrine is reserved for severe reactions such as anaphylaxis.

body.prompt: While monitoring a patient after a contrast injection, which reading falls outside normal adult limits?
options: Oxygen saturation of 91 percent
Blood pressure of 118 over 76
Oxygen saturation of 97 percent
Resting pulse of 72 per minute
body.explain: An SpO2 above 95 percent is considered normal, and 92 percent or less suggests hypoxemia. Normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.

body.prompt: A patient reports feeling warm and flushed during the gadolinium-based contrast injection but has no other symptoms. What does this represent?
options: A common sensation, not a true reaction
An early mild reaction needing medication
The first stage of anaphylactic response
A vasovagal episode needing leg raising
body.explain: Transient warmth and flushing are expected sensations, not true reactions. Reassurance is usually all that is needed, and calming anxious patients before injection can prevent escalation.

body.title: Brain MRI: routine protocol and when to enhance
body.html:
A routine brain study uses the head coil and covers from the skull base to the vertex, roughly one slice above the top of the skull. Axial slices are angled along the AC-PC line, drawn through the anterior and posterior commissures, so that anatomy is displayed in a reproducible plane. Many departments now acquire 3D sagittal volumes (T1 or MPR, FLAIR, and T2) and reformat them into axial and coronal planes, which reduces repeat scanning and gives isotropic detail.

The non-contrast set is built around a signal triad. Diffusion detects acute infarct: true restriction is bright on the high b-value image (for example b1000) and dark on the ADC map. SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) shows hemorrhage and cerebral microbleeds in trauma and microhemorrhage. FLAIR is a fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequence that nulls CSF so CSF appears dark, and it highlights multiple sclerosis and other white-matter disease. The spine equivalent for demyelination is STIR.

Gadolinium is dosed by body weight per department protocol. Structures that normally enhance confirm that contrast was delivered: the pituitary gland and infundibulum, choroid plexus, nasal mucosa and turbinates, dural venous sinuses, and vessels. Contrast is added by indication, such as routine with and without for headache or infection, tumor follow-up, pre-operative and immediate post-operative studies, metastatic or meningioma work-up in a patient with a cancer history, and demyelinating disease. Isolated memory loss usually does not receive contrast.
keypoints: Head coil, coverage skull base to vertex, axial slices angled on the AC-PC line.
Diffusion restriction means bright on high b-value AND dark on ADC.
SWI shows hemorrhage and microbleeds; FLAIR nulls CSF and shows MS.
3D sagittal volumes are reformatted into axial and coronal planes.
Gadolinium is weight-based; pituitary, choroid plexus, mucosa, sinuses, and vessels normally enhance.
body.worked_example: A patient arrives with sudden left-sided weakness. On the high b-value diffusion image a right frontal region is bright, and the same region is dark on the ADC map. That combination confirms an acute infarct with true restricted diffusion, so the finding is reported as acute stroke rather than dismissed as an artifact.
memory_hooks: Diffusion for stroke, SWI for blood, FLAIR for plaques.
True restriction is bright high-b, dark ADC.
AC to PC keeps every brain in the same plane.
exam_traps: FLAIR nulls CSF so CSF is dark, unlike T2 where CSF is bright.
High b-value brightness alone is not restriction without a dark ADC; bright high-b with bright ADC is T2 shine-through.

body.title: Specialized neuro studies: pituitary, IAC, and stereotactic planning
body.html:
The dynamic pituitary study uses the head coil and full-dose contrast. A microadenoma is smaller than 10 mm and a macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger. A dynamic contrast-enhanced sequence acquires rapid repeated images just after injection to catch microadenomas, which enhance later than the normal gland. On early dynamic frames the lesion therefore looks relatively dark against the briskly enhancing normal pituitary. Do not alter the dynamic sequence parameters. The gland has an anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and a posterior lobe (neurohypophysis), the posterior lobe is often intrinsically T1-bright, and the gland sits in the sella turcica.

The internal auditory canal study also uses the head coil and full-dose contrast. The IAC carries cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear). Indications include sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo or balance problems, tinnitus, and acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Technique combines thin-section heavily T2-weighted cisternal imaging, a steady-state CISS or FIESTA type sequence that outlines the nerves within bright CSF, plus thin post-contrast T1 with fat saturation. A related variant targets trigeminal neuralgia or facial-nerve problems such as facial pain or Bell's palsy involving CN VII.

Stereotactic or neuronavigation planning is a pre-surgical study. Keep the head straight and do not angle the slice packages, and acquire an isotropic 3D volume with full coverage. Do not clip the nose, ears, or back of the head, because the surgical navigation system registers the whole head surface. Sub-variants add perfusion for tumor grading or a dynamic sequence for metastases and meningioma, and a seizure pre-operative study angles coronals perpendicular to the hippocampus.
keypoints: Microadenoma is under 10 mm, macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger.
Dynamic pituitary catches microadenomas by their delayed enhancement, dark early against the normal gland.
IAC carries CN VII and VIII; indications include hearing loss and acoustic neuroma.
IAC uses thin-section CISS or FIESTA cisternal imaging plus post-contrast T1 fat-sat.
Stereotactic studies keep the head straight, do not angle packages, and never clip nose, ears, or occiput.
body.worked_example: A patient with a rising prolactin level has a normal-looking sella on routine images. The dynamic pituitary sequence is run, and on the earliest post-injection frames a small 6 mm region stays dark while the rest of the gland enhances briskly. That delayed enhancement pattern identifies a microadenoma that a single delayed image would have missed.
memory_hooks: Micro is under 10, macro is ten or more.
Seven and Eight run through the IAC gate.
Straight head, full head for navigation.
exam_traps: A microadenoma enhances later than the gland, so it looks dark early, not bright early.
Do not angle or crop the stereotactic packages; clipping the nose, ears, or occiput breaks surface registration.

body.prompt: Which coil and coverage are standard for a routine brain MRI?
options: Head coil, covering from the skull base to the vertex
Neck coil, covering from the orbits down to the carina
Body coil, covering from the vertex to the mandible only
Surface coil, covering the occiput and upper cervical spine
body.explain: Routine brain imaging uses a dedicated head coil and covers the skull base up to the vertex, about one slice above the top of the skull. The other coils and coverages do not include the whole brain.

body.prompt: Axial slices in a routine brain study are typically angled along which reference line?
options: The AC-PC line from the anterior to the posterior commissure
The orbitomeatal line from the outer canthus to the ear canal
The hard palate line drawn parallel to the maxillary teeth
The interhemispheric line drawn through the falx midline
body.explain: Axials are prescribed along the AC-PC line, drawn through the anterior and posterior commissures, giving a reproducible plane. The other lines are used for different purposes or planning steps.

body.prompt: On MRI, what confirms true acute restricted diffusion in a suspected stroke?
options: Bright signal on high b-value with dark signal on the ADC map
Bright signal on high b-value with bright signal on the ADC map
Dark signal on high b-value with dark signal on the ADC map
Dark signal on high b-value with bright signal on the ADC map
body.explain: True restriction is bright on the high b-value image and dark on the ADC map. Bright on both high-b and ADC is T2 shine-through, not restriction, and the dark-on-high-b patterns do not indicate acute infarct.

body.prompt: Which sequence is most sensitive for cerebral microbleeds and hemorrhage?
options: SWI, a susceptibility-weighted gradient technique
FLAIR, a fluid-attenuated inversion recovery technique
DWI, a diffusion-weighted echo-planar technique
STIR, a short tau inversion recovery fat-suppression technique
body.explain: SWI is highly sensitive to blood products and detects hemorrhage and microbleeds. FLAIR targets white-matter disease, DWI targets infarct, and STIR is used for fat-suppressed edema and cord imaging.

body.prompt: On a FLAIR image, how does normal CSF appear and what does FLAIR highlight?
options: CSF appears dark because it is nulled, highlighting MS plaques
CSF appears bright because it is enhanced, highlighting fresh blood
CSF appears gray because it is partly nulled, highlighting fat
CSF appears dark because it is saturated, highlighting cortical bone
body.explain: FLAIR nulls CSF so it appears dark, which makes periventricular MS plaques and white-matter disease stand out. FLAIR does not enhance CSF or specifically target blood, fat, or bone.

body.prompt: Many brain protocols acquire 3D sagittal volumes and then do what with them?
options: Reformat them into axial and coronal planes after acquisition
Discard them once the axial two-dimensional scans are complete
Send them only to the technologist workstation for archiving
Convert them into diffusion maps for stroke quantification only
body.explain: Isotropic 3D sagittal volumes such as T1, FLAIR, and T2 are reformatted into axial and coronal planes, giving multiplanar review from one acquisition. They are not discarded, merely archived, or turned into diffusion maps.

body.prompt: How is the gadolinium contrast dose for a brain MRI determined?
options: By the patient body weight, per the department protocol
By the patient age, using a fixed pediatric adult split
By the patient height, using a standard body surface chart
By a single fixed volume given to every patient equally
body.explain: Gadolinium is dosed on body weight following department protocol. It is not set by age, height, or a single fixed volume for all patients.

body.prompt: Which structure normally enhances and can confirm that gadolinium was given?
options: The pituitary gland and infundibulum, which enhance normally
The cerebral cortex, which enhances briskly in every patient
The normal white matter tracts, which enhance after injection
The lateral ventricle CSF, which enhances soon after injection
body.explain: The pituitary and infundibulum lack a blood-brain barrier and enhance normally, along with choroid plexus, nasal mucosa, dural sinuses, and vessels. Normal cortex, white matter, and CSF do not enhance.

body.prompt: Which clinical situation typically does NOT warrant contrast on a brain MRI?
options: Isolated memory loss without other concerning history
Follow-up of a known brain tumor after prior treatment
Work-up for metastatic disease in a known cancer patient
Immediate post-operative imaging after a tumor resection
body.explain: Isolated memory loss is usually imaged without contrast. Tumor follow-up, metastatic work-up, and immediate post-operative studies all routinely use gadolinium.

body.prompt: What size threshold separates a pituitary microadenoma from a macroadenoma?
options: 10 mm, with micro under 10 and macro 10 or larger
20 mm, with micro under 20 and macro 20 or larger
5 mm, with micro under 5 and macro 5 or larger
15 mm, with micro under 15 and macro 15 or larger
body.explain: A microadenoma is smaller than 10 mm and a macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger. The 20, 5, and 15 mm figures are not the accepted threshold.

body.prompt: On an early dynamic pituitary frame, how does a microadenoma usually appear?
options: Relatively dark, because it enhances later than the normal gland
Brightly enhancing, because it fills with contrast before the gland
Isointense, because it enhances exactly with the normal gland
Completely absent, because it never takes up any contrast agent
body.explain: A microadenoma shows delayed enhancement, so on early dynamic frames it looks relatively dark against the briskly enhancing normal gland. It does not enhance first, match the gland, or fail to enhance entirely.

body.prompt: Which statement about the normal pituitary gland is correct?
options: The posterior lobe is often T1-bright and the gland sits in the sella turcica
The anterior lobe is always T1-dark and the gland sits in the cavernous sinus
The posterior lobe is always T2-bright and the gland sits above the clivus
The anterior lobe is often T1-bright and the gland sits in the frontal sinus
body.explain: The posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) is frequently intrinsically T1-bright, and the gland lies within the sella turcica. The other pairings misplace the gland or misassign the bright signal.

body.prompt: Which cranial nerves run through the internal auditory canal?
options: The facial nerve VII and the vestibulocochlear nerve VIII
The trigeminal nerve V and the abducens nerve VI together
The glossopharyngeal nerve IX and the vagus nerve X together
The optic nerve II and the oculomotor nerve III together
body.explain: The IAC carries CN VII (facial) and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear). The other pairs travel through different skull base routes, not the internal auditory canal.

body.prompt: Which finding is a classic indication for an internal auditory canal study?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss with suspected acoustic neuroma
Sudden thunderclap headache with suspected aneurysm rupture
Progressive memory loss with suspected early dementia change
New focal seizures with suspected cortical developmental lesion
body.explain: The IAC protocol targets sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, and acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Aneurysm, dementia, and seizure work-ups use other protocols.

body.prompt: Which technique best displays the CN VII and VIII within the IAC?
options: Thin-section heavily T2-weighted CISS or FIESTA steady-state imaging
Thick-slab T1-weighted spin echo imaging without any fat saturation
Standard axial gradient echo imaging matched to the routine brain
Low-resolution single-shot diffusion imaging through the posterior fossa
body.explain: Thin-section heavily T2-weighted steady-state imaging (CISS or FIESTA) outlines the nerves against bright CSF, and thin post-contrast T1 fat-sat is added. Thick T1, routine gradient echo, and diffusion do not resolve the nerves.

body.prompt: When planning a stereotactic neuronavigation study, how should slices be prescribed?
options: Keep the head straight and do not angle the slice packages at all
Angle the axial package along the AC-PC line as in routine brain
Angle the coronal package perpendicular to the hippocampal body
Tilt the whole package toward the side of the suspected lesion
body.explain: Navigation studies require the head straight with unangled packages so the volume registers cleanly to the surgical system. AC-PC angling and hippocampal angling belong to other protocols, and lesion tilting is not done.

body.prompt: Why must a stereotactic planning volume include the entire head surface?
options: The navigation system registers the whole head surface for guidance
The radiologist needs the neck vessels included for perfusion mapping
The scanner requires full coverage to correct for gradient nonlinearity
The surgeon uses the sinuses alone to align the operative approach
body.explain: The surgical navigation system registers the full head surface, so the nose, ears, and occiput must not be clipped. The other reasons do not drive the full-coverage rule for planning volumes.

body.prompt: The trigeminal-neuralgia and facial-nerve variant of the IAC study targets which nerve?
options: The facial nerve CN VII in patients with facial pain or Bell's palsy
The optic nerve CN II in patients with sudden painless vision loss
The hypoglossal nerve CN XII in patients with tongue deviation signs
The accessory nerve CN XI in patients with shoulder droop weakness
body.explain: The variant evaluates CN VII for facial pain or Bell's palsy, alongside trigeminal assessment. The optic, hypoglossal, and accessory nerves are not the focus of this protocol.

body.title: Spine MRI protocols: cervical, thoracic, and lumbar
body.html:
The cervical spine is imaged with a combined head and neck coil for indications such as neck pain, herniated disc (HNP), degenerative disc disease (DDD), radiculopathy, stenosis, cord compression, MS, tumor, Chiari malformation, syrinx, and radiating arm pain. Sagittal coverage runs from the pons and fourth ventricle down to about T2 to T3, pedicle to pedicle, and axials extend from C2 to C3 through C7 to T1, angled to each disc space. Core sequences are Sag T2 and Sag T1 for herniation, DDD, lesions, tumor, and syrinx, plus Sag STIR for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection. Axial GRE displays the nerve roots and osteophytes, and Ax T2 shows cord lesions and syrinx. An anterior saturation band placed in front of the vertebral bodies suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion and also reduces CSF pulsation artifact.

The thoracic spine covers roughly C7 to L1 for mid back pain and the same degenerative and cord indications. Because the thoracic levels are hard to count, a vitamin E capsule (a common skin or table marker) is placed to help count vertebral bodies so the correct level is localized. Sag STIR is the best sequence for MS, infection, fracture, and bony metastases. Add Cor T2 for scoliosis and Cor STIR when neurofibromatosis (NF1 or NF2) is suspected. Axials may use right to left phase encoding to push breathing motion artifact away from the cord.

The lumbar spine covers about T12 to S2 with axials from L1 to S1 for low back pain, HNP, DDD, radiculopathy, stenosis, tumor, radiating leg pain, prior surgery, and tethered cord. Use an odd number of slices per disc (for example 5) so one slice runs through the disc center. Contrast is required for infection, post-operative scarring, and tumor. After back surgery, contrast separates enhancing scar (fibrosis) from non-enhancing recurrent disc. Tethered cord studies extend coverage down to the coccyx.
keypoints: Cervical uses a head and neck coil; sagittals run from the pons and fourth ventricle to about T2 to T3.
Sag STIR is best for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection in every region of the spine.
Axial GRE shows nerve roots and osteophytes but blooms near metal, so avoid it there.
An anterior saturation band suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion plus CSF pulsation.
A vitamin E capsule marker counts thoracic levels; lumbar covers about T12 to S2 with odd slices per disc.
body.worked_example: A patient returns with recurrent leg pain one year after an L4 to L5 discectomy. A plain non-contrast study cannot tell whether the epidural soft tissue is scar or a new disc fragment. Contrast is given, and the tissue enhances uniformly, which identifies fibrosis rather than recurrent disc. Because scar enhances while recurrent disc does not, the post-operative lumbar spine is protocoled with contrast from the start.
memory_hooks: STIR lights up the bad marrow: MS, mets, fracture, infection.
Vitamin E dot lets you count the vertebral bodies and find the level.
Post-op scar glows, recurrent disc stays dark.
exam_traps: Do not run GRE near spinal hardware, because metal blooms and hides the anatomy.
The post-operative lumbar spine gets contrast because scar enhances while recurrent disc does not.

body.title: Total spine and technique: bone versus neuro, drop metastases, and metal reduction
body.html:
A total spine is assembled from two sagittal packages, an upper and a lower set, that overlap by about two disc spaces at 3 mm with no gap. The upper package uses a smaller field of view than the lower one. Always use the smallest field of view that still covers the anatomy, and adjust resolution whenever the FOV changes. Remember the counts: the spine has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar vertebrae.

Metastatic disease splits into two patterns. Drop metastases seed down the CSF from a primary brain tumor, so the study images the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum and typically omits the pre-contrast axials. Bony metastases arise from primary cancers such as lung, colon, or breast, usually need no contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence can help characterize marrow. Cor STIR is added when neurofibromatosis is suspected. For post-contrast technique, use a fat-saturated T1 to improve differentiation of enhancing tissue, and do not simply append a pre-contrast inversion recovery T1 as the post series.

Near hardware, a metal reduction toolkit recovers the image. Use TSE (turbo spin echo) rather than gradient echo, increase the receive bandwidth, and raise the turbo or echo train factor. Decrease the slice thickness, switch fat-saturated T2 to STIR for more uniform fat suppression, and decrease the TE. Raise the resolution, change the phase encode direction, and increase the number of signal averages to recover lost signal.
keypoints: Total spine sagittals use two packages overlapping by about two disc spaces at 3 mm with no gap.
Drop mets seed from a brain tumor and require imaging the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum.
Bony mets from lung, colon, or breast usually need no contrast; in and out of phase can help.
Near metal, use TSE not gradient echo, raise bandwidth, and switch fat-sat T2 to STIR.
body.worked_example: A patient with a known posterior fossa primary is sent for spine imaging to look for CSF seeding. Because drop metastases fall through the CSF and collect at the bottom of the thecal sac, the coverage is extended to include the entire sacrum, and the pre-contrast axials are omitted so the post-contrast series does the work. A patient with lung cancer and back pain, by contrast, is worked up for bony metastases, usually without contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence helps confirm marrow replacement.
memory_hooks: Drop mets fall to the floor, so scan all the way to the sacrum.
Fight metal with TSE, wide bandwidth, and STIR.
exam_traps: Near metal, prefer STIR over fat-saturated T2 and use TSE rather than gradient echo.

body.prompt: Which coil is standard for imaging the cervical spine?
options: A combined head and neck coil covering the cervical region
A dedicated extremity coil wrapped around the lower neck
A single small loop surface coil taped over the throat
The transmit body coil alone with no surface coil added
body.explain: The cervical spine is imaged with a head and neck coil, which places receive elements over the whole cervical region for adequate signal and coverage.

body.prompt: On a cervical spine study, how far superiorly should the sagittal coverage extend?
options: To the pons and fourth ventricle, then down to about T2 to T3
To the vertex of the skull, then down to the mid lumbar spine
To the hard palate only, then down to the level of the carina
To the frontal sinus region, then down to the top of the sacrum
body.explain: Cervical sagittals cover from the pons and fourth ventricle down to about T2 to T3, pedicle to pedicle, so the cervicomedullary junction and cervicothoracic junction are included.

body.prompt: Which sagittal sequence is best for showing MS plaques, metastases, fracture, and infection?
options: Sagittal STIR, which brightens cord edema and marrow lesions
Sagittal T1 gradient echo tuned with a very long echo time
Axial gradient echo optimized only to display the nerve roots
A low resolution localizer acquired with wide slice gaps only
body.explain: STIR suppresses fat and makes edema conspicuous, so it is the best sequence for MS, metastases, fracture, and infection where marrow or cord signal is abnormal.

body.prompt: Axial GRE shows nerve roots and osteophytes well, but should be avoided when what is present?
options: Metallic hardware, because susceptibility causes signal blooming
A simple midline disc bulge without any associated bony change
Cerebrospinal fluid pulsation moving along the cervical cord
Mild degenerative scoliosis of the lower thoracic spinal column
body.explain: Gradient echo is very sensitive to susceptibility, so metal blooms and obscures the anatomy. Near hardware a TSE based sequence is used instead.

body.prompt: An anterior saturation band placed in front of the vertebral bodies primarily reduces what?
options: Swallowing, breathing, and cardiac motion, plus CSF pulsation
Chemical shift misregistration at the fat and water boundaries
Magnetic susceptibility blooming caused by dental restorations
Gibbs truncation ringing seen at sharp high contrast interfaces
body.explain: A saturation band in front of the spine nulls signal from the moving throat, heart, and chest, which suppresses swallowing, cardiac, and breathing motion and also reduces CSF pulsation artifact.

body.prompt: On a thoracic spine study, why is a vitamin E capsule marker placed on the patient?
options: To count vertebral bodies so the correct level is localized
To suppress fat signal along the anterior chest wall region
To trigger the acquisition to the patient breathing cycle
To calibrate the transmit gain before the scan is started
body.explain: The thoracic levels are hard to count, so a bright vitamin E marker gives a fixed reference on the images that lets the reader count vertebral bodies and localize the correct level.

body.prompt: What is the usual sagittal coverage range for a lumbar spine study?
options: About T12 down to S2, covering the conus and the thecal sac
About C7 down to L1, covering the mid spinal column segments
About L3 down to the coccyx, a narrow and focused lower block
About the pons down to L1, matching a cervical spine package
body.explain: Lumbar sagittals span about T12 to S2 so the conus medullaris and the lower thecal sac are both included, with axials typically from L1 to S1.

body.prompt: Why does the post-operative lumbar spine require contrast?
options: Scar tissue enhances while recurrent disc material does not
Contrast shortens the total scan time for the whole examination
Contrast removes all of the motion artifact from axial images
Recurrent disc enhances brightly while scar tissue stays dark
body.explain: After back surgery, enhancing fibrosis and non-enhancing recurrent disc look similar without contrast. Because scar enhances and recurrent disc does not, contrast separates the two.

body.prompt: A herniated disc or a syrinx is best demonstrated on which weighting?
options: T2, where bright fluid makes a syrinx and disc herniation stand out
T1 without contrast, where fluid appears uniformly dark instead
Gradient echo alone, which is reserved mainly for metallic clips
A proton density map optimized purely for marrow fat contrast
body.explain: T2 makes fluid bright, so a syrinx and a herniated disc against dark structures stand out clearly, which is why Sag and Ax T2 are core to spine protocols.

body.prompt: How are the sagittal packages of a total spine study assembled?
options: Two packages that overlap by about two disc spaces, no gap
Two packages that abut with a wide gap between the two sets
Two packages that overlap by about half the entire spinal column
One single package for the whole spine, so overlap never applies
body.explain: The upper and lower sagittal packages overlap by about two disc spaces at 3 mm with no gap, so no level is missed at the junction between them.

body.prompt: What field of view guidance applies to spine sagittal imaging?
options: Use the smallest FOV that still covers the target anatomy
Use the largest FOV available to capture nearby structures
Match the FOV to the bore size regardless of the anatomy
Keep the FOV fixed at 40 cm for every spine examination
body.explain: The smallest field of view that still covers the anatomy gives the best spatial resolution. When the FOV changes, resolution is adjusted to keep image quality consistent.

body.prompt: Drop metastases seed down the CSF from a primary brain tumor, so the study must do what?
options: Image the whole thecal sac including the entire sacrum
Image only the cervical cord where the seeding begins first
Stop coverage at L1 since the cord ends around that level
Cover the brain alone because the sacrum stays unaffected
body.explain: Drop metastases fall through the CSF and can collect anywhere in the thecal sac, so coverage extends to include the entire sacrum, and pre-contrast axials are typically omitted.

body.prompt: Bony metastases from lung, colon, or breast primaries usually require what?
options: No contrast, often with an in and out of phase sequence added
A double dose of contrast with delayed post-contrast imaging
Intrathecal contrast injected before the sagittal series runs
Oral contrast timed to the start of the axial image acquisition
body.explain: Bony metastases from primaries such as lung, colon, or breast usually need no contrast, and an in and out of phase sequence helps show marrow replacement.

body.prompt: Which change reduces metal artifact near spinal hardware?
options: Increase the receive bandwidth to tighten the readout window
Decrease the receive bandwidth to widen each frequency voxel
Lower the echo train factor toward a single spin echo readout
Increase the slice thickness to average the artifact together
body.explain: A higher receive bandwidth shortens the readout and reduces the spatial spread of susceptibility, which cuts metal artifact. Raising the echo train factor and thinner slices also help.

body.prompt: Near metallic hardware, fat-saturated T2 should be switched to what?
options: STIR, which suppresses fat more uniformly around the metal
A spectral fat-sat T1 acquired with a very short echo time
Gradient echo, which handles the susceptibility more cleanly
A plain T2 with no fat control and a very long echo time set
body.explain: Spectral fat saturation fails near metal because the field is distorted. STIR uses an inversion time to null fat and gives more uniform suppression around hardware.

body.prompt: Which sequence family is preferred over gradient echo near hardware?
options: TSE, because its refocusing pulses limit susceptibility loss
GRE, because its single pulse shortens the readout echo time
Echo planar imaging, because it fills k space very rapidly
Balanced steady state, because it maximizes the fluid signal
body.explain: TSE (turbo spin echo) applies refocusing pulses that recover signal lost to susceptibility, so it is preferred over gradient echo near metal.

body.prompt: How many vertebrae are in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions?
options: Seven cervical, twelve thoracic, and five lumbar vertebrae
Five cervical, seven thoracic, and twelve lumbar vertebrae
Twelve cervical, five thoracic, and seven lumbar vertebrae
Eight cervical, ten thoracic, and six lumbar vertebrae total
body.explain: The spine has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar vertebrae, a count used constantly when localizing levels and planning coverage.

body.title: Brain MRA and MRV: time-of-flight, coverage, and reconstructions
body.html:
Brain MRA is usually a non-contrast time-of-flight (TOF) study. The bright vessel signal comes from fresh, unsaturated blood flowing into the imaging slab, while the stationary background tissue is repeatedly saturated by the rapid pulses and stays dark. No gadolinium is needed for this contrast. A TOF angiogram can be added to a routine brain study or run on its own, and typical indications include aneurysm, brain hemorrhage, and arteriovenous malformation (AVM), which may need extra coverage to include the feeding and draining vessels.

Coverage for the arterial study runs from about the top of the corpus callosum down to the skull base, and the TOF acquisition should be kept isotropic so reformats are clean in any plane. To extend coverage, do not raise the number of slices per slab much above 40, because too many slices per slab causes the Venetian blind artifact, a stripe of signal drop at the slab boundaries. Instead, add more slabs. Reconstructions include rotating maximum intensity projections (MIPs) of the Circle of Willis plus targeted MIPs of the bilateral and individual carotid arteries. An aneurysm is best shown on TOF MRA, while an AVM or a cavernoma is better characterized on SWI or diffusion.

Brain MRV is the venous half of the vascular study and evaluates dural venous sinus thrombosis and central sinus obstruction. Venous coverage runs from the top of the skull down to below the foramen magnum. A non-contrast venogram uses a straight sagittal and a straight coronal 2D TOF acquisition, while a contrast venogram uses an axial fast 3D T1 gradient echo planned along the AC-PC line. For a contrast MRV, the pre and post series must match exactly so a MIP subtraction removes the background tissue, and the nose is cropped out of the reconstruction.
keypoints: TOF is bright because inflowing blood is unsaturated while background tissue is saturated dark, with no contrast used.
Arterial brain MRA coverage runs from the top of the corpus callosum down to the skull base and is kept isotropic.
Extend TOF coverage by adding more slabs, not more slices per slab, to avoid the Venetian blind artifact.
Aneurysm is best shown on TOF MRA, while AVM or cavernoma is better shown on SWI or diffusion.
Brain MRV evaluates dural sinus thrombosis; contrast MRV needs matched pre and post series for MIP subtraction.
body.worked_example: A technologist needs to extend a TOF brain MRA superiorly to capture the upper branches of an AVM. Rather than increasing the slices per slab to 60, which would leave dark horizontal bands where the slabs meet, the technologist keeps each slab near 40 slices and adds a second and third slab to reach the added coverage. The Circle of Willis and the malformation are then reconstructed as rotating MIPs without slab-boundary signal loss.
memory_hooks: TOF glows because inflowing blood is fresh and unsaturated, not because of dye.
More coverage means more slabs, not more slices.
Aneurysm on TOF, AVM and cavernoma on SWI.
exam_traps: To extend TOF coverage, add more slabs rather than more slices per slab, because too many slices per slab causes the Venetian blind artifact at the slab boundaries.
TOF vessels are bright because inflowing blood is unsaturated, not because contrast was given.

body.title: Neck MRA and carotid technique: contrast timing, saturation bands, and dissection
body.html:
Neck MRA indications include prior stroke or CVA, carotid stenosis or occlusion, and carotid dissection. A limited non-contrast TOF of the neck can cover just above and below the carotid bifurcation, while a full non-contrast neck MRA covers from the skull base down to the aortic arch. As with brain MRA, coverage is extended by adding slabs rather than slices per slab. Contrast-enhanced neck MRA uses a thin coronal 3D gradient echo, on the order of 1.5 mm, covering from the top of the Circle of Willis down to the aortic arch and including both carotids. Gadolinium is weight-based, and the acquisition is timed to the arterial bolus using a test bolus or a bolus-tracking method so the arteries are captured before venous contamination.

Saturation band direction sets which vessels are displayed. A saturation band placed superior to the slab, a "sat up," suppresses inflow from above and displays arterial flow, while a band placed inferior to the slab, a "sat down," displays venous flow. This is how subclavian steal is demonstrated, a condition where vertebral artery flow reverses because of a compromised subclavian artery, so the vertebral fills from the wrong direction.

Carotid dissection is a tear that lets blood track into the vessel wall. It is best shown on a pre-contrast fat-saturated T1, typically a coronal 3D T1, or an axial T1 fat-sat if the coronal fails, covering the carotids and the entire aortic arch. The classic sign is a normally dark flowing vessel with a crescent of bright signal in the wall, the intramural hematoma, at the site of the dissection. Because the finding lives in the wall and not the lumen, it is imaged before contrast is given.
keypoints: Neck MRA indications include prior stroke, carotid stenosis or occlusion, and carotid dissection.
Full non-contrast neck MRA covers from the skull base to the aortic arch, extended by adding slabs.
Contrast neck MRA is weight-based and timed to the arterial bolus so arteries fill before veins.
A superior saturation band (sat up) shows arterial flow, an inferior band (sat down) shows venous flow.
Carotid dissection is best shown on pre-contrast fat-sat T1 as a bright crescent of intramural hematoma.
body.worked_example: A patient presents with neck pain and stroke symptoms after a fall, and the radiologist suspects a carotid dissection. Before any gadolinium is given, the technologist runs a coronal 3D fat-saturated T1 covering the carotids from the skull base through the aortic arch. On the images the normally dark carotid shows a bright crescent along its wall, the intramural hematoma, confirming the dissection while the lumen still appears patent.
memory_hooks: Sat up sees arteries, sat down sees veins.
Steal means the vertebral runs backward from a bad subclavian.
Dissection is a bright crescent in the wall on fat-sat T1, done before dye.
exam_traps: A superior saturation band (sat up) shows arterial flow, while an inferior saturation band (sat down) shows venous flow.
Carotid dissection shows a bright crescent of intramural hematoma on fat-saturated T1 and is imaged before contrast.

body.prompt: In a non-contrast time-of-flight brain MRA, why do the arteries appear bright?
options: Inflowing blood is unsaturated while stationary background tissue is saturated dark
Gadolinium contrast shortens the T1 of blood within the imaged arteries
Flowing blood loses signal so vessels are darker than the tissue
Fat saturation removes marrow signal so vessels stand out brightly
body.explain: TOF relies on flow-related enhancement. Fresh, unsaturated blood flows into the slab and gives high signal, while repeatedly excited stationary tissue stays saturated and dark. No contrast is used.

body.prompt: What is the standard superior-to-inferior coverage for the arterial brain MRA?
options: From about the top of the corpus callosum down to the skull base
From the top of the skull down to below the foramen magnum
From the skull base down to the aortic arch and carotids
From above and below the carotid bifurcation only
body.explain: The arterial TOF study for the Circle of Willis runs roughly from the top of the corpus callosum to the skull base. The wider top-of-skull to below-foramen-magnum range belongs to the venous MRV study.

body.prompt: To extend TOF MRA coverage without causing the Venetian blind artifact, the technologist should do what?
options: Add more slabs while keeping the slices per slab near 40 or fewer
Increase the slices per slab well above 40 within a single slab
Remove fat saturation and widen each individual slice thickness
Switch to a single thick two-dimensional slab covering everything
body.explain: Too many slices per slab causes saturation toward the slab exit and produces the Venetian blind artifact, a signal drop at slab boundaries. Adding more slabs extends coverage while avoiding it.

body.prompt: The Venetian blind artifact in TOF MRA appears as what?
options: Bands of signal drop at the boundaries between adjacent slabs
A bright crescent of signal within the wall of a vessel
Complete loss of all arterial signal across the whole slab
Ghosting repeated along the phase-encoding direction only
body.explain: When too many slices are packed into one slab, spins saturate near the slab exit, so signal drops where slabs meet. This produces horizontal stripes resembling a Venetian blind.

body.prompt: How should the TOF acquisition voxel be set for high-quality reconstructions?
options: Isotropic, so reformats and MIPs are clean in any plane
Highly anisotropic, with thick slices and thin in-plane pixels
Two-dimensional only, with wide gaps between the slices
Weighted toward the phase direction to shorten the scan time
body.explain: Keeping the TOF voxel isotropic lets the volume be reformatted and projected in any orientation without stair-step blurring, which is essential for rotating MIPs of the Circle of Willis.

body.prompt: Which vascular lesion is best demonstrated on a TOF MRA?
options: An intracranial aneurysm arising from a Circle of Willis vessel
A cavernoma with its typical blood-product susceptibility signal
An acute infarct showing restricted diffusion of water
A chronic microbleed scattered through the white matter
body.explain: Aneurysms are luminal outpouchings well shown by the flow signal of TOF MRA. Cavernomas and microbleeds are better characterized on SWI, and infarcts on diffusion.

body.prompt: An AVM or a cavernoma is generally better characterized on which sequence?
options: SWI or diffusion, which show blood products and susceptibility
TOF MRA, which shows only the bright flowing arterial lumen
A weight-based contrast MRV with matched subtraction images
A plain sagittal two-dimensional TOF venogram of the sinuses
body.explain: SWI is sensitive to blood products and the susceptibility of a cavernoma, and diffusion adds tissue information. TOF shows flowing lumen but characterizes these lesions less well.

body.prompt: Which reconstructions are routinely produced from a brain TOF MRA?
options: Rotating MIPs of the Circle of Willis and targeted carotid MIPs
Subtraction images built from matched pre and post venous series
Fat-saturated T1 crescent views of the carotid vessel walls
Bolus-timing test images tracked at the level of the arch
body.explain: The TOF volume is reconstructed as rotating maximum intensity projections of the Circle of Willis plus targeted MIPs of the bilateral and individual carotid arteries.

body.prompt: A brain MRV is primarily performed to evaluate what?
options: Dural venous sinus thrombosis and central sinus obstruction
Carotid bifurcation stenosis and downstream arterial occlusion
A saccular aneurysm arising along the Circle of Willis
Reversed vertebral artery flow caused by subclavian steal
body.explain: The MRV evaluates the venous system, chiefly dural venous sinus thrombosis and central sinus obstruction. Stenosis, aneurysm, and subclavian steal are arterial questions.

body.prompt: For a contrast-enhanced brain MRV, why must the pre and post series match exactly?
options: So a MIP subtraction can remove the background and isolate the veins
So the arterial bolus can be timed with a tracking test scan
So the saturation band can be flipped to display arterial flow
So the slices per slab can be raised safely well above 40
body.explain: Matched geometry lets the pre series be subtracted from the post series, removing stationary background so a clean venous MIP remains. The nose is also cropped from the reconstruction.

body.prompt: Which of the following is a recognized indication for a neck MRA?
options: Carotid stenosis or dissection in a patient with prior stroke
Dural venous sinus thrombosis presenting with a headache
A microadenoma suspected on a rising serum prolactin level
An acute lacunar infarct showing bright diffusion restriction
body.explain: Neck MRA is ordered for prior stroke or CVA, carotid stenosis or occlusion, and carotid dissection. Sinus thrombosis is an MRV question, and the others are unrelated.

body.prompt: A full non-contrast neck MRA covers which superior-to-inferior range?
options: From the skull base down to the aortic arch
From the top of the corpus callosum to the skull base
From the top of the skull to below the foramen magnum
From just above to just below the carotid bifurcation
body.explain: A full neck MRA extends from the skull base to the aortic arch. A limited TOF may cover only around the bifurcation, and the other ranges describe brain arterial or venous studies.

body.prompt: How is gadolinium dosed and timed for a contrast-enhanced neck MRA?
options: Weight-based dose timed to the arterial bolus before venous filling
Fixed volume for every patient injected after the venous phase
Weight-based dose delayed until the veins have fully enhanced
Fixed volume timed to the late equilibrium washout phase
body.explain: Contrast neck MRA uses a weight-based gadolinium dose and times the thin 3D acquisition to the arterial bolus with a test bolus or bolus tracking, capturing arteries before venous contamination.

body.prompt: A saturation band placed superior to the slab (a sat up) will display which flow?
options: Arterial flow, by suppressing venous inflow coming from above
Venous flow, by suppressing arterial inflow coming from above
Both arterial and venous flow with equal signal intensity
Neither vessel, because all inflowing signal is nulled out
body.explain: A superior band saturates blood entering from above (venous return), leaving upward arterial inflow to appear bright. A sat up therefore displays arterial flow.

body.prompt: A saturation band placed inferior to the slab (a sat down) will display which flow?
options: Venous flow, by suppressing arterial inflow coming from below
Arterial flow, by suppressing venous inflow coming from below
Both venous and arterial flow at the same brightness level
Neither vessel, since inferior bands cannot affect any flow
body.explain: An inferior band saturates blood entering from below (upward arterial flow), leaving descending venous flow bright. A sat down therefore displays venous flow.

body.prompt: Subclavian steal is best described as what?
options: Reversed vertebral artery flow from a compromised subclavian artery
A tear allowing blood to track into the carotid vessel wall
Thrombosis blocking a central dural venous sinus of the brain
A saccular outpouching along a Circle of Willis artery branch
body.explain: In subclavian steal, a proximal subclavian narrowing causes vertebral artery flow to reverse and supply the arm, robbing the posterior circulation. Saturation band direction demonstrates the reversed flow.

body.prompt: Which sequence best demonstrates a suspected carotid dissection?
options: A pre-contrast fat-saturated T1 covering the carotids and the arch
A post-contrast subtracted MIP of the dural venous sinuses
A high b-value diffusion image paired with its ADC map
A rotating TOF MIP of the Circle of Willis arteries
body.explain: Dissection lives in the vessel wall, so a pre-contrast fat-saturated T1 (coronal 3D, or axial if coronal fails) covering the carotids and entire aortic arch shows the mural hematoma best.

body.prompt: On fat-saturated T1, the classic sign of a carotid dissection is what?
options: A crescent of bright intramural hematoma in the vessel wall
A band of signal drop where two adjacent slabs meet
A bright lumen from inflowing unsaturated arterial blood
A dark filling defect within an enhancing dural sinus
body.explain: The dissection tear lets blood into the wall, forming an intramural hematoma that appears as a bright crescent around a normally dark flowing lumen on fat-saturated T1, imaged before contrast.

body.title: MSK MRI protocols: shoulder, knee, hip, wrist, and foot
body.html:
The shoulder is imaged for rotator cuff tear, bursitis, and arthritis. Position the arm at the side, palm up, in external rotation supported by a sandbag, which gives a cleaner profile of the labrum without the bicipital groove overlapping. The arm should lie parallel to the chest without sagging, and if the patient cannot externally rotate, image in neutral. Coverage runs from above the sternoclavicular joint to below the glenoid. The coronal is angled perpendicular to the glenohumeral joint and the sagittal is parallel to it. The four rotator cuff muscles are Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, and Subscapularis (SITS).

The knee is imaged for pain, ACL or PCL tear, meniscal tear, torn cartilage, arthritis, and internal derangement. Center the laser at the inferior border of the patella (the apex), not the joint center. Coverage runs from the quadriceps femoris attachment above to the patellar tendon and fat pad below. The hip is imaged for pain, bursitis, avascular necrosis (AVN), and labral tear. Place the phased-array coil with its top at the iliac crest and the hip joint over a posterior coil element, and locate the hip midway between the ASIS and the greater trochanter. Tie the feet together with toes in and heels apart to hold gentle internal rotation. Axial coverage runs from a few inches above the hip joint to below the lesser trochanter.

The wrist is imaged for triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tear, carpal fracture, carpal tunnel syndrome, ganglion cyst, and ligament tear. Position with the hand overhead (the superman position) or head-first supine, and cover all the carpal bones from the carpometacarpal joints to the wrist joint. The foot and ankle protocols are forefoot or midfoot, ankle or hindfoot, and whole foot, using a foot and ankle coil, feet-first supine. Indications include pain, fracture, ligament tear, Morton neuroma, bone infection, edema, Lisfranc injury, and Achilles tendon tear.
keypoints: Shoulder: arm at the side, palm up in external rotation on a sandbag for a clean labral profile.
The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis (SITS).
Knee laser centers on the inferior border of the patella (the apex), not the joint center.
Hip coil top sits at the iliac crest; feet are tied for gentle internal rotation.
Wrist uses the superman position covering all carpals; foot and ankle coil runs feet-first supine.
body.worked_example: A patient with shoulder pain and suspected rotator cuff tear is positioned with the arm at the side, palm turned up so the shoulder sits in external rotation, and a sandbag holds the position. Because external rotation swings the bicipital groove out of the way, the labrum is profiled cleanly and the supraspinatus tendon is seen along its length. If the patient cannot tolerate external rotation, the arm is left neutral rather than forced. Coverage extends from above the sternoclavicular joint to below the glenoid.
memory_hooks: SITS spells the four rotator cuff muscles: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.
Palm up opens the labrum by turning the biceps groove out of the way.
Knee laser sits on the point of the patella, its inferior apex.
exam_traps: The knee laser is centered at the inferior border of the patella (the apex), not the joint center.
The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis.

body.title: MSK technique: fat suppression, metal reduction, and arthrograms
body.html:
Fat suppression choice matters when the field is inhomogeneous. Spectral fat-saturated T2 fails in a distorted field, so use STIR instead of fat-saturated T2 when there is metal near the area of interest, when the fat suppression looks inhomogeneous, or when unsuspected metal is causing inhomogeneity. STIR nulls fat by inversion time and is far more uniform in a distorted field.

Metal reduction escalates with the amount of metal. A small amount such as a single screw can be handled with a routine metal-reduction protocol, often at 1.5T because susceptibility artifact is smaller at lower field. A large metal implant such as a joint replacement (hip or knee) needs a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type) that corrects through-plane and in-plane distortion. An in and out of phase sequence is added when a bone tumor or marrow replacement is the question.

An MR arthrogram is a two-part procedure. First, contrast is injected directly into the joint (an intra-articular injection), then the joint is imaged. Distending the joint with fluid outlines the cartilage, labrum, and ligaments so tears and degeneration are seen. Arthrograms are performed on the shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, and ankle, and they help decide whether arthroscopy, surgery, or joint replacement is needed.
keypoints: Switch fat-saturated T2 to STIR when metal or inhomogeneous fat suppression is present.
STIR nulls fat by inversion time and stays uniform even in a distorted field.
A single screw needs routine metal reduction, often done at 1.5T for smaller susceptibility.
A joint replacement needs a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type).
An MR arthrogram injects contrast directly into the joint, then images the distended joint.
body.worked_example: A patient with a prior hip screw is scanned and the fat-saturated T2 images show patchy, uneven fat suppression around the metal. The technologist switches to STIR, which nulls fat by inversion time rather than by frequency, so the suppression becomes uniform despite the field distortion. If the same patient had a full hip replacement instead of a single screw, the routine metal-reduction protocol would not be enough, and a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type) would be used to correct the larger distortion.
memory_hooks: Metal or messy fat-sat, reach for STIR every time.
One screw is routine; a whole joint replacement needs SEMAC or MAVRIC.
Arthrogram means inject into the joint first, then image.
exam_traps: Switch from fat-saturated T2 to STIR when metal or inhomogeneous fat suppression is present.
An MR arthrogram injects contrast directly into the joint (intra-articular), not into a vein.

body.prompt: Which set of indications best fits a routine shoulder MRI?
options: Rotator cuff tear, bursitis, and arthritis of the shoulder
Tethered cord, syrinx, and cervical radiculopathy findings
Morton neuroma, Lisfranc injury, and an Achilles tendon tear
Carpal tunnel syndrome, a ganglion cyst, and a TFCC tear
body.explain: The shoulder is imaged for rotator cuff tear, bursitis, and arthritis. The other lists belong to spine, foot, and wrist protocols.

body.prompt: How is the arm positioned for a standard shoulder MRI, and why?
options: Palm up in external rotation, to profile the labrum cleanly
Palm down in internal rotation, to open the acromial arch
Elbow flexed across the chest, to relax the deltoid muscle
Arm raised overhead, to stretch the supraspinatus tendon
body.explain: The arm lies at the side, palm up in external rotation on a sandbag. External rotation swings the bicipital groove out of the way, giving a cleaner profile of the labrum.

body.prompt: What is the standard superior to inferior coverage for a shoulder MRI?
options: From above the sternoclavicular joint to below the glenoid
From the mid clavicle down to the mid shaft of the humerus
From the top of the acromion down to the deltoid insertion
From the cervical spine down to the level of the axillary fold
body.explain: Shoulder coverage runs from above the sternoclavicular joint to below the glenoid so the whole glenohumeral joint and cuff are included.

body.prompt: Which four muscles make up the rotator cuff?
options: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis
Supraspinatus, teres major, deltoid, and the coracobrachialis
Infraspinatus, teres major, pectoralis minor, and subscapularis
Deltoid, biceps brachii, teres minor, and the latissimus dorsi
body.explain: The rotator cuff is the SITS group: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. Teres major and deltoid are not part of the cuff.

body.prompt: Where is the laser centered for a routine knee MRI?
options: At the inferior border of the patella, which is the apex
At the center of the joint line between the femur and tibia
At the superior pole of the patella near the quadriceps
At the tibial tuberosity where the patellar tendon inserts
body.explain: The knee laser is centered at the inferior border of the patella, the apex, not the joint center, so coverage captures from the quadriceps attachment to the fat pad.

body.prompt: Which indications are typical reasons to order a knee MRI?
options: ACL or PCL tear, meniscal tear, and internal derangement
TFCC tear, carpal fracture, and carpal tunnel syndrome pain
Rotator cuff tear, subacromial bursitis, and biceps groove pain
Labral tear, avascular necrosis, and trochanteric bursitis pain
body.explain: The knee is imaged for pain, ACL or PCL tear, meniscal tear, torn cartilage, arthritis, and internal derangement. The other lists are wrist, shoulder, and hip indications.

body.prompt: How is the hip coil placed and the leg held for a hip MRI?
options: Coil top at the iliac crest, feet tied for internal rotation
Coil top at the greater trochanter, feet left free in neutral
Coil centered on the knee, feet tied for external rotation
Coil low over the thigh, feet crossed to abduct the joint
body.explain: The phased-array coil top sits at the iliac crest with the joint over a posterior element, and the feet are tied with toes in and heels apart to hold gentle internal rotation.

body.prompt: What is the usual axial coverage range for a hip MRI?
options: From a few inches above the joint to below the lesser trochanter
From the iliac crest down only to the top of the femoral head
From the mid femoral shaft up only to the acetabular roof
From the sacroiliac joints down to the mid femoral condyles
body.explain: Axial hip coverage runs from a few inches above the hip joint to below the lesser trochanter so the joint and proximal femur are fully included.

body.prompt: What is the superman position used for in a wrist MRI?
options: Hand overhead to cover the carpals from the CMC to the wrist
Hand at the side to cover the elbow and the distal humerus
Hand on the abdomen to shorten the distance to the coil
Hand behind the head to extend the fingers away from bone
body.explain: In the superman position the hand is placed overhead (or head-first supine), and coverage includes all the carpal bones from the carpometacarpal joints to the wrist joint.

body.prompt: How is a foot and ankle study set up, and what does it evaluate?
options: Feet-first supine in a foot coil for Morton neuroma or Lisfranc injury
Head-first supine in a knee coil for a meniscal tear or ACL injury
Feet-first prone in a body coil for a labral tear or AVN of the hip
Head-first prone in a wrist coil for a TFCC tear or carpal fracture
body.explain: Foot and ankle protocols use a dedicated foot and ankle coil, feet-first supine, for indications such as Morton neuroma, Lisfranc injury, fracture, ligament tear, and Achilles tendon tear.

body.prompt: When metal is near the area of interest, fat-saturated T2 should be replaced by what?
options: STIR, which nulls fat by inversion time and stays uniform
A spectral fat-sat T1 tuned with a very short echo time set
A gradient echo T2 star, which tolerates the distortion better
A plain T2 with no fat control and a long echo time selected
body.explain: Spectral fat saturation fails when metal distorts the field. STIR nulls fat by inversion time rather than frequency, so it stays uniform near metal.

body.prompt: The fat suppression on a fat-saturated T2 looks patchy and uneven. What is the fix?
options: Switch to STIR for more uniform suppression across the field
Raise the flip angle on the same fat-saturated T2 sequence
Add a second spectral fat-sat pulse before each readout train
Lengthen the repetition time and keep the spectral fat-sat on
body.explain: Inhomogeneous fat suppression signals a distorted or non-uniform field. STIR uses an inversion time to null fat and gives far more uniform suppression than spectral fat-sat.

body.prompt: A patient has a single small screw in the area of interest. What protocol fits?
options: A routine metal-reduction protocol, often performed at 1.5T
A dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence for large implants
A standard gradient echo protocol with no metal adjustments made
An intra-articular arthrogram before any metal-reduction imaging
body.explain: A small amount of metal such as a single screw is handled with a routine metal-reduction protocol. A dedicated sequence is reserved for large implants.

body.prompt: A patient has a full joint replacement. Which approach is needed?
options: A dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence, a SEMAC or MAVRIC type
A routine metal-reduction protocol run at a slightly higher field
A plain fat-saturated T2 with the receive bandwidth turned down
A gradient echo sequence chosen to bloom and mark the implant
body.explain: A large implant such as a hip or knee replacement needs a dedicated metal-artifact-reduction sequence (a SEMAC or MAVRIC type) that corrects through-plane and in-plane distortion.

body.prompt: Why is a metal-reduction study often performed at 1.5T rather than a higher field?
options: Susceptibility artifact is smaller at the lower field strength
Signal to noise is always far higher at the lower field strength
Fat and water separate more widely at the lower field strength
Scan times are much shorter at the lower field strength setting
body.explain: Susceptibility artifact scales with field strength, so it is smaller at 1.5T. That is why metal-reduction imaging is often done at the lower field.

body.prompt: When a bone tumor or marrow replacement is the question, which sequence is added?
options: An in and out of phase sequence to characterize the marrow
A time of flight angiogram to map the feeding tumor vessels
A diffusion tensor sequence to trace the marrow fiber tracts
A phase contrast flow study to quantify the marrow perfusion
body.explain: An in and out of phase sequence is added when a bone tumor or marrow replacement is the question, because it helps show replacement of normal marrow fat.

body.prompt: In an MR arthrogram, where is the contrast placed?
options: Directly into the joint, which is an intra-articular injection
Into a peripheral vein, which is a standard venous injection
Into the joint space by way of the arterial blood supply first
Into the muscle beside the joint, which is an intramuscular route
body.explain: An MR arthrogram injects contrast directly into the joint, an intra-articular injection, not into a vein. The distended joint outlines cartilage, labrum, and ligaments.

body.prompt: What are the two parts of an MR arthrogram procedure?
options: Inject contrast into the joint first, then image the joint
Image the joint first, then inject contrast into a vein after
Inject contrast into a vein first, then aspirate the joint fluid
Image the joint twice, once before and once after oral contrast
body.explain: An MR arthrogram is a two-part procedure. Contrast is injected directly into the joint first, and then the distended joint is imaged.

body.prompt: What kind of injuries does an MR arthrogram best demonstrate?
options: Labral, TFCC, or cartilage tears outlined by the joint fluid
Bony metastases spreading through the vertebral marrow spaces
Cerebrospinal fluid leaks tracking along the nerve root sleeves
Muscle strains and deep hematomas within the soft tissue planes
body.explain: Distending the joint with contrast outlines the cartilage, labrum, and ligaments, so labral, TFCC, and cartilage tears and degeneration are clearly demonstrated.

body.prompt: How is the coronal plane oriented on a shoulder MRI?
options: Angled perpendicular to the glenohumeral joint for the labrum
Angled parallel to the glenohumeral joint along the scapula
Held straight in the true body coronal without any joint angle
Angled parallel to the acromion to profile the deltoid muscle
body.explain: The shoulder coronal is angled perpendicular to the glenohumeral joint, while the sagittal is angled parallel to it, so the cuff and labrum are seen in profile.

body.title: Body MRI protocols: liver, MRCP, and abdomen/pelvis coverage
body.html:
Dedicated liver MRI is ordered for suspected hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis surveillance, hemangioma characterization, fatty liver, and hepatitis. The patient lies supine with the liver positioned over the posterior spine coil elements and an anterior phased-array body coil placed on top. Whatever the indication, the prescribed slices must cover the entire liver, from the dome down past the inferior tip. A lesion you cannot see is a lesion you cannot report.
