Spins at different positions along its axis precess at different rates while it is on, and when it switches off they keep a position-dependent phase shift. The gradient is stepped to a different amplitude every TR, and each step writes one line of the raw data matrix. Finally the frequency-encode (readout) gradient runs during the echo itself, so that signal frequency encodes position along the third axis while the echo is digitized.

That raw data matrix is k-space. It is a map of spatial frequencies, not a picture. The central lines hold the low spatial frequencies: bulk signal, overall brightness, and contrast. The peripheral lines hold the high spatial frequencies: edges and fine detail. Every point in k-space contains signal from the entire slice.

Once every planned line is filled, a two-dimensional Fourier transform converts k-space into the image, turning spatial frequencies into pixel intensities. Excite, encode, sample, repeat per TR, transform: that is how every 2D image is built.
keypoints: The slice-select gradient is on during the RF pulse; only spins whose local Larmor frequency matches the RF are excited.
Slice thickness is set by the RF bandwidth and the steepness of the slice-select gradient.
The phase-encode gradient is a brief pulse after excitation, stepped to a new amplitude every TR; each step fills one line of k-space.
The frequency-encode (readout) gradient is on during the echo, so frequency encodes position while the echo is sampled.
k-space center holds contrast and bulk signal (low spatial frequencies); the periphery holds edges and fine detail; a 2D Fourier transform reconstructs the image.
body.worked_example: You run an axial brain series with 192 phase-encode steps. Each TR, the z gradient switches on with the RF pulse to excite the chosen slice, a phase-encode blip along right-left takes a new amplitude, and the readout gradient along anterior-posterior runs while the echo is sampled. After 192 TRs the 192 lines of k-space are full and the scanner Fourier transforms them into the image. The patient coughs halfway through, right when the central lines are being acquired. Because those lines carry the low spatial frequencies for the whole slice, the result is not a smudge at one spot but degraded contrast and ghosting across the entire image.
memory_hooks: Slice with the RF, phase in between, frequency while you listen.
Center of k-space = contrast; corners = crisp edges.
One TR, one phase step, one line.
exam_traps: The slice-select gradient is on during the RF pulse and the readout gradient is on during the echo; swapping the two is the classic error.
k-space center = contrast and signal, periphery = fine detail. Exams love to reverse them.
k-space is raw spatial-frequency data, not a scrambled photo: no single k-space point maps to a single pixel.

body.title: The image-formation pipeline: excite, encode, sample, reconstruct
body.html:
Every MR image, whatever the sequence name on the console, is built by the same loop. Excite the chosen slice with an RF pulse while the slice-select gradient is on. Encode the signal spatially: a phase-encode step, then frequency encoding during the readout. Sample the echo into one line of k-space. Repeat every TR with a new phase-encode amplitude until k-space is full, then reconstruct with the Fourier transform. Sequences differ mainly in how they form the echo that gets sampled.

A gradient echo sequence forms its echo by reversing the polarity of the readout gradient: the first lobe dephases the spins, the flipped lobe rephases them. There is no 180 degree pulse, so the signal decays with T2*, and the excitation typically uses a flip angle under 90 degrees, which leaves longitudinal magnetization in reserve and allows a very short TR.

A spin echo sequence forms its echo with a 180 degree refocusing pulse applied after the excitation. Inversion recovery adds a different 180: a preparatory inversion pulse placed before the excitation. After the inversion, the sequence waits a chosen time so that one tissue's longitudinal magnetization is crossing zero at the moment of excitation, and that tissue gives no signal. STIR uses this to null fat, FLAIR to null CSF.

Keep the two 180s apart: the inversion 180 prepares the magnetization before excitation, while the spin-echo 180 refocuses it afterward. And whatever the echo mechanism, they all end the same way: fill k-space, then reconstruct with a Fourier transform. A conventional scan fills one phase-encode line per TR; a fast or turbo scan fills several lines per TR (an echo train), which is how it saves time.
keypoints: Pipeline: excite the slice, phase then frequency encode, sample the echo into k-space, repeat per TR, Fourier transform to reconstruct.
Gradient echo forms its echo by reversing the readout gradient: no 180 degree pulse, T2* decay, flip angle usually under 90 degrees.
Spin echo forms its echo with a 180 degree refocusing pulse applied after the excitation.
Inversion recovery adds a preparatory 180 degree inversion before the excitation; the nulled tissue is excited at its zero crossing (STIR nulls fat, FLAIR nulls CSF).
Whatever the echo mechanism, the filled k-space is reconstructed with a Fourier transform; a conventional scan fills one phase-encode line per TR, a fast or turbo scan several (an echo train).
body.worked_example: You start a brain exam with a gradient-echo localizer: no refocusing pulse and a small flip angle let the TR drop to a few milliseconds, so the scout finishes in seconds, though the patient's dental work blooms because nothing refocuses the local field errors. Next comes a spin echo series, where a 180 degree pulse after each excitation forms the echo. Then the FLAIR: now a 180 degree inversion goes in before each excitation, with the wait time chosen so CSF is at its zero crossing and comes out black. Three different echo mechanisms, yet all three fill the same k-space matrix line by line and hand the filled matrix to the Fourier transform.
memory_hooks: GRE flips gradients, SE flips spins, IR flips first.
Excite, encode, sample, repeat, transform.
exam_traps: Gradient echo forms its echo by gradient reversal; there is no refocusing pulse in it to remove.
The inversion 180 comes before the excitation as preparation; the spin-echo 180 comes after it to refocus. Two different pulses, two different jobs.
One phase-encode line per TR is only the conventional case: a fast or turbo spin echo fills several lines per TR (an echo train), which is how it shortens the scan.

body.prompt: Which gradient is switched on at the same time as the RF excitation pulse?
options: The slice-select gradient
The phase-encode gradient
The frequency-encode gradient
The rewinder gradient
body.explain: The slice-select gradient runs with the RF pulse so that only one plane of tissue is on resonance. The phase and frequency gradients come later, after the slice is already excited.

body.prompt: An RF pulse applied while the slice-select gradient is on excites only one slice because:
options: only spins at that location precess at the RF frequency
only spins at that location align with the main field
the gradient shields the other slices from the RF energy
the receive coil is sensitive to that location alone
body.explain: With the gradient on, Larmor frequency varies along the patient, and the RF pulse tips only the spins whose frequency matches its own. Field alignment and coil sensitivity are the same for every slice, so neither can select one.

body.prompt: With the RF bandwidth unchanged, making the slice-select gradient steeper produces:
options: a thinner slice
a thicker slice
a noisier image
a brighter image
body.explain: A steeper gradient spreads Larmor frequencies over a shorter distance, so the fixed RF bandwidth maps onto a thinner band of tissue. A thicker slice would need a flatter gradient or a wider bandwidth.

body.prompt: The brief phase-encode gradient pulse leaves spins along its axis with:
options: a position-dependent phase shift
a position-dependent flip angle
a position-dependent T1 change
a position-dependent coil gain
body.explain: While the gradient is on, spins at different positions precess at different rates; when it switches off they keep a phase shift that tags their position. An encoding gradient changes neither flip angle nor T1.

body.prompt: In a standard 2D acquisition, each TR period fills how much of k-space?
options: One line
One pixel
One quadrant
The whole matrix
body.explain: Each TR acquires one echo under one phase-encode setting, which writes exactly one k-space line. Filling the whole matrix takes as many TRs as there are phase-encode steps.

body.prompt: A patient moves during the TRs that sample the central lines of k-space. The damage mainly appears in:
options: overall image contrast
fine edge detail only
the number of slices
the receiver bandwidth
body.explain: The central lines carry the low spatial frequencies that set overall contrast and brightness, so corrupting them degrades the whole image. Fine edges live in the periphery and would suffer if motion hit the outer lines instead.

body.prompt: A single data point in k-space represents:
options: one spatial frequency summed from the whole slice
one pixel at the same position in the final image
one slice location along the selection gradient
one coil element's share of the total signal
body.explain: Every k-space point stores the strength of one spatial frequency contributed by the entire slice, which is why k-space looks nothing like the picture. There is no one-to-one link between a k-space point and an image pixel.

body.prompt: Within one TR of a 2D sequence, the correct order of gradient events is:
options: slice-select, then phase-encode, then frequency-encode
phase-encode, then slice-select, then frequency-encode
frequency-encode, then phase-encode, then slice-select
phase-encode, then frequency-encode, then slice-select
body.explain: The slice-select gradient runs with the RF pulse, the phase-encode blip follows the excitation, and the frequency-encode gradient runs during the echo. This timing repeats every TR.

body.prompt: Which order matches the image-formation pipeline for one slice?
options: Excite, encode, sample the echo, reconstruct
Encode, excite, sample the echo, reconstruct
Reconstruct, excite, encode, sample the echo
Sample the echo, encode, excite, reconstruct
body.explain: The slice is excited first, spatial encoding is applied to the excited signal, the echo is sampled into k-space, and reconstruction happens last. There is no signal to encode or sample before the excitation.

body.prompt: The Fourier transform can reconstruct the image only after:
options: every planned k-space line has been sampled
the longitudinal magnetization fully recovers
the transverse magnetization fully decays
the gradients have returned to their baseline
body.explain: Reconstruction needs the complete set of spatial frequencies, so the transform waits until every planned line is in k-space. Relaxation happens every TR and is not what gates reconstruction.

body.prompt: During the readout period, the scanner's receiver digitises:
options: the echo, stored as one line of k-space
the RF excitation pulse as it is applied
the full image, one pixel at a time
the gradient waveform for that TR
body.explain: The receiver samples the echo while the readout gradient runs, and those samples become one k-space line. The scanner never digitises the image directly; the image exists only after the Fourier transform.

body.prompt: A gradient-echo sequence forms its echo by:
options: reversing the polarity of the readout gradient
applying a second RF pulse at half the TE
waiting for T1 recovery to rebuild the signal
stepping the phase-encode gradient amplitude
body.explain: Gradient echo dephases the spins with one readout lobe and rephases them with the flipped lobe, so no second RF pulse is needed. An RF pulse at half the TE describes spin echo, not gradient echo.

body.prompt: Compared with the 90 degree excitation of spin echo, gradient-echo sequences typically use:
options: a flip angle below 90 degrees
a flip angle above 90 degrees
a pair of 180 degree pulses
no excitation pulse at all
body.explain: Gradient echo usually excites with less than 90 degrees, which leaves longitudinal magnetization in reserve and allows a very short TR. Larger flip angles or paired 180s belong to other sequence types.

body.prompt: Which sequence family forms its echo with an RF refocusing pulse rather than a gradient reversal?
options: Spin echo
Gradient echo
Spoiled gradient echo
Balanced gradient echo
body.explain: Spin echo refocuses the signal with a 180 degree RF pulse. All the gradient-echo variants listed form their echoes by reversing the readout gradient instead.

body.prompt: In inversion recovery, the 180 degree pulse placed before the excitation serves to:
options: invert magnetization so a chosen tissue can be nulled
refocus dephasing so the echo forms exactly at TE
double the transverse signal before the readout
excite two slices at once to halve the scan time
body.explain: The inversion pulse flips magnetization negative before the excitation, and waiting the right time lets one tissue reach zero so it gives no signal. Refocusing at TE is the job of the spin-echo 180, a separate pulse with a different purpose.

body.prompt: STIR and FLAIR make their target tissue dark by timing the excitation:
options: when the tissue's longitudinal magnetization is zero
when the tissue's longitudinal recovery is complete
when the tissue's transverse magnetization peaks
when the tissue's resonant frequency is suppressed
body.explain: A tissue excited at the moment its inverted longitudinal magnetization crosses zero has nothing to tip into the transverse plane, so it appears black. If recovery were complete the tissue would be bright, not dark.

body.prompt: In a 3D volumetric acquisition, wrap-around along the slice-select (partition) direction is prevented by:
options: Oversampling in the slice-encode direction so tissue outside the slab does not fold into it
Lowering the receive bandwidth to widen the range of frequencies sampled at each partition
Shortening the echo time so that fewer partitions are needed to fill the excited slab
Raising the flip angle to saturate the signal from tissue beyond the edges of the slab
body.explain: A 3D acquisition phase-encodes the slice direction, so anatomy beyond the excited slab can alias onto the end partitions. Slice-direction oversampling extends encoding past the slab edges and discards the extra partitions, removing the wrap. Bandwidth, TE, and flip angle do not address slice-direction aliasing.

body.prompt: Compared with a single 2D slice, a 3D acquisition that phase-encodes the slice direction increases scan time mainly because:
options: Each partition adds a full set of phase-encoding steps, so the second phase axis multiplies the acquisition
The whole slab must be re-shimmed between every repetition to keep the partitions aligned
A longer echo time is forced on every partition to allow the slab to be excited fully
The receiver has to sample each frequency point several extra times to reach the same resolution
body.explain: 3D scan time is TR times the in-plane phase-encode steps times the number of slice-encode partitions (times NEX). The extra slice phase-encode loop multiplies acquisition time, which is why 3D usually pairs with short-TR gradient echo. Re-shimming, TE, and oversampled readout are not the reason.

body.prompt: Why can a 3D acquisition produce contiguous slices with no interslice gap, unlike a typical 2D acquisition?
options: The slab is partitioned by phase encoding rather than by separate selective excitations, so partitions do not need a gap to avoid cross-talk
The 3D readout gradient is strong enough to prevent any overlap between neighbouring slices
3D sequences are always run with a much longer TR, which lets each adjacent slice fully recover its longitudinal magnetization before the next excitation
The Fourier transform automatically inserts blank partitions between the reconstructed slices
body.explain: In 3D the slab is excited once and divided into partitions by a second phase-encoding gradient, so there is no imperfect slice profile overlapping a neighbour and no gap is needed. 2D uses separate selective excitations whose profiles overlap, which is why a gap or interleaving is used. Readout strength, TR, and the transform do not create the gap-free partitions.

body.prompt: A 3D acquisition tends to have higher SNR than an equivalent 2D acquisition mainly because:
options: Signal is collected from the entire slab on every excitation and averaged over all the slice-encode steps
The excited slab undergoes far less T2 decay than the individual 2D slices experience during their own separate readout windows
3D imaging uses a much larger voxel, which always raises the signal it receives
Gradient spoiling is unnecessary in 3D, so no transverse signal is ever discarded
body.explain: Because a 3D sequence excites and samples the whole slab for every slice-encode step, signal is effectively averaged over all partitions, giving an SNR gain that scales with the square root of the number of partitions. Larger voxels would raise SNR but are not the mechanism here, and the T2 and spoiling statements are incorrect.

body.prompt: In a contrast-enhanced 3D MR angiogram, a mask subtraction is performed by:
options: Subtracting a precontrast 3D data set from the postcontrast set so that only enhancing vessels remain
Removing every second partition from the postcontrast set to suppress the background tissue
Inverting the k-space of the postcontrast set before the Fourier transform to cancel the fat
Applying a saturation band over the aorta so that arterial inflow is nulled on the mask
body.explain: Subtraction MRA acquires a precontrast mask and a postcontrast set with identical geometry, then subtracts them so stationary background cancels and only the gadolinium-filled vessels remain. Dropping partitions, inverting k-space, and saturation bands do not produce a subtraction angiogram.

body.prompt: Reformatting a data set into an arbitrary oblique plane keeps full spatial resolution only when the source acquisition is:
options: 3D with isotropic voxels, because equal dimensions in all three axes reformat without blurring
2D with a large slice gap, because the gaps give the reformat room to interpolate cleanly
2D with thick slices, because thicker slices carry more signal into the reformatted plane
3D with a very high receive bandwidth, because bandwidth sets the through-plane resolution
body.explain: Isotropic 3D voxels have the same size along every axis, so a reformat in any plane preserves resolution. Thick 2D slices reformat poorly because the through-plane dimension is coarse and the oblique plane blurs. Slice gap and receive bandwidth do not give clean multiplanar reformats.

body.prompt: A balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) sequence is often run as a 3D acquisition because it:
options: Uses a very short TR with high signal, so the many partitions of a 3D slab can be collected quickly
Is immune to banding artifact, so field inhomogeneity across the slab never matters
Requires no gradient spoiling, which means it cannot be used for 2D imaging at all
Produces pure T1 weighting, which only becomes visible in a volumetric acquisition
body.explain: bSSFP has a very short TR and high signal efficiency, which suits the many slice-encode steps of a 3D slab and keeps total time reasonable. It is actually prone to banding from B0 inhomogeneity, can be run in 2D, and gives mixed T2/T1 contrast rather than pure T1.

body.prompt: In a 3D data set, k-space is filled along:
options: One frequency-encode axis and two phase-encode axes, one in-plane and one for the partitions
Three frequency-encode axes, one for each spatial dimension of the excited slab
One phase-encode axis only, with the other two directions taken from the readout
Two frequency-encode axes and a single phase-encode axis shared across all partitions
body.explain: A 3D acquisition frequency-encodes one axis and phase-encodes the other two, the in-plane phase direction and the slice (partition) direction, so k-space is a 3D matrix. The other options misstate how the three axes are encoded.

body.prompt: A drawback of STIR compared with spectral (chemical) fat saturation is that STIR:
options: Suppresses any tissue whose T1 is near that of fat, so enhancing tissue and some blood products are also nulled
Depends heavily on a uniform main magnetic field and fails badly wherever the field is inhomogeneous
Cannot be used at low field strength because the fat and water peaks are then too far apart
Requires a very long echo time, which unavoidably makes the whole sequence heavily T1 weighted
body.explain: STIR nulls signal based on T1, not on chemical frequency, so it is not tissue-specific: anything with a T1 near fat's is also suppressed, including gadolinium-enhancing tissue and some hemorrhage. Field uniformity dependence describes spectral sat, and the low-field and echo-time statements are wrong.

body.prompt: A practical advantage of the Dixon method over spectral fat saturation is that Dixon:
options: Tolerates field inhomogeneity better and yields water, fat, in-phase and opposed-phase images from one acquisition
Needs no reference to the fat and water resonant frequencies at all, so it can even be applied to nonproton imaging studies
Suppresses fat using a single inversion pulse and therefore takes much less time to run
Removes chemical-shift artifact by lowering the receive bandwidth used during the readout
body.explain: Dixon reconstructs water and fat from in-phase and opposed-phase data, so it is more robust to B0 inhomogeneity than frequency-selective saturation and produces four image sets at once. It still relies on the fat and water frequency difference, does not use an inversion pulse, and does not work by changing bandwidth.

body.prompt: The resonant frequency difference between fat and water protons is about 3.5 ppm, which at 1.5 T corresponds to roughly:
options: 220 Hz, and it roughly doubles to about 440 Hz at 3 T because the difference scales with field strength
70 Hz, and it stays the same at 3 T because a chemical shift in ppm is independent of the field
1000 Hz, and it falls to about 500 Hz at 3 T because higher fields narrow the separation
15 Hz, and it is far too small to be exploited by any frequency-selective saturation pulse
body.explain: At 1.5 T (about 64 MHz) a 3.5 ppm shift is roughly 220 Hz, and because the shift in hertz scales with field strength it roughly doubles to 440 Hz at 3 T. This larger separation is why spectral fat saturation is easier at higher field. The other values and their field dependence are incorrect.

body.prompt: On a 1.5 T gradient echo, fat and water signals are opposed in phase (India-ink boundary) at an echo time near:
options: 2.2 ms, with the two returning in phase near 4.4 ms as they precess back together
10 ms, with the two returning in phase near 20 ms after further dephasing
0.5 ms, with the two returning in phase near 1.0 ms during the first readout
50 ms, with the two never returning in phase because T2 star decay has removed the signal
body.explain: Fat and water differ by about 220 Hz at 1.5 T, so they are opposed in phase near 2.2 ms and back in phase near 4.4 ms. These in and opposed phase echo times halve at 3 T. The larger echo-time values given in the distractors do not match the fat-water beat period.

body.prompt: SPAIR and SPIR improve on a simple frequency-selective fat-saturation pulse mainly by:
options: Using a spectrally selective inversion that is more tolerant of B1 (transmit) nonuniformity than a plain saturation pulse
Nulling fat purely by its T1, so no knowledge of the fat frequency is needed at all
Acquiring two separate echoes so that the fat and water signals can be separated arithmetically after the scan is complete
Applying the fat pulse only to the center of k-space, which halves the added scan time
body.explain: SPAIR (and SPIR) use a spectrally selective inversion of fat, and the adiabatic version is relatively insensitive to B1 nonuniformity, giving more uniform suppression than a plain saturation pulse. They remain frequency-selective (unlike STIR), do not separate echoes arithmetically (that is Dixon), and are not limited to the center of k-space.

body.prompt: Fat stays relatively bright on fast (turbo) spin echo compared with conventional spin echo because:
options: The closely spaced refocusing pulses disrupt J-coupling in fat, which slows its T2 decay and keeps it bright
The long echo train lets fat recover far more of its longitudinal magnetization in between each of the successive echoes
Fast spin echo uses a much shorter effective TE, so little fat signal is ever lost
The multiple echoes average out the fat signal, which raises its apparent brightness
body.explain: The train of closely spaced 180 degree pulses in fast spin echo interferes with the J-coupling that normally speeds fat's T2 decay, so fat retains signal and appears brighter than on conventional spin echo. This is a common reason fat suppression is added to FSE. The recovery, effective-TE, and averaging explanations are incorrect.

body.prompt: First-order gradient moment nulling (flow compensation) corrects the phase of spins that are:
options: Moving at a constant velocity, leaving higher-order motion such as acceleration uncorrected
Completely stationary, so that only the fixed background tissue is rephased at the echo
Accelerating rapidly, which is the only motion that a first-order correction can address
Moving in random directions, so that fully turbulent flow is rephased at the readout
body.explain: Nulling the first gradient moment rephases spins moving at constant velocity, so flow-related dephasing from steady flow is corrected while acceleration and higher-order motion are not. Stationary spins are already rephased without it, and turbulent (random) flow is not corrected by a first-order scheme.

body.prompt: On a symmetric multi-echo spin echo sequence, even-echo rephasing describes how flowing spins:
options: Regain phase coherence on the even-numbered echoes, so those echoes show less flow-related signal loss
Lose all coherence by the second echo, so that the even echoes are always darker than the odd ones
Are fully saturated after the first echo, so that no vascular signal remains on any of the later echoes
Shift position between echoes, so the vessel appears in a slightly different place on each even echo
body.explain: With symmetric echo spacing, the phase that constant-velocity spins accumulate is undone on the even echoes, so flowing blood regains coherence and shows less signal loss there. It is a rephasing, not a saturation or a spatial shift, and it makes even echoes brighter for flow, not darker.

body.prompt: To reduce ghosting from blood flowing into the imaging volume, a spatial saturation band is best placed:
options: On the side the unwanted blood flows in from, so it is saturated before it enters the imaged slab
Directly over the region of interest, so the pulsing vessel inside it is nulled along with the ghosts
As far away from the vessel as possible, so that the saturation pulse cannot disturb the imaged anatomy
Only along the frequency-encode direction, since that is where the flow ghosts always propagate
body.explain: A pre-saturation band is placed on the side from which the unwanted blood enters (for example superior to the slab for descending venous flow), so the inflowing spins are already saturated and produce no ghost. Placing it over the region would null the anatomy, distance defeats the purpose, and flow ghosts propagate along phase, not frequency.

body.prompt: Increasing the number of signal averages (NEX) tends to reduce pulsatile flow ghosting because:
options: Averaging repeated acquisitions lowers the ghost intensity relative to the consistent true signal
A higher NEX shortens the total scan time, giving the pulsating vessel much less time to move
The extra averages move the ghosts into the frequency-encode direction, where they are hidden
Averaging raises the effective receive bandwidth, which spreads the ghost energy out of the image
body.explain: Ghosts arise from view-to-view inconsistency, so averaging several acquisitions reinforces the consistent stationary signal while the variable ghost contribution partly cancels, lowering ghost intensity. Higher NEX lengthens rather than shortens the scan, and it does not change the ghost direction or the bandwidth.

body.prompt: Respiratory compensation for body imaging can be achieved with all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Raising the flip angle so that the moving abdominal wall tissue no longer contributes any signal
A bellows that reorders phase encoding to the respiratory cycle (respiratory-ordered phase encoding)
A navigator echo that tracks diaphragm position and accepts data only within a set gating window
A breath-hold acquisition that is fast enough to freeze respiratory motion within a single hold
body.explain: Respiratory-ordered phase encoding (bellows), navigator echoes, and breath-holding all reduce respiratory motion artifact. Simply raising the flip angle does not suppress moving-tissue signal or compensate for breathing, so it is the exception.

body.prompt: Pseudogating, which can reduce pulsation ghosts without any physiologic monitor, occurs when the:
options: Repetition time happens to fall close to a multiple of the patient's cardiac cycle length
Echo time is set exactly equal to the duration of one full cardiac cycle of the patient
Receive bandwidth is deliberately matched to the frequency of the arterial pulsation
Slice thickness is chosen to be equal to the diameter of the pulsating vessel imaged
body.explain: If the TR coincides with (a multiple of) the cardiac period, each phase-encode view is sampled at the same point in the pulse cycle, so flow looks consistent and ghosting drops, effectively gating by accident. TE, bandwidth, and slice thickness do not create this effect.

body.prompt: Pulsatile flow ghosts appear as discrete repeating copies whose spacing along the phase-encode axis depends chiefly on the:
options: Ratio of the pulsation period to the repetition time, together with the number of phase-encode steps
Strength of the frequency-encode gradient that is used during the sampling of each echo
Overall receive bandwidth, which sets how far apart the copies fall in the readout direction
Absolute field strength of the magnet, which fixes the ghost spacing regardless of timing
body.explain: Because motion modulates the phase-encoded views, the ghost spacing is governed by how the pulsation period relates to the TR and the number of phase-encode steps. Readout gradient strength and bandwidth act in the frequency direction, and field strength does not set the ghost spacing.

body.prompt: Under the ASTM labeling system, an item marked MR Safe is one that:
options: Poses no known hazard in any MR environment because it is nonconducting, nonmetallic and nonmagnetic
Is safe only within the specific field strength and conditions that are printed on its label
May be taken to the bore as long as it stays outside the 5-gauss line at all times
Has been shown to be safe in a 1.5 T scanner but has not yet been tested at 3 T
body.explain: MR Safe (green square) means the object is nonconducting, nonmetallic and nonmagnetic and poses no known hazard in all MR environments. An item safe only under stated conditions is MR Conditional, and the field-strength and gauss-line statements describe conditional or unlabeled items.

body.prompt: An item labeled MR Unsafe is best described as one that:
options: Poses a known hazard in all MR environments and must be kept out of the scanner room
Is hazardous only at 3 T but may still be used safely at 1.5 T with careful monitoring
May enter the room provided that it is secured well outside the bore during scanning
Has simply not yet been tested and should therefore be treated cautiously until it is
body.explain: MR Unsafe (red circle with a bar) means the item is known to pose a hazard in all MR environments, such as a ferromagnetic oxygen cylinder, and it must never enter the scanner room. An untested item is unlabeled, not MR Unsafe, and the field-strength and bore statements are wrong.

body.prompt: The specific conditions printed on an MR Conditional implant label typically include all of the following EXCEPT the:
options: Ambient room temperature that must be maintained throughout the entire examination
Maximum static field strength, such as 1.5 T or 3 T, at which it was demonstrated safe
Maximum spatial field gradient that the device may be exposed to in the fringe field
Limit on RF power (SAR) and sometimes a restriction on the total scanning time
body.explain: MR Conditional labeling specifies the static field strength, the maximum spatial field gradient, and RF (SAR) and timing limits that must all be met. Room temperature for the patient is not one of the stated implant conditions, so it is the exception.

body.prompt: A worker who grinds metal reports possible metal fragments in the eye. Before an MRI, the appropriate screening step is:
options: Obtain orbital radiographs to exclude a ferromagnetic foreign body before entering the magnet
Proceed directly to scanning because a fragment that small simply cannot move inside the eye
Flush the eyes with saline, which will safely remove any metal before the examination begins
Use a handheld magnet near the face to confirm whether any fragment present is ferromagnetic
body.explain: A history of metal grinding raises the risk of an intraocular ferromagnetic foreign body, which can move and damage the eye in the magnet. Orbital radiographs are the standard screen. Saline flushing does not remove an embedded fragment, and a handheld magnet near a possible ocular fragment is dangerous.

body.prompt: Level 2 MR personnel differ from Level 1 personnel in that they have:
options: More extensive safety training, allowing them to make decisions about screening and Zone III and IV access
Completed only a basic safety orientation and must always be escorted while inside the scanner room
Authorization to enter the room only after every patient examination has been finished for the day
Clearance limited strictly to the control room that never extends into the magnet room itself at all
body.explain: Level 2 personnel have broader MR safety training and can take responsibility for screening and for controlling access to the restricted Zones III and IV. Basic orientation with supervision describes Level 1 personnel, and the other options misstate their access.

body.prompt: The translational (attractive) force that pulls a ferromagnetic object toward the bore is driven mainly by the:
options: Spatial gradient of the static fringe field, which is steepest around the mouth of the bore
Uniform static field at isocenter, where the field is strongest and the most homogeneous
Switching of the imaging gradients that are used for spatial encoding during the scan
Radiofrequency field transmitted by the body coil during each excitation pulse of the scan
body.explain: Translational force depends on the spatial gradient of the static field (how fast the field changes with position), which is greatest in the fringe field near the bore opening, not on the uniform field at isocenter. Imaging gradients and the RF field do not produce the projectile effect.

body.prompt: An elongated ferromagnetic object near isocenter experiences torque, which tends to:
options: Rotate the object so that its long axis comes into alignment with the main magnetic field
Pull the object in a straight line toward the nearest wall of the magnet room
Heat the object very rapidly through radiofrequency currents induced within it
Push the object outward toward the low-field region that lies beyond the bore
body.explain: Torque rotates an elongated ferromagnetic object to align its long axis with B0 and is greatest where the field is strong and uniform, near isocenter. Translational pull toward walls is the separate projectile force, and heating and outward push are not torque effects.

body.prompt: The elevated T wave sometimes seen on an ECG trace inside the magnet is caused by the:
options: Magnetohydrodynamic effect, a voltage induced as conductive blood flows through the static field
Onset of a genuine cardiac arrhythmia that requires the scan to be stopped right away
Radiofrequency pulses of the running sequence directly stimulating the heart muscle
Gradient switching that induces peripheral nerve stimulation across the chest wall
body.explain: Blood is a conductor, so as it flows through the static field a voltage is induced (the magnetohydrodynamic effect) that augments the T wave on the ECG. It is a benign artifact, not a true arrhythmia, and it is unrelated to RF stimulation or gradient nerve stimulation.

body.prompt: Brief flashes of light (magnetophosphenes) that a patient may notice are produced by:
options: Rapidly switching gradients (dB/dt) stimulating the retina, and they stop when the gradients do
The static magnetic field slowly warming the vitreous of the eye during a long acquisition
Radiofrequency energy that deposits heat in the optic nerve at high SAR levels
Cryogen vapor briefly entering the bore and irritating the surface of the eye
body.explain: Magnetophosphenes are transient visual flashes from rapidly changing gradient fields (dB/dt) stimulating the retina; they cease when gradient activity stops and are harmless. The static field, RF heating, and cryogen vapor do not cause them.

body.prompt: A skin-to-skin contact point, such as clasped hands or crossed calves, is a burn risk during scanning because it can:
options: Form a closed conductive loop in which the changing fields induce a current that heats the tissue
Focus the static magnetic field down to a single point and freeze the tissue at that spot
Block the gradient fields so that the surrounding tissue then receives a much larger dose
Reflect the radiofrequency pulse back into the coil and damage the transmit hardware
body.explain: Skin-to-skin contact can close a conductive loop; the time-varying RF and gradient fields then induce a current in that loop that heats the tissue and can burn it. Padding to break the contact prevents it. The static-field, gradient-blocking, and RF-reflection explanations are incorrect.

body.prompt: To reduce the risk of a burn from a surface coil or ECG lead cable, the technologist should:
options: Keep cables straight and insulated, avoiding loops and direct contact with the patient's skin
Coil the excess cable neatly into several loops and rest them against the patient's skin
Run every one of the cables across the bare skin so that heat can dissipate more quickly
Cross the cables over one another so that any induced current is spread between them
body.explain: Cables should run straight, be insulated from skin, and never be looped, because loops and skin contact allow induced currents to concentrate and burn. Coiling, skin contact, and crossing cables all increase the burn risk.

body.prompt: The most immediate life-threatening hazard when helium vents into the scanner room during a quench is:
options: Displacement of the oxygen in the room by the expanding gas, which can cause asphyxiation
A sudden strengthening of the static field as the coil rapidly loses its liquid coolant
An electric shock delivered through the magnet housing to anyone who is touching it
Ignition of the helium gas, which becomes highly flammable at normal room temperature
body.explain: Liquid helium expands enormously as it boils off, and if the vent fails it displaces oxygen in the room, risking asphyxiation (evacuate immediately). A quench actually collapses the field, helium is inert and nonflammable, and electric shock is not the primary quench hazard.

body.prompt: Pressing the magnet quench button should be reserved for situations where:
options: A person is pinned by a ferromagnetic object and the field must be removed to free them
A routine examination is running late and the daily schedule needs to be caught up quickly
An MR Conditional implant needs to be scanned outside of its stated static field limits
The room feels warm and the static field should be lowered in order to cool it down
body.explain: A deliberate quench dumps the cryogen and destroys the superconducting field, is costly and hazardous, and is reserved for true emergencies such as a person trapped against the magnet by a ferromagnetic object. It is never used for scheduling, to exceed implant limits, or for comfort.

body.prompt: If a fire starts in or near the scanner room, a key MRI-specific precaution is that:
options: Only nonferromagnetic extinguishers and equipment may be brought anywhere near the magnet
A standard steel oxygen cylinder should be rushed in at once to support the patient
The static field will automatically shut itself off as soon as smoke is first detected
Firefighters may enter freely because the magnet poses no real risk during a fire
body.explain: The magnet stays energized during a fire, so only nonferromagnetic extinguishers and gear may approach; a steel cylinder or conventional extinguisher becomes a projectile. Responders must be warned and, if needed, the magnet is quenched before ferromagnetic equipment enters.

body.prompt: Zone III of an MRI facility is best described as the area that:
options: Has restricted, badge-controlled access and where unscreened people can be seriously harmed
Is fully open to the general public and contains the waiting room and the reception desk
Is the magnet room itself, containing the bore where the static field is at its strongest
Lies entirely outside the building, beyond the outermost fringe of the magnetic field
body.explain: Zone III is the controlled-access region (physically restricted to screened MR personnel and patients) that surrounds the magnet room, where unscreened individuals or ferromagnetic objects can be dangerous. The public area is Zone I, and the magnet room itself is Zone IV.

body.prompt: Compared with the normal operating mode, first-level controlled mode:
options: Allows higher SAR and gradient output but requires medical supervision of the patient
Removes all of the limits on RF and gradient output for any routine clinical scan
Is used only for phantom testing and may never be applied to a live patient at all
Lowers the field strength of the magnet in order to keep energy deposition very small
body.explain: First-level controlled mode permits higher SAR and gradient (dB/dt) output than normal mode but requires medical supervision because the physiologic stress is greater. Second-level mode (still higher) needs research approval. No mode removes all limits or changes the magnet's field strength.

body.prompt: Hearing protection is required for patients during most sequences because the acoustic noise:
options: From the vibrating gradient coils can exceed safe sound levels and damage the hearing
Comes from the radiofrequency coil and rises sharply with any higher SAR settings
Is produced by the cryogen pump and becomes loudest during a magnet quench event
Results from the static field and grows steadily louder as the field strength increases
body.explain: Acoustic noise comes from the gradient coils vibrating as they switch rapidly against the static field (Lorentz forces), and it can exceed safe levels, so earplugs or headphones are required. It is not produced by the RF coil, the cryogen pump, or the static field itself.

body.prompt: Ancillary equipment such as a patient monitor, IV pole or wheelchair used in the scanner room must be:
options: Labeled MR Safe or MR Conditional and kept within any conditions stated on its own label
Any standard hospital equipment, since items that are on wheels cannot become projectiles
Removed from the room only after the patient has already been positioned in the bore
Kept just outside the 5-gauss line, where ferromagnetic items are known to be safe to use
body.explain: Only equipment labeled MR Safe or MR Conditional (used within its stated conditions) may be taken into the scanner room; ordinary ferromagnetic equipment can become a projectile. Wheels do not make an item safe, and the 5-gauss line concerns pacemaker and device exposure, not projectile safety.

body.prompt: Zone II of an MRI facility is best described as the area where:
options: patients are under general supervision and are greeted, screened, and interviewed before entering the controlled zones
the scanner and magnet sit, and only screened Level 2 personnel may move about freely without an escort
the general public has free and unrestricted access with no screening, supervision, or MR staff present
the console and equipment room are located and where physical access is actively controlled by MR staff
body.explain: Zone II is the interface between the freely accessible Zone I and the restricted Zones III and IV. Patients are greeted, screened, and interviewed here under supervision but are not yet in a controlled area. Free public access describes Zone I, the controlled console area is Zone III, and the magnet room is Zone IV.

body.prompt: Operation of an MRI system in the second-level controlled mode:
options: exceeds first-level limits and is permitted only under an approved human-research (IRB or ethics board) protocol
is the routine clinical default and requires no additional supervision or physiologic monitoring of the patient
applies only to the static field strength and has no bearing on the SAR or gradient output limits used
is selected automatically whenever the whole-body SAR stays within the normal operating mode range
body.explain: The second-level controlled operating mode allows output above first-level limits and, because of the added risk, is restricted to approved human-subject research under IRB or ethics-board oversight. Normal mode is the routine clinical default; first-level requires medical supervision.

body.prompt: After MRI of a patient with a programmable CSF shunt valve, the technologist should ensure that:
options: the valve setting is checked and reprogrammed as needed, because the magnetic field can change its pressure setting
the shunt tubing is flushed with saline, because the field can introduce air into the ventricular system
the valve is replaced after every scan, because MRI permanently demagnetizes the adjustable mechanism inside
no action is taken, because programmable shunt valves are fixed devices unaffected by the static magnetic field
body.explain: Many programmable (adjustable) CSF shunt valves use a magnetic mechanism whose pressure setting can be altered by the scanner field. The setting must be verified and reprogrammed after the exam. The field does not introduce air, permanently demagnetize the valve, or leave adjustable valves unaffected.

body.prompt: If a patient goes into cardiac arrest inside the scanner room, the correct response is to:
options: move the patient out of Zone IV to a safe area and begin resuscitation there, since ferromagnetic crash carts cannot enter
bring the ferromagnetic crash cart up to the bore and begin full resuscitation without moving the patient at all
quench the magnet first and wait for the static field to fully dissipate before beginning any resuscitation efforts
call the code team into the magnet room and defibrillate the patient while still positioned inside the scanner bore
body.explain: Standard crash carts, defibrillators, and code equipment are ferromagnetic projectile hazards, so the patient is removed from Zone IV and resuscitated in a safe area. Quenching is slow and unnecessary, and bringing ferromagnetic gear to the bore endangers everyone.

body.prompt: A patient has an intracranial aneurysm clip and no documentation of its composition. MRI should be:
options: deferred until the clip is confirmed to be non-ferromagnetic, because a ferromagnetic clip can torque and cause hemorrhage
performed at 1.5 T but not at 3 T, since torque on an aneurysm clip only occurs at the higher field strength
performed after the patient signs a consent form accepting the small risk of clip movement during the scan itself
performed with SAR minimized, because heating rather than movement is the main hazard posed by an aneurysm clip
body.explain: An aneurysm clip of unknown ferromagnetic status is an absolute contraindication until documentation confirms it is non-ferromagnetic. A ferromagnetic clip can experience torque and tear the vessel. Torque occurs at 1.5 T as well, consent does not remove the hazard, and movement, not heating, is the primary risk.

body.prompt: A static field strength of 1 tesla is equivalent to:
options: 10,000 gauss
1,000 gauss
100 gauss
100,000 gauss
body.explain: One tesla equals 10,000 gauss. This is why the 5-gauss safety line lies well outside the bore: 5 gauss is only 0.0005 T, a tiny fraction of a 1.5 T or 3 T field.

body.prompt: At levels well above the peripheral-nerve-stimulation threshold, the dominant hazard of rapidly switched gradient fields is:
options: cardiac stimulation, which is why gradient slew rates are capped below the level that could induce an arrhythmia
tissue heating, because rapidly switched gradient fields deposit most of their energy as radiofrequency power
a projectile effect, because fast gradient switching briefly raises the static magnetic field strength near the bore
acoustic damage alone, because gradient switching has no direct effect on excitable nerve or cardiac muscle tissue
body.explain: Time-varying gradient fields induce currents in tissue. The first effect is peripheral nerve stimulation; at higher dB/dt the concern is cardiac stimulation, so slew rates are limited below that threshold. Heating is an RF (SAR) effect, not a gradient effect, and gradients do not change the static field.

body.prompt: An oxygen monitor mounted in the scanner room contributes to safety mainly by:
options: alarming when the room oxygen level falls, giving early warning of cryogen (helium) displacing the breathable air
measuring the patient's blood oxygen saturation continuously throughout the entire duration of the examination
detecting ferromagnetic objects carried into the room before they can accelerate and become dangerous projectiles
confirming that the piped medical oxygen supply feeding the anesthesia machine remains at the correct pressure
body.explain: A room oxygen monitor warns of asphyxiation risk: during a quench, cold helium gas can displace air. It measures ambient oxygen, not patient SpO2, and does not detect metal or monitor piped medical gases.

body.prompt: When an unconscious patient with no available history must be screened for MRI, the safest approach is to:
options: treat implant status as unknown and obtain records or radiographs before scanning, rather than relying on any verbal history
proceed with the scan at reduced SAR, since low radiofrequency power output makes any undocumented implant safe to image
rely on a careful visual skin inspection alone, because any MRI-relevant implant will leave a visible external scar or mark
scan only at 1.5 T and skip the questionnaire, since undocumented implants are considered safe below 3 T field strength
body.explain: With no history, implant status is unknown and must be established from records or radiographs before scanning. Reduced SAR does not address projectile or torque hazards, not every implant leaves a visible scar, and a lower field does not make an unknown implant safe.

body.prompt: The peripheral (outer) regions of k-space predominantly encode:
options: fine detail and sharp edges, that is, the high-spatial-frequency information of the image
overall image brightness and gross contrast, that is, the low-spatial-frequency information
the receiver-coil sensitivity maps used for the parallel-imaging reconstruction of the image
nothing usable, because only the exact center point of k-space contributes to the final image
body.explain: The outer regions of k-space hold high-spatial-frequency data, which defines edges and fine detail. The center holds low-spatial-frequency data, which governs overall contrast and signal. Both are needed to reconstruct the image.

body.prompt: The chemical-shift misregistration artifact appears along which axis, and why?
options: the frequency-encode axis, because fat and water resonate at slightly different frequencies and are mismapped
the phase-encode axis, because fat and water accumulate different amounts of phase during each repetition
the slice-select axis, because fat and water are excited by slightly different slice-selection profiles
no particular axis, because the shift is random and spreads evenly across the entire imaging field of view
body.explain: Spatial position along the frequency-encode axis is derived from precessional frequency. Because fat resonates about 3.5 ppm below water, its signal is mapped to the wrong location along that axis, producing the chemical-shift (of the first kind) artifact.

body.prompt: For a given scanner, how does signal-to-noise ratio relate to voxel volume?
options: SNR is directly proportional to voxel volume, so larger voxels (thicker slices or a coarser matrix) raise SNR
SNR is inversely proportional to voxel volume, so smaller voxels always give a higher signal-to-noise ratio
SNR is independent of voxel volume and depends only on the receiver bandwidth chosen at the scanner console
SNR scales with the square root of voxel volume, mirroring the way that signal averaging improves the ratio
body.explain: More protons contribute to a larger voxel, so signal (and SNR) is directly proportional to voxel volume. Thicker slices, larger FOV, or a coarser matrix all raise SNR at the cost of spatial resolution.

body.prompt: Compared with a large body coil, a small surface coil placed over the region of interest generally provides:
options: higher SNR near the coil but rapidly falling signal with depth and limited anatomic coverage
higher SNR uniformly throughout the entire imaging volume regardless of the distance from the coil
lower SNR everywhere but a much larger usable field of view than the body coil is able to achieve
identical SNR to the body coil, differing only in the acoustic noise that is produced during the scan
body.explain: A small surface coil sits close to the anatomy and collects high SNR near its surface, but sensitivity falls off steeply with depth and its coverage is limited. The body coil gives more uniform but lower peak SNR.

body.prompt: In a fast (turbo) spin-echo sequence, increasing the echo train length:
options: shortens scan time but increases T2-related blurring, because the later echoes have progressively decayed signal
lengthens scan time but sharpens fine detail, because each additional echo adds true spatial resolution to the image
has no effect on scan time and only changes the number of slices that can be acquired within each repetition time
eliminates the chemical-shift artifact, because a longer echo train realigns the fat and water signals in phase
body.explain: A longer echo train fills more k-space lines per TR, cutting scan time, but the later echoes have lower signal due to T2 decay, which blurs fine detail (T2 blurring). It does not add resolution or remove chemical shift.

body.prompt: The magic-angle artifact produces artificially high signal in a tendon or ligament when it is:
options: oriented near 55 degrees to B0 and imaged with a short TE, which lengthens its apparent T2 relaxation time
oriented parallel to B0 and imaged with a long TE, which in turn shortens its apparent T2 relaxation time
oriented perpendicular to B0 and imaged with any TE, because collagen shows no dependence on orientation
positioned at the exact center of the bore, where the static magnetic field is strongest and most uniform
body.explain: When collagen fibers lie near 55 degrees to B0, dipolar interactions are minimized and the tissue's apparent T2 lengthens, so a normally dark tendon looks bright on short-TE sequences. Using a longer TE reduces the artifact.

body.prompt: In a STIR sequence, the inversion time (TI) is chosen to:
options: null fat by setting TI near 0.69 times the T1 of fat, which is roughly 150 to 170 ms at 1.5 T
null water by setting TI near 0.69 times the T1 of water, which is roughly 2000 ms at 1.5 T field
match the TE so that the fat and water signals are exactly opposed in phase at the chosen echo time
equal the TR so that the longitudinal magnetization is fully recovered before the next excitation pulse
body.explain: STIR nulls fat by placing the readout at fat's magnetization zero-crossing after inversion, TI is about 0.69 x T1(fat), roughly 150 to 170 ms at 1.5 T. It targets fat, not water, and TI is unrelated to matching TE or TR.

body.prompt: A single two-point Dixon acquisition can be reconstructed into:
options: in-phase, opposed-phase, water-only, and fat-only image sets computed from the same raw data
a water-only image only, with the fat information permanently discarded during reconstruction
a fat-saturated image whose quality depends entirely on the static-field shimming over the region
a single proton-density image that blends fat and water without ever separating the two signals
body.explain: Dixon uses the phase difference between fat and water to compute water-only and fat-only images along with the in-phase and opposed-phase images, all from one acquisition. This is why Dixon also yields robust fat suppression from a single scan.

body.prompt: STIR is often preferred over spectral (chemical-shift) fat saturation when:
options: B0 is inhomogeneous or the field of view is large or off-isocenter, since inversion nulling is frequency independent
the highest possible SNR is required, because STIR preserves far more signal than a spectral saturation pulse does
gadolinium has already been given, because STIR selectively suppresses fat while leaving enhancing tissue bright
scan time must be minimized, because STIR adds no inversion pulse and therefore no extra time to each repetition
body.explain: STIR suppresses fat by T1 nulling, which does not depend on field homogeneity, so it excels with a large or off-center FOV or a poorly shimmed field. It has lower SNR, must not be combined with gadolinium (it nulls anything with fat's T1), and adds an inversion pulse.

body.prompt: On a 1.5 T gradient-echo sequence, fat and water signals are aligned (in phase) at an echo time near:
options: 4.4 ms, when their differing precession has realigned after one full cycle
2.2 ms, when their differing precession has just reached opposition (India ink)
0 ms only, because fat and water can never realign once the echo has begun
10 ms, matching the point where T2 decay has equalized the fat and water signal
body.explain: At 1.5 T the fat and water precession frequencies differ by about 220 Hz, so they oppose at roughly 2.2 ms and realign (in phase) at about 4.4 ms. Opposed-phase echoes show the India-ink boundary; in-phase echoes do not.

body.prompt: SPAIR differs from a basic SPIR or frequency-selective fat-saturation pulse mainly in that SPAIR:
options: uses an adiabatic inversion pulse, which makes its fat suppression more tolerant of B1 (RF) field inhomogeneity
uses a spatial saturation band, which makes its fat suppression depend on the position of the slice in the bore
requires gadolinium to be present, which makes its fat suppression effective only on post-contrast acquisitions
removes any need for a homogeneous static field, which lets it work identically at any field strength or shim
body.explain: SPAIR (spectral attenuated inversion recovery) uses an adiabatic, spectrally selective inversion pulse that is relatively insensitive to B1 non-uniformity, giving more uniform fat suppression than a simple SPIR or fat-sat pulse. It is not a spatial band and does not need contrast.

body.prompt: On a gradient-echo in- and opposed-phase pair, a signal drop within a lesion on the opposed-phase image indicates:
options: microscopic (intravoxel) fat and water sharing the same voxel, as seen in an adrenal adenoma or a fatty liver
a purely cystic lesion with no internal fat, because simple fluid loses signal only on the opposed-phase image
the presence of calcification, which cancels the signal specifically when fat and water are out of phase
magnetic susceptibility from hemorrhage, which becomes visible only on the in-phase image of the acquired pair
body.explain: When fat and water coexist in one voxel, their signals cancel on the opposed-phase image, producing a signal drop relative to in-phase. This is the basis for diagnosing lipid-rich adrenal adenomas and hepatic steatosis. Cysts, calcium, and hemorrhage do not behave this way.

body.prompt: The acquisition time of a 3D volumetric sequence is proportional to:
options: TR multiplied by the number of in-plane phase encodes, the number of partition (slice) encodes, and NEX
TR multiplied by the number of in-plane phase encodes and NEX only, exactly as for a single 2D slice
the number of slices alone, because a 3D sequence excites the entire slab in one repetition of the sequence
the receiver bandwidth multiplied by the field of view, independent of the number of phase-encoding steps
body.explain: A 3D acquisition phase-encodes in two directions, so scan time is TR x Ny x Nz x NEX. The extra partition-encoding loop is what makes 3D acquisitions longer than a single 2D slice for the same TR.

body.prompt: A limitation of the maximum-intensity projection (MIP) is that:
options: overlapping high-signal structures obscure one another and small or low-signal vessels can be lost
it can only be generated from a 2D acquisition and never from a true 3D volumetric data set
it discards all of the bright voxels and instead displays only the darkest voxel along each ray
it doubles the acquisition time, because the projection has to be recomputed for every source slice
body.explain: A MIP keeps only the brightest voxel along each ray, so superimposed bright structures overlap and faint or small vessels can drop out. Subtraction and editing help. A MIP keeps the brightest (not darkest) voxel and is a post-processing step that does not lengthen acquisition.

body.prompt: Zero-fill interpolation (slice interpolation) applied to a 3D acquisition:
options: creates apparently thinner and more numerous slices without adding any true spatial resolution or scan time
increases the true through-plane spatial resolution by acquiring additional partition-encoding steps in k-space
removes wrap-around in the slice direction by oversampling the outer edges of the imaging volume during readout
shortens the acquisition by discarding the outer high-spatial-frequency lines of the acquired k-space data set
body.explain: Zero-filling pads unmeasured k-space with zeros, interpolating extra thinner slices for smoother reformats. It improves apparent continuity but adds no real resolution and no scan time, unlike acquiring more partitions.

body.prompt: In a 3D contrast-enhanced MR angiogram, centric (low-high) k-space ordering is used to:
options: sample the center of k-space at the moment of peak arterial enhancement, maximizing the arterial signal
sample the periphery of k-space first, so that fine vessel edges are acquired before the contrast arrives
spread the acquisition evenly over time, so that the arterial and venous phases contribute signal equally
shorten the scan by skipping the center of k-space, which contributes little to the final angiographic image
body.explain: The center of k-space determines image contrast, so centric ordering acquires it first, timed to peak arterial gadolinium concentration. This maximizes arterial signal and minimizes venous contamination.

body.prompt: Volume rendering (VR) differs from a maximum-intensity projection in that VR:
options: assigns opacity and shading to voxels to preserve depth, instead of projecting only the single brightest voxel
projects only the brightest voxel along each ray, giving a flat image with no depth information whatsoever
can be produced only from a 2D multislice acquisition and never from an isotropic 3D volumetric data set
requires intravenous contrast, whereas a maximum-intensity projection is always performed without any contrast
body.explain: Volume rendering maps voxel intensities to opacity and color and applies shading, preserving three-dimensional depth. A MIP simply projects the brightest voxel along each ray and loses depth cues. Neither technique is limited to 2D or requires contrast.

body.prompt: In time-of-flight MR angiography, a multiple overlapping thin-slab acquisition (MOTSA) is used to:
options: combine the flow sensitivity of thin slabs with the coverage of a thick volume, reducing inflow saturation
acquire one very thick slab quickly, accepting the resulting saturation of the slowly flowing spins within it
replace the need for any phase encoding by projecting the whole volume onto a single flat plane at one time
suppress the stationary background tissue by injecting gadolinium before the overlapping slabs are acquired
body.explain: In 3D TOF, spins saturate as they travel deep into a thick slab, dimming distal vessels. MOTSA acquires several thin overlapping slabs, keeping inflow enhancement high while covering a large volume. TOF is a flow (not contrast) technique.

body.prompt: The Larmor (resonance) frequency of hydrogen at 1.5 T is closest to:
options: about 64 MHz, and it scales in direct proportion to the static field strength
about 128 MHz, and it scales in inverse proportion to the static field strength
about 21 MHz, and it stays fixed regardless of the static field strength used
about 300 MHz, and it depends only on the gyromagnetic ratio, not the field
body.explain: The Larmor frequency equals the gyromagnetic ratio (42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen) times B0, giving about 64 MHz at 1.5 T and 128 MHz at 3 T. It is directly proportional to field strength.

body.prompt: Compared with a linearly polarized coil, a quadrature (circularly polarized) coil provides:
options: a signal-to-noise improvement of roughly the square root of two and more uniform excitation
exactly double the signal-to-noise ratio and no change at all in the excitation uniformity
lower signal-to-noise ratio but a much wider field of view than any linear coil can cover
identical performance to a linear coil, differing only in the amount of RF power deposited
body.explain: A quadrature coil transmits and receives on two orthogonal channels, gaining about a factor of root-two in SNR and improving RF field uniformity compared with a single-channel linear coil.

body.prompt: As static field strength increases from 1.5 T to 3 T, image signal-to-noise ratio tends to:
options: increase roughly in proportion to field strength, which is a principal reason for using 3 T
decrease roughly in proportion to field strength, because noise grows faster than signal does
stay essentially constant, since signal and noise both scale identically with field strength
change only for gradient-echo sequences and not for any spin-echo based acquisition at all
body.explain: Baseline SNR rises approximately linearly with B0, so 3 T offers roughly twice the SNR of 1.5 T. This can be traded for higher resolution or speed, though SAR and susceptibility effects also increase.

body.prompt: Eddy currents induced in nearby conductors by rapid gradient switching are best reduced by:
options: actively shielded gradient coils together with waveform pre-emphasis of the gradient pulses
raising the receiver bandwidth so that the readout finishes before the eddy currents can form
increasing the number of signal averages so that the eddy-current effects average out to zero
using a lower static field strength, since eddy currents scale with the main magnetic field
body.explain: Switching gradients induces eddy currents in surrounding conductors, distorting the intended waveform. Actively shielded gradients confine the field, and pre-emphasis pre-distorts the drive current to compensate.

body.prompt: The slew rate of a gradient system is defined as:
options: the gradient amplitude divided by its rise time, expressed in tesla per meter per second
the gradient amplitude multiplied by its rise time, expressed in tesla per meter per second
the maximum gradient amplitude alone, expressed simply in millitesla per meter of length
the receiver bandwidth divided by the field of view, expressed in hertz per meter of length
body.explain: Slew rate is how fast a gradient reaches full amplitude, amplitude divided by rise time, in T/m/s. Higher slew rates speed up imaging but raise the risk of peripheral nerve stimulation, which caps the limit.

body.prompt: Compared with a superconducting magnet, a resistive (electromagnet) system:
options: requires continuous electrical power and cooling to sustain its field and is limited to lower field strengths
needs no electrical power once energized and readily reaches field strengths of 3 T and above for imaging
uses liquid helium to keep its windings cold and holds its field indefinitely without any power supplied
produces no fringe field at all and therefore needs neither active nor passive magnetic shielding around it
body.explain: A resistive magnet creates its field by current through ordinary (non-superconducting) windings, so it consumes power continuously and generates heat, limiting it to low field strengths. Superconducting magnets need no sustaining power once ramped.

body.prompt: The cold head (cryocooler) on a modern superconducting magnet functions to:
options: recondense evaporating helium so that cryogen boil-off and the need for refills are minimized
generate the static magnetic field by cooling the resistive drive coils to room temperature
switch the imaging gradients on and off rapidly during the readout portion of the sequence
shield the scan room from outside radiofrequency interference entering through the wall panels
body.explain: The cold head continuously recondenses helium gas back to liquid, greatly reducing boil-off. Many current 'zero-boil-off' magnets rarely need refills as long as the cold head keeps running.

body.prompt: The difference between passive and active shimming of the static field is that:
options: passive shimming uses ferromagnetic pieces placed at installation, while active shimming uses current in shim coils
passive shimming uses current in shim coils, while active shimming uses ferromagnetic pieces placed at installation
passive shimming corrects the gradients, while active shimming corrects the radiofrequency transmit field only
passive shimming is done for every patient, while active shimming is performed just once when the magnet is sited
body.explain: Passive shims are small ferromagnetic plates positioned during installation to homogenize B0. Active shims are electromagnetic coils whose currents are adjusted, often per patient, to fine-tune homogeneity over the imaging volume.

body.prompt: The magnetic field homogeneity of an MRI magnet is typically specified as:
options: parts per million measured over a defined diameter spherical volume at the magnet isocenter
tesla per meter measured along the bore axis from one end of the magnet to the other end
hertz per pixel measured across the reconstructed image at the chosen receiver bandwidth
a percentage of the maximum gradient amplitude available on the strongest gradient axis
body.explain: Homogeneity is quoted in parts per million of field variation over a diameter spherical volume (DSV) centered at isocenter. Tighter ppm over a larger DSV means a more uniform field for accurate imaging and fat suppression.

body.prompt: A dual-echo spin-echo sequence acquires two echoes per TR in order to produce:
options: proton-density and T2-weighted images together, using a short first TE and a long second TE
T1-weighted and T2-weighted images together, using a short TR paired with a single short TE
two identical T2-weighted images that are then averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio
in-phase and opposed-phase images for fat quantification within a single breath-hold acquisition
body.explain: With a long TR, a short first TE yields proton-density weighting and a long second TE yields T2 weighting, so both contrasts come from one acquisition. It is not a T1/T2 pair, and the echoes have different TEs, not identical ones.

body.prompt: MP-RAGE (magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo) is best described as a:
options: 3D inversion-prepared spoiled gradient echo used for high-resolution T1-weighted brain volumes
2D fast spin echo used mainly for heavily T2-weighted imaging of fluid in the spinal canal
single-shot echo-planar sequence used for diffusion-weighted imaging of acute cerebral infarct
balanced steady-state sequence used for bright-blood cardiac cine imaging across the heartbeat
body.explain: MP-RAGE applies an inversion preparation pulse then reads out a fast 3D spoiled gradient echo, giving isotropic high-resolution T1 contrast widely used for brain volumetrics and neuronavigation.

body.prompt: A magnetization transfer (MT) pulse improves images by:
options: saturating protons bound to macromolecules, which suppresses background tissue and boosts vessel or lesion conspicuity
adding a second refocusing pulse that recovers signal lost to static field inhomogeneity across the slice
nulling the signal from mobile free water so that only fat-bound protons contribute to the final image
increasing the flip angle beyond the Ernst angle to maximize the available longitudinal magnetization
body.explain: An off-resonance MT pulse saturates the broad pool of macromolecule-bound protons; magnetization transfer to free water lowers background signal. This improves TOF angiography background suppression and highlights tissues with MT contrast such as cartilage.

body.prompt: A driven-equilibrium (DRIVE / fast-recovery) pulse is added to a fast spin echo mainly to:
options: flip residual transverse magnetization back along B0 so fluid signal recovers faster and TR can be shortened
spoil any residual transverse magnetization so that the next repetition starts from a clean baseline state
invert the longitudinal magnetization before excitation so that fat is nulled at the chosen inversion time
apply diffusion-sensitizing gradients so that the sequence becomes sensitive to water molecular motion
body.explain: A driven-equilibrium module ends the echo train with a negative flip-back pulse that returns transverse magnetization to the longitudinal axis, speeding recovery of long-T2 fluid. This brightens CSF or joint fluid while allowing a shorter TR.

body.prompt: Ultrashort-echo-time (UTE) sequences are designed to:
options: capture signal from very short-T2 tissues such as cortical bone, tendon, and ligament before it decays
eliminate chemical-shift artifact by acquiring fat and water at two separate long echo times each
provide the heaviest possible T2 weighting for detecting free fluid in joints and around tendons
reduce SAR at 3 T by replacing every refocusing pulse with a low-flip-angle gradient reversal instead
body.explain: Tissues like cortical bone and tendon have T2 values of well under a millisecond, so conventional TEs show no signal. UTE sampling begins microseconds after excitation, capturing that fast-decaying signal for imaging.

body.prompt: Which combination of parameters produces a T2-weighted image on a spin-echo sequence?
options: a long TR and a long TE, which lets tissues with longer T2 retain more transverse signal
a short TR and a short TE, which emphasizes differences in the T1 recovery of the tissues
a long TR and a short TE, which minimizes both the T1 and the T2 contribution to contrast
a short TR and a long TE, which is generally avoided because it yields very little total signal
body.explain: T2 weighting needs a long TR (to reduce T1 effects) and a long TE (to let T2 differences develop). Short TR/short TE gives T1 weighting, and long TR/short TE gives proton-density weighting.

body.prompt: SENSE and GRAPPA are two forms of parallel imaging that differ in that:
options: SENSE unwraps aliased pixels in the image domain, while GRAPPA fills missing lines in k-space
SENSE fills missing lines in k-space, while GRAPPA unwraps aliased pixels in the image domain
SENSE requires only one receive channel, while GRAPPA requires at least sixteen receive channels
SENSE shortens the echo time, while GRAPPA instead shortens the repetition time of the sequence
body.explain: Both accelerate scans by undersampling phase encoding and using coil sensitivity information. SENSE reconstructs in the image domain by unfolding aliasing; GRAPPA reconstructs in k-space by synthesizing the skipped lines from calibration data.

body.prompt: The g-factor in parallel imaging refers to:
options: the spatially varying noise amplification introduced by the parallel-imaging reconstruction
the acceleration factor set by how many phase-encode lines are skipped during the scan
the geometric distortion produced by nonlinearity at the periphery of the gradient field
the gradient duty cycle that limits how quickly the coils can be switched before overheating
body.explain: Beyond the intrinsic root-R signal loss from undersampling, the g-factor captures extra, position-dependent noise amplification during unfolding. A high g-factor causes localized noisy patches, often central, at higher acceleration.

body.prompt: A spiral k-space trajectory acquires data by:
options: sampling outward from the center of k-space along a spiral, which is efficient but sensitive to off-resonance blurring
acquiring one straight horizontal line of k-space per repetition, exactly as a standard 2D sequence does
collecting only the outer edges of k-space, so that image contrast must be recovered from a separate scan
filling k-space in two orthogonal phase-encode directions, which is why it is used only for 3D imaging
body.explain: Spiral readouts trace a spiral from the k-space center outward, using gradient time very efficiently and tolerating motion. Their main weakness is sensitivity to off-resonance, which produces blurring rather than the discrete ghosts of Cartesian scans.

body.prompt: Raising the receiver bandwidth (widening the bandwidth per pixel) has which set of effects?
options: a shorter minimum TE and reduced chemical shift, at the cost of lower signal-to-noise ratio
a longer minimum TE and increased chemical shift, together with a higher signal-to-noise ratio
no change to TE or chemical shift, but a large increase in the total acquisition scan time
a shorter scan time and higher spatial resolution, with no penalty to the signal-to-noise ratio
body.explain: A higher receiver bandwidth samples the echo faster, allowing a shorter TE and reducing chemical-shift misregistration and susceptibility distortion, but it admits more noise per pixel, lowering SNR.

body.prompt: The N/2 (Nyquist) ghost seen in echo-planar imaging arises from:
options: inconsistencies between the odd and even echo lines collected by the alternating EPI readout
bulk patient motion occurring specifically while the central lines of k-space are being sampled
chemical-shift displacement of fat, which always shifts by exactly half of the field of view
gadolinium arriving in the arteries after the center of k-space has already been acquired
body.explain: EPI reads alternate k-space lines in opposite directions; slight timing or phase mismatches between odd and even lines produce a ghost displaced by half the FOV in the phase direction, the N/2 or Nyquist ghost.
