body.prompt: Keyhole (view-sharing) acquisition raises temporal resolution in dynamic imaging by:
options: fully sampling central k-space each frame while sharing the peripheral lines across several time frames
fully sampling peripheral k-space each frame while sharing the central lines across several time frames
acquiring every line of k-space twice per frame and averaging the two copies to reduce image noise
skipping the readout gradient entirely so that each frame is reconstructed from phase encoding alone
body.explain: Since the k-space center carries most contrast information, keyhole methods update the center frequently and reuse (share) the slowly changing periphery across frames, boosting frame rate for dynamic contrast studies at some spatial-detail cost.

body.prompt: A zipper artifact, a band of alternating bright and dark spots running across the image, most often results from:
options: radiofrequency energy entering the scan room, such as through a door left open during the scan
patient motion occurring only while the outermost lines of k-space are being sampled by the coil
fat and water becoming misregistered along the frequency-encode axis at a low receiver bandwidth
gadolinium reaching the veins before the center of k-space has finished being acquired by the scanner
body.explain: A zipper is stray RF contaminating the data, classically from a broken Faraday seal or an open scan-room door. It appears as a line of alternating dots along one axis. Closing the door or fixing the RF shield resolves it.

body.prompt: A herringbone (crisscross or corduroy) artifact spread across the whole image is caused by:
options: a single corrupted data point (a spike) in k-space, often from electrical arcing or a static discharge
pulsatile arterial flow that produces discrete repeating ghosts along the phase-encode direction
fat and water canceling within each voxel on an opposed-phase gradient-echo acquisition of the region
a metallic implant creating a signal void with surrounding geometric distortion of the nearby anatomy
body.explain: One bad k-space point transforms into a regular stripe pattern across the entire image after the Fourier transform. Sources include electrostatic discharge or arcing. Finding and removing the spike (or fixing the cause) clears it.

body.prompt: A bright dot in the exact center of the image (a DC artifact) is produced by:
options: a constant direct-current offset in the received signal, which maps to the center point of k-space
aliasing of tissue lying outside the field of view along the phase-encode direction of the scan
chemical-shift misregistration of fat, which always concentrates its signal at the image center
a standing-wave (dielectric) effect that removes signal from the periphery of a large body part
body.explain: The center of k-space corresponds to the zero-frequency (DC) component. A constant offset in the receiver electronics deposits extra signal there, appearing as a bright central dot in the reconstructed image.

body.prompt: Moire fringes (a zebra-stripe interference pattern) are most commonly seen when:
options: aliasing combines with B0 inhomogeneity on a gradient-echo image acquired with a large field of view
cardiac pulsation produces evenly spaced ghosts along the frequency-encode direction of a spin echo
a receiver channel fails, so that half of the phased-array elements contribute no signal to the image
the slice-select gradient is too steep, so adjacent slices excite and saturate one another during scanning
body.explain: Moire fringes arise where aliased signal overlaps true signal and the two have differing phase because of field inhomogeneity, producing a banded interference pattern. This is typical of gradient-echo imaging with a large FOV.

body.prompt: Geometric distortion that becomes progressively worse toward the edges of a large field of view is due to:
options: gradient nonlinearity, and it is reduced by the vendor's gradient (distortion) correction algorithm
chemical shift, and it is reduced simply by lowering the receiver bandwidth for the acquisition
patient motion, and it is reduced by adding cardiac and respiratory gating to the pulse sequence
RF inhomogeneity, and it is reduced by placing high-permittivity dielectric pads next to the patient
body.explain: Gradients deviate from perfect linearity away from isocenter, warping anatomy near the FOV edges. Vendor gradient-warp (distortion) correction remaps the image to compensate; keeping anatomy near isocenter also helps.

body.prompt: Central signal loss from a dielectric (standing-wave) effect, seen on large-body imaging at 3 T, can be reduced by:
options: placing high-permittivity dielectric pads against the patient or using RF (B1) shimming with parallel transmit
lowering the receiver bandwidth so that the readout captures more signal from the center of the body
increasing the number of signal averages so that the central signal loss averages out across repetitions
switching from a gradient-echo to a spin-echo readout, which is completely immune to any B1 nonuniformity
body.explain: At 3 T the RF wavelength in tissue approaches body dimensions, so standing waves cause central B1 dropout, especially in large abdomens or with ascites. Dielectric pads or parallel-transmit RF shimming even out the B1 field.

body.prompt: Which acquisition parameter most directly controls the degree of T1 weighting?
options: TR, because a short TR emphasizes differences in how quickly tissues recover longitudinal magnetization
TE, because a short TE emphasizes differences in how quickly tissues lose transverse magnetization
the flip angle alone, because it fixes how much signal each tissue produces regardless of TR or TE
the receiver bandwidth, because it sets how much T1 relaxation occurs during the signal readout
body.explain: T1 contrast develops during the recovery period between excitations, so TR governs it: a short TR does not let long-T1 tissues fully recover, exaggerating their difference from short-T1 tissues. TE controls T2 weighting.

body.prompt: On a T1-weighted image, fat appears bright because it:
options: has a short T1, so it recovers longitudinal magnetization quickly and gives high signal at a short TR
has a long T1, so it recovers longitudinal magnetization slowly and gives high signal at a short TR
has a long T2, so it retains transverse magnetization far longer than the surrounding tissues do
contains very little hydrogen, so it produces almost no signal and is displayed as a bright region
body.explain: Fat has a short T1, recovering its longitudinal magnetization quickly between pulses, so it yields high signal on T1-weighted sequences. This is why subcutaneous fat is bright on a non-fat-suppressed T1 image.

body.prompt: As static field strength increases from 1.5 T to 3 T, tissue T1 values generally:
options: lengthen, which slightly reduces T1 contrast and often calls for a longer TR or TI
shorten, which increases T1 contrast and allows a much shorter TR to be used safely
stay exactly the same, since T1 is an intrinsic property independent of field strength
drop to nearly zero, which is why 3 T scanners cannot produce T1-weighted images at all
body.explain: T1 relaxation times increase with field strength, so at 3 T tissues recover more slowly and T1 contrast is slightly reduced. Sequences are adjusted (for example a longer inversion time for FLAIR) to compensate.

body.prompt: A superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) contrast agent alters image signal by:
options: shortening T2 and T2*, which makes tissue that takes up the agent lose signal and appear dark
shortening T1 only, which makes tissue that takes up the agent gain signal and appear bright
increasing the proton density of tissue, which raises signal on every pulse sequence equally
having no effect on relaxation times, acting purely as a mechanical marker within the vessel
body.explain: SPIO agents create strong local field disturbances that shorten T2 and T2*, so tissue taking up the agent (for example normal liver Kupffer cells) loses signal. They act as negative (dark) contrast agents, unlike gadolinium.

body.prompt: Proton-density weighting is achieved by minimizing T1 and T2 effects so that contrast reflects:
options: the concentration of mobile hydrogen protons in each tissue, using a long TR and a short TE
the T1 recovery rate of each tissue, using a short TR paired together with a short TE value
the T2 decay rate of each tissue, using a long TR paired together with a long TE value
the diffusion of water molecules in each tissue, using a pair of strong motion-probing gradients
body.explain: A long TR reduces T1 influence and a short TE reduces T2 influence, leaving contrast that depends mainly on how many mobile protons each tissue contains, the proton (spin) density.

body.prompt: Fat has a short T1 (relaxes quickly) because:
options: its molecules tumble at a rate close to the Larmor frequency, allowing efficient energy transfer to the lattice
its molecules tumble far faster than the Larmor frequency, which prevents any energy transfer to the lattice
it contains almost no hydrogen, so there is very little magnetization that needs to recover after a pulse
it is a solid at body temperature, and solids always have the shortest T1 of any tissue in the body
body.explain: T1 recovery is fastest when molecular tumbling frequencies match the Larmor frequency, letting protons dump absorbed energy into the surrounding lattice. Mid-sized fat molecules tumble near this rate, giving fat its short T1. Free water tumbles too fast, giving it a long T1.

body.prompt: Ranked from brightest to darkest on a standard T1-weighted brain image, the correct order is:
options: fat, then white matter, then gray matter, then cerebrospinal fluid
cerebrospinal fluid, then gray matter, then white matter, then fat
gray matter, then fat, then cerebrospinal fluid, then white matter
white matter, then cerebrospinal fluid, then fat, then gray matter
body.explain: On T1, signal tracks short T1 as bright: fat is brightest, white matter (more myelin lipid) is brighter than gray matter, and CSF with its very long T1 is darkest. This ordering reverses on a T2-weighted image.

body.prompt: Contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) is best defined as:
options: the difference in signal between two tissues divided by the background noise level of the image
the signal of a single tissue divided by the background noise level of the surrounding image
the difference in signal between two tissues multiplied by the total scan time of the sequence
the ratio of the largest voxel to the smallest voxel achievable at the chosen field of view
body.explain: CNR is the signal difference between two tissues normalized by noise. Because detecting a lesion depends on how well it stands out from adjacent tissue, CNR predicts conspicuity better than raw SNR (which concerns one tissue against background).

body.prompt: The in-plane pixel size along one axis is equal to:
options: the field of view divided by the matrix size along that axis
the field of view multiplied by the matrix size along that axis
the slice thickness divided by the number of signal averages used
the receiver bandwidth divided by the number of phase-encode steps
body.explain: Pixel size equals FOV / matrix. Shrinking the FOV or enlarging the matrix makes pixels smaller, improving spatial resolution but reducing SNR because each smaller voxel holds fewer protons.

body.prompt: Reducing the phase matrix (for example choosing 75 percent phase resolution) will:
options: shorten scan time but lower spatial resolution along the phase-encode direction of the image
shorten scan time while actually improving spatial resolution along the phase-encode direction
lengthen scan time but greatly improve resolution along the frequency-encode direction instead
leave both scan time and resolution unchanged, affecting only the receiver bandwidth per pixel
body.explain: Fewer phase-encode steps mean fewer TR periods, so scan time falls, but coarser sampling of the phase direction lowers resolution there. The scanner may interpolate to a square pixel, but true resolution is reduced.

body.prompt: Using parallel imaging at acceleration factor R shortens the scan but:
options: reduces SNR by roughly the square root of R, with an additional local penalty from the g-factor
increases SNR by roughly the square root of R, because fewer noisy lines are sampled overall
leaves SNR unchanged, because the missing k-space lines are recovered perfectly by the coils
reduces spatial resolution, because parallel imaging always enlarges the reconstructed voxels
body.explain: Undersampling collects less data, so SNR drops by about root-R, and the unfolding reconstruction adds spatially varying noise through the g-factor. Resolution is preserved; the cost is SNR and possible residual artifact.

body.prompt: At clinical field strengths, the dominant source of image noise is:
options: thermal (Johnson) noise from the patient's own body, which is why coil loading matters so much
quantization noise from the analog-to-digital converter, which sets a hard floor on achievable SNR
quantum shot noise from the small number of photons emitted by the excited hydrogen protons
gradient vibration noise, which couples mechanically into the receive chain during the readout
body.explain: Most MRI noise is thermal (Brownian) motion of charges in the conductive tissue of the patient, picked up by the receive coil. This is why a properly loaded coil and imaging the smallest necessary volume improve SNR.

body.prompt: Overall signal-to-noise ratio in MRI is approximately proportional to:
options: voxel volume times the square root of (phase steps x frequency steps x averages), divided by the square root of bandwidth
voxel volume divided by the square root of (phase steps x frequency steps x averages), times the square root of bandwidth
the receiver bandwidth times the matrix size, independent of the voxel volume or the number of averages
the field of view divided by the slice thickness, independent of how many signal averages are collected
body.explain: SNR rises with voxel volume (more protons) and with the square root of the total number of samples collected (phase steps, frequency steps, and averages), and falls with the square root of receiver bandwidth (more bandwidth admits more noise).

body.prompt: With all other parameters held constant, increasing TE will:
options: lower SNR, because more of the transverse signal has decayed by the time the echo is read
raise SNR, because a longer echo time allows more signal to build up before the readout
leave SNR unchanged, because TE affects only image contrast and never the signal amplitude
raise spatial resolution, because a longer echo time samples more lines of k-space per TR
body.explain: Signal is read at the echo, and transverse magnetization decays with T2 (or T2*) as TE lengthens, so a longer TE means less remaining signal and lower SNR. TE also increases T2 weighting.

body.prompt: Relative to water, the hydrogen protons in fat precess at:
options: a lower frequency, about 3.5 parts per million below water, because they are more shielded
a higher frequency, about 3.5 parts per million above water, because they are less shielded
exactly the same frequency as water, differing only in their T1 and T2 relaxation times
a frequency that depends only on the receiver bandwidth chosen for the particular sequence
body.explain: Fat protons sit in a more shielded chemical environment, so they resonate about 3.5 ppm lower than water protons. Spectral fat-saturation pulses are tuned to this lower fat frequency to selectively saturate it.

body.prompt: At 3 T, the frequency separation between fat and water is about:
options: 440 Hz, roughly double the separation at 1.5 T, which makes spectral fat saturation easier
220 Hz, the same as at 1.5 T, because the separation is independent of the field strength
110 Hz, roughly half the separation at 1.5 T, which makes spectral fat saturation harder
3.5 Hz, a fixed value set by the chemical-shift difference regardless of the field strength
body.explain: The 3.5 ppm chemical shift scales with field strength, so the fat-water gap is about 220 Hz at 1.5 T and about 440 Hz at 3 T. The wider separation at 3 T makes selective fat saturation more reliable.

body.prompt: A chemically selective fat-saturation pulse works by, just before the excitation pulse:
options: applying a narrow-band 90-degree pulse at fat's frequency, then a spoiler gradient to dephase the fat signal
applying a broad-band 180-degree pulse at water's frequency, then reading the echo without any spoiler
inverting all of the tissue in the slice, then waiting for fat to reach its longitudinal null point
switching the slice-select gradient off so that only fat within the isocenter becomes saturated
body.explain: A spectral fat-sat pulse tips fat's magnetization into the transverse plane with a frequency-selective 90-degree pulse, then a spoiler gradient dephases it so fat contributes no signal to the following excitation. Water, at a different frequency, is left alone.

body.prompt: Spectral (chemical-shift) fat saturation is least reliable:
options: at the periphery of a large field of view or near metal and air, where local B0 is inhomogeneous
at the exact center of the bore, where the static field is strongest and most perfectly uniform
on thin slices, because reducing slice thickness always widens the fat and water frequency gap
on T1-weighted sequences, because T1 weighting removes the frequency difference between fat and water
body.explain: Selective saturation depends on fat sitting at a predictable frequency, which requires a homogeneous B0. Near the FOV edges, metal, or air-tissue interfaces, local field shifts move fat off the saturation band and suppression fails.

body.prompt: STIR is considered non-specific for fat because it also nulls the signal from:
options: any tissue whose T1 resembles fat, such as subacute hemorrhage, melanin, or gadolinium-enhanced tissue
any tissue with a very long T2, such as simple cysts, cerebrospinal fluid, and joint effusions
any tissue containing calcium, because calcium and fat happen to share the same resonant frequency
only pure water, leaving fat and every other soft tissue completely unaffected by the inversion pulse
body.explain: STIR nulls tissue at fat's T1, so anything with a similarly short T1, methemoglobin, melanin, proteinaceous fluid, or gadolinium-enhanced tissue, is also suppressed. That is why STIR is not combined with contrast and is called non-specific.

body.prompt: A multi-point (multi-echo / IDEAL-type) Dixon method improves on two-point Dixon mainly by:
options: being more robust to B0 inhomogeneity and enabling accurate quantitative fat-fraction measurement
removing the need for any phase-encoding steps, which shortens the scan time by roughly half
eliminating the water-only and fat-only images so that only a single fat-saturated image remains
working only at very low field strengths, where the fat and water frequencies are far apart
body.explain: Acquiring more echoes lets the reconstruction separate fat and water while also solving for field-map errors, making it robust to B0 inhomogeneity and yielding a reliable proton-density fat fraction.

body.prompt: To evaluate a suspected ruptured silicone breast implant, the technologist would use a sequence that:
options: selectively images silicone (or suppresses water) so that silicone signal is highlighted against the breast
suppresses silicone and fat together, leaving only glandular tissue and any implant capsule visible
applies a standard STIR, since silicone and fat share an identical resonant frequency and T1 value
relies on gadolinium enhancement, because silicone only becomes visible after intravenous contrast
body.explain: Silicone resonates at its own frequency, distinct from fat and water. A silicone-selective (or water-suppressed) sequence makes silicone bright, revealing extracapsular silicone or the linguine sign of an intracapsular rupture.

body.prompt: Proton-density fat fraction (PDFF), computed from Dixon images, is clinically used to:
options: quantify hepatic steatosis as the fraction fat / (fat + water) within the liver
measure the total blood volume in the liver by comparing arterial and venous phases
estimate the patient's whole-body SAR before a long fat-suppressed abdominal protocol
calculate the receiver bandwidth needed to keep chemical shift below one pixel of shift
body.explain: PDFF expresses fat signal as a fraction of total (fat plus water) signal, giving a reproducible measure of liver fat. It has become a noninvasive standard for grading hepatic steatosis.

body.prompt: Curved planar reformation (CPR) is used to:
options: display a tortuous vessel by reformatting along its centerline onto a single flat image
project only the brightest voxel along each ray to show a bright-blood angiographic view
render a threshold-based solid surface of an organ for a three-dimensional external view
remove wrap-around in the slice direction by oversampling the edges of the imaging volume
body.explain: CPR traces a curved path along a vessel's centerline and flattens it into one plane, so a tortuous artery that would otherwise leave the imaging plane can be shown end to end in a single image.

body.prompt: A surface-shaded display (SSD) reconstruction is limited because it:
options: renders only voxels above a chosen threshold, so it is highly sensitive to that threshold and hides internal detail
projects only the single brightest voxel along each ray, so it discards all of the depth information
can be produced only from a 2D multislice acquisition and never from a true 3D volumetric data set
requires intravenous contrast, so it cannot be applied to any non-enhanced volumetric acquisition
body.explain: SSD picks a threshold and renders a surface of everything above it, giving a 3D external view but losing internal intensity information and exaggerating or hiding structures depending on the threshold chosen.

body.prompt: Compared with a full-volume MIP, a thin-slab (subvolume) MIP:
options: reduces the overlap of superimposed vessels by projecting only a limited depth of tissue
increases the overlap of superimposed vessels by projecting a much greater depth of tissue
removes the need for any source 3D data, generating the projection from a single 2D slice
always requires twice the acquisition time, because two separate projections must be computed
body.explain: A thin-slab MIP projects only a limited depth, so overlying bright structures are less likely to obscure the vessel of interest, at the cost of showing a smaller volume per image.

body.prompt: 3D fast-spin-echo variants (such as CUBE, SPACE, or VISTA) use variable refocusing flip angles across the echo train mainly to:
options: limit SAR and reduce blurring while still acquiring a long echo train for an isotropic volume
increase SAR deliberately so that the images gain the heaviest possible T2 weighting available
eliminate the need for phase encoding, which is what makes these sequences inherently three-dimensional
suppress fat without any dedicated fat-saturation pulse being added to the pulse sequence at all
body.explain: Long echo trains in 3D FSE would otherwise deposit high SAR and blur from T2 decay. Sweeping the refocusing flip angles (low then rising) controls the signal evolution, keeping SAR manageable and reducing blurring for a high-resolution isotropic volume.

body.prompt: A practical workflow advantage of acquiring a single isotropic 3D data set is that it:
options: can be reformatted into axial, sagittal, and coronal planes, often replacing three separate 2D acquisitions
requires no reconstruction at all, since the raw k-space is already displayed as the final image
always has lower SNR than any 2D acquisition, which is offset only by its much shorter scan time
can only ever be viewed in the plane in which it was originally acquired, exactly like a 2D scan
body.explain: Isotropic voxels reformat equally well in any plane, so one 3D acquisition yields axial, sagittal, and coronal images. This can replace multiple 2D scans and often shortens overall exam time.

body.prompt: Compared with 2D time-of-flight angiography, 3D time-of-flight:
options: gives higher resolution and SNR but saturates slow flow more, so 2D is preferred for slow venous flow
gives lower resolution and SNR but never saturates slow flow, so it is always preferred for veins
requires intravenous gadolinium, whereas 2D time-of-flight is the only truly non-contrast technique
cannot be reformatted into other planes, whereas 2D time-of-flight produces an isotropic volume
body.explain: 3D TOF acquires a volume with high resolution and SNR and short TE (less dephasing), ideal for fast arterial flow, but spins saturate as they traverse the slab, dimming slow flow. 2D TOF, exciting one thin slice at a time, better preserves slow venous flow.

body.prompt: In 3D contrast-enhanced MR angiography, correct bolus timing is usually achieved by:
options: using a test bolus or automated bolus tracking so acquisition of central k-space coincides with peak arterial enhancement
starting the acquisition at a fixed 60 seconds after injection for every patient regardless of cardiac output
acquiring continuously for several minutes and selecting the best frame after the scan has finished
injecting the gadolinium only after the central lines of k-space have already been fully acquired
body.explain: Because central k-space sets contrast, it must be filled at peak arterial concentration. A small test bolus or real-time bolus tracking measures transit time and triggers the scan accordingly, adapting to each patient's circulation.

body.prompt: Reformatting an anisotropic (thick-partition) 3D data set into an orthogonal plane tends to produce:
options: stair-step artifact and blurring, which is why isotropic voxels are preferred for multiplanar reformation
a perfectly sharp image in every plane, since 3D data can always be reformatted without any quality loss
wrap-around along the frequency-encode axis, which is corrected by increasing the receiver bandwidth
chemical-shift misregistration, which is corrected by adding a spectral fat-saturation pulse to the scan
body.explain: When partitions are thicker than the in-plane pixels, reformatting across them samples coarsely, giving a stair-step, blurred appearance. Acquiring isotropic voxels avoids this and preserves resolution in any reformatted plane.

body.prompt: Why is a receive coil placed as close to the anatomy as possible?
options: Signal-to-noise ratio drops as coil-to-anatomy distance grows
It increases the static magnetic field strength locally
It shortens the T1 relaxation time of the nearby tissue
It automatically widens the usable field of view
body.explain: SNR is highest when the coil sits close to the part and is no larger than needed.

body.prompt: Which coil gives the best result for a small joint such as the wrist?
options: A small dedicated extremity coil sized to the part
The whole-body transmit coil used on its own
The largest available torso phased-array coil
A head coil, chosen for its high uniformity
body.explain: A smaller coil matched to the part maximizes SNR over that small volume.

body.prompt: What is the main advantage of a phased-array coil over one large coil?
options: High SNR over a large field of view plus parallel-imaging capability
A stronger transmit pulse that allows a substantially shorter TR
Complete immunity to patient motion during the whole scan
It removes the need for gradient coils during the imaging
body.explain: Multiple small elements give local SNR across a wide FOV and enable SENSE/GRAPPA.

body.prompt: Where is the centering landmark for a routine brain examination?
options: At the nasion, with the head held straight in the coil
At the sternal notch, with the chin slightly raised
At the iliac crest, with the pelvis level
At the thyroid cartilage, with the neck extended
body.explain: The brain is centered near the nasion or glabella.

body.prompt: Where is the centering landmark for a cervical spine examination?
options: At the thyroid cartilage, roughly the C4 to C5 level
At the xiphoid process, at the lower sternum
At the umbilicus, in the midline of the abdomen
At the symphysis pubis, at the lower pelvis
body.explain: The thyroid cartilage centers the mid cervical spine.

body.prompt: Where is the centering landmark for a lumbar spine examination?
options: At the iliac crest, roughly the L4 to L5 level
At the thyroid cartilage, high in the neck
At the nasion, between the eyebrows
At the sternal notch, at the top of the sternum
body.explain: The iliac crest marks the lower lumbar level for centering.

body.prompt: Why is the anatomy of interest placed at magnet isocenter?
options: Field homogeneity and gradient linearity are best at isocenter
Only the isocenter of the bore receives any RF energy
The SNR of the image is unaffected by patient position
Receive coils are able to function only at isocenter
body.explain: Anatomy far off-center sees geometric distortion and poorer shimming.

body.prompt: What is the preferred shoulder position for a routine exam?
options: Arm at the side in neutral to slight external rotation, palm up
Arm fully abducted and raised overhead above the head
Hand tucked behind the back with the elbow flexed
Elbow flexed with the forearm resting across the chest
body.explain: A neutral to externally rotated arm held at the side is standard and comfortable.

body.prompt: The knee is placed in about 15 degrees of external rotation mainly to?
options: Unwind the ACL so it lies within a single imaging plane
Reduce the specific absorption rate seen by the patient
Shorten the T2 relaxation time of the joint cartilage
Move the patella completely out of the field of view
body.explain: External rotation aligns the obliquely oriented ACL for sagittal imaging.

body.prompt: What is the standard patient position for breast MRI?
options: Prone with the breasts pendant in a dedicated breast coil
Supine with a general-purpose body array over the chest
Lateral decubitus with the arms folded across the body
Prone with the arms at the sides inside a head coil
body.explain: Prone positioning with the breasts pendant in the breast coil is standard.

body.prompt: How is the ankle positioned for a routine ankle examination?
options: Neutral, near 90 degrees of dorsiflexion, coil around the ankle
Full plantar flexion with the toes pointed firmly well away
Everted and taped down flat against the table surface
Weight-bearing with the patient standing up in the bore
body.explain: A neutral, roughly 90-degree position limits magic-angle effect and keeps anatomy in plane.

body.prompt: What describes correct positioning for a pituitary or sella exam?
options: Small field of view with thin coronal and sagittal slices at the nasion
Large field of view axial images covering the whole head and neck
Centering at the external auditory meatus with thicker slices
A sagittal-only survey of the entire brain and the skull base
body.explain: Sella imaging uses a small FOV and thin slices centered near the nasion.

body.prompt: What coil setup suits temporomandibular joint (TMJ) imaging?
options: Bilateral small surface coils over the joints, imaged open and closed
A single large body coil used with the mouth kept closed only
A knee coil placed right around the head for extra uniformity
A spine array positioned under the neck and the shoulders
body.explain: Paired surface coils capture both joints, and open and closed views show the disc.

body.prompt: What is the purpose of immobilization pads and straps?
options: Reduce voluntary and involuntary motion and improve comfort
Increase the local magnetic field strength near the part
Raise the signal-to-noise ratio of deep-lying structures
Automatically shorten the repetition time of the scan
body.explain: Comfortable immobilization improves compliance and reduces motion artifact.

body.prompt: Why is cardiac imaging synchronized to the ECG signal?
options: To freeze cardiac motion by acquiring data at set points in the cycle
To raise the magnetic field strength during ventricular systole
To remove the need for a receive coil over the chest
To shorten the T1 relaxation time of the myocardium
body.explain: Gating times acquisition to consistent phases of the cardiac cycle.

body.prompt: What is a typical way to control respiratory motion in the abdomen?
options: Breath-holding, or respiratory navigators and triggering
Injecting an additional dose of gadolinium contrast
Increasing the slice thickness for every sequence
Removing the surface coil to lower the signal
body.explain: Breath-hold sequences or navigator gating limit respiratory blurring.

body.prompt: Where is the centering landmark for a routine abdomen examination?
options: Midway between the xiphoid and the umbilicus, with a torso array
At the pubic symphysis, near the very bottom of the pelvis
At the thyroid cartilage, high up toward the neck
At the nasion, in the midline of the upper face
body.explain: The midpoint between xiphoid and umbilicus centers the upper abdomen.

body.prompt: What is best practice when an extremity sits off to the side of the bore?
options: Bring it as close to isocenter as the patient can tolerate to limit distortion
Leave it out near the bore edge simply because that feels more comfortable
Ignore its position entirely, since distortion does not depend on location
Switch to the whole-body coil so that the extremity coil is not needed
body.explain: Off-isocenter anatomy suffers gradient nonlinearity and geometric distortion.

body.title: How are the internal auditory canals imaged?
body.html:
The internal auditory canals are imaged to look for an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) in a patient with one sided hearing loss. The workhorse is a thin section heavily T2 weighted sequence such as CISS or FIESTA, acquired at high resolution with a small field of view. Cerebrospinal fluid in the canal is bright, and the tiny nerves stand out as dark structures against it.

When a mass is suspected, thin post contrast T1 weighted images are added, because a schwannoma enhances strongly. The small field of view and thin slices are what make a two or three millimetre lesion visible.
keypoints: Heavily T2 weighted thin sections such as CISS or FIESTA show the nerves against bright fluid.
A small field of view and thin slices resolve millimetre sized lesions.
Post contrast T1 is added because an acoustic neuroma enhances strongly.

body.title: How is the pituitary gland imaged?
body.html:
The pituitary sits in a small space, so it is imaged with a small field of view and thin coronal and sagittal slices, usually T1 weighted. The normal gland enhances quickly and uniformly after gadolinium.

To find a microadenoma, a dynamic post contrast series is run, capturing several early phases. The adenoma enhances more slowly than the normal gland, so it appears as a relatively dark focus in the first minute before it fills in later. Coronal images best show the relationship to the optic chiasm and the cavernous sinuses.
keypoints: Use a small field of view with thin coronal and sagittal slices.
A microadenoma enhances slower than the normal gland, so dynamic imaging catches it early.
Coronal planes show the optic chiasm and cavernous sinuses.

body.title: What is MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)?
body.html:
MRCP shows the biliary tree and the pancreatic duct without contrast. It uses a heavily T2 weighted sequence with a very long TE, so only slow moving or static fluid stays bright. Bile and pancreatic juice are bright while the surrounding solid organs and flowing blood are dark.

It is acquired either as a thick slab single shot in one breath hold, or as thin sections with respiratory triggering that can be reconstructed into projections. No gadolinium is needed because the fluid in the ducts is the contrast.
keypoints: MRCP is heavily T2 weighted with a long TE so static fluid is bright.
Bile and pancreatic juice are bright against dark background tissue.
It needs no contrast because ductal fluid provides the signal.

body.title: How is the shoulder and rotator cuff imaged?
body.html:
The rotator cuff is imaged in planes aligned to the scapula. The oblique coronal plane follows the supraspinatus tendon and best shows cuff tears, while the oblique sagittal plane displays the arch and the axial plane shows the labrum and biceps tendon. Fluid sensitive fat suppressed sequences make a tear bright.

For the labrum, MR arthrography is often added, injecting dilute gadolinium into the joint so it outlines a labral tear. The contrast distends the joint and leaks into any defect.
keypoints: Oblique coronal follows the supraspinatus and shows cuff tears.
Fluid sensitive fat suppressed images make tears bright.
MR arthrography distends the joint to reveal labral tears.

body.title: How is the knee imaged for internal derangement?
body.html:
The knee is imaged in three planes. The sagittal plane shows the cruciate ligaments and the menisci, the coronal plane shows the collateral ligaments and the meniscal roots, and the axial plane shows the patellofemoral joint. The anterior cruciate ligament runs obliquely, so a slightly angled sagittal helps display it in one slice.

Fluid sensitive fat suppressed sequences highlight cartilage damage, bone marrow oedema, and joint effusion, while proton density images give the fine detail of the menisci.
keypoints: Sagittal shows the cruciate ligaments and menisci.
Coronal shows the collateral ligaments and meniscal roots.
Fat suppressed fluid sensitive images reveal marrow oedema and cartilage loss.

body.title: How is a focal liver lesion characterised?
body.html:
Characterising a liver lesion depends on a dynamic multiphase post contrast study. A fat suppressed T1 weighted sequence is repeated through arterial, portal venous, and delayed phases after a gadolinium bolus, so the pattern of enhancement over time points to the diagnosis. A haemangioma fills in slowly from the edge, while many malignancies wash out.

The dynamic series is combined with T2 weighted and diffusion weighted images. Fluid rich lesions such as cysts and haemangiomas are very bright on heavily T2 weighted images, which helps separate them from solid tumours.
keypoints: A dynamic multiphase T1 study captures arterial, portal venous, and delayed enhancement.
The timing of enhancement and washout characterises the lesion.
T2 and diffusion weighted images help separate cysts and haemangiomas from tumours.

body.title: What is in a routine brain MRI protocol?
body.html:
A routine brain study samples several contrasts. It typically includes T1 weighted, T2 weighted, FLAIR, and diffusion weighted images, along with a gradient echo or susceptibility weighted sequence to look for blood. FLAIR nulls cerebrospinal fluid so that periventricular lesions are not hidden by bright fluid.

Contrast is added when tumour, infection, or inflammation is suspected, giving post contrast T1 weighted images. The set of contrasts lets the reader tell oedema, blood, infarction, and enhancing tissue apart.
keypoints: A routine brain protocol covers T1, T2, FLAIR, and diffusion.
FLAIR suppresses CSF so periventricular lesions show.
Post contrast T1 is added for tumour, infection, or inflammation.

body.title: Which sequence is essential for acute stroke?
body.html:
For suspected hyperacute stroke the indispensable sequence is diffusion weighted imaging. Within minutes of an arterial occlusion the affected tissue develops restricted diffusion, appearing bright on the diffusion image and dark on the ADC map, well before any change is visible on T2 or FLAIR.

A stroke protocol pairs diffusion with FLAIR and a gradient echo or susceptibility sequence to exclude haemorrhage, and often a time of flight MRA to look for the occluded vessel. Speed matters, so the protocol is kept short.
keypoints: Diffusion weighted imaging is the essential sequence in acute stroke.
Infarct is bright on diffusion and dark on ADC within minutes.
A blood sensitive sequence is added to exclude haemorrhage.

body.title: What does a multiple sclerosis protocol emphasise?
body.html:
A multiple sclerosis protocol emphasises FLAIR, especially in the sagittal plane, because it shows the ovoid periventricular plaques that lie along the deep veins. Thin sagittal FLAIR displays these lesions well, and the brainstem and spinal cord are also covered.

Post contrast T1 images separate active from old disease, because a plaque with active inflammation and a broken blood brain barrier enhances. Counting enhancing and non enhancing lesions helps stage the disease over time.
keypoints: FLAIR, particularly sagittal, best shows periventricular plaques.
Enhancing lesions on post contrast T1 indicate active inflammation.
The protocol also covers the brainstem and spinal cord.

body.title: How do you reduce artifact when imaging around metal?
body.html:
Metal hardware distorts the field and causes signal loss and bright pile up. To reduce this a technologist uses a high receive bandwidth, a short TE, thin slices, and a smaller voxel, and favours spin echo over gradient echo because the 180 degree pulse recovers some of the lost signal.

For fat suppression near metal, STIR is preferred over chemical saturation, which fails where the field is distorted. Dedicated metal reduction sequences such as view angle tilting further limit the distortion.
keypoints: Use a high bandwidth, short TE, and thin slices to limit distortion.
Spin echo suffers less signal loss than gradient echo near metal.
Choose STIR rather than chemical fat saturation around metal.

body.title: How do you reduce CSF pulsation artifact on spine MRI?
body.html:
Pulsating cerebrospinal fluid creates ghosting that runs along the phase encoding direction on spine images. A technologist can apply flow compensation (gradient moment nulling), place saturation bands above and below the imaged region, and use cardiac gating so data are collected at the same point in the cycle.

Swapping the phase and frequency directions can also move the ghosts away from the cord so they do not mimic disease. These steps are routine on T2 weighted spine sequences where the bright fluid pulsates most.
keypoints: CSF ghosts run along the phase encoding direction.
Flow compensation, saturation bands, and gating reduce the ghosting.
Swapping phase and frequency can move ghosts off the cord.

body.title: How does time of flight MRA make arteries bright?
body.html:
Time of flight MRA is a non contrast technique that relies on flow related enhancement. Stationary tissue in the slice is saturated by rapid repeated radiofrequency pulses and stays dark, while fresh unsaturated blood flowing into the slice has full signal and appears bright. No contrast is injected.

A saturation band placed on one side removes signal from vessels flowing the other way, so arteries can be shown without veins. Time of flight works best for flow perpendicular to the slice and can lose signal where flow is slow or in plane.
keypoints: Time of flight brightens inflowing unsaturated blood against saturated tissue.
It needs no contrast and is sensitive to through plane flow.
A saturation band suppresses veins to leave only arteries.

body.title: What is unique about phase contrast MRA?
body.html:
Phase contrast MRA encodes the velocity of moving blood into the phase of the signal using a bipolar gradient. Because it measures velocity, it can show both the vessel and the direction and speed of flow, and it can be made quantitative. An operator sets the velocity encoding value to match the expected flow.

If the velocity encoding is set too low, fast flow aliases and the measured velocity wraps around and reads wrongly. Phase contrast is slower than time of flight but gives flow information that time of flight cannot.
keypoints: Phase contrast encodes blood velocity into the signal phase.
It can measure the direction and speed of flow, not just show the vessel.
A velocity encoding set too low causes aliasing of fast flow.

body.title: What matters most in contrast enhanced MRA?
body.html:
Contrast enhanced MRA brightens the vessels by shortening the blood T1 with a gadolinium bolus, then imaging with a fast T1 weighted gradient echo. The single most important factor is timing: the centre of k space, which sets contrast, must be filled while the contrast is at peak concentration in the target arteries.

Timing is set with a small test bolus or with bolus tracking that triggers the scan when contrast reaches the vessel. Image too early and the arteries are faint, too late and the veins fill in and obscure them.
keypoints: Contrast enhanced MRA shortens blood T1 with a gadolinium bolus.
Timing the central k space to peak arterial contrast is critical.
Bolus tracking or a test bolus sets the delay.

body.title: How is MR venography performed?
body.html:
MR venography shows veins rather than arteries, most often to look for dural sinus thrombosis. It can be done with time of flight tuned to slow venous flow, with phase contrast at a low velocity encoding, or with a contrast enhanced acquisition timed to the venous phase.

On a time of flight venogram a saturation band is placed to remove arterial inflow so only veins remain. A clot appears as an absence of the normal flow signal within the sinus.
keypoints: MR venography images veins, often to find dural sinus thrombosis.
It uses time of flight, phase contrast, or contrast enhanced methods.
A thrombus shows as missing flow signal in the sinus.

body.title: Why is the anatomy centred at the magnet isocentre?
body.html:
The isocentre is the middle of the magnet where the static field is most uniform and the gradients are most linear. Positioning the region of interest at isocentre gives the best field homogeneity, which matters most for fat suppression and for any technique that depends on a uniform field.

The technologist places the coil over the anatomy, sets the landmark at the centre of the region, and advances the table so that landmark sits at isocentre. Poor centring degrades fat saturation and can cut off the edges of the imaged volume.
keypoints: The isocentre has the most uniform field and most linear gradients.
Centring the region of interest there improves fat suppression.
The landmark is set at the middle of the anatomy and moved to isocentre.

body.title: How do you choose and place the receiver coil?
body.html:
Signal to noise is best when the receiver coil is close to the anatomy and no larger than it needs to be. A small surface or dedicated coil placed right over the region collects strong signal, while an oversized coil adds noise from tissue it does not need to see.

Modern phased array coils combine several small elements to cover a larger area while keeping the high signal of small coils, and they enable parallel imaging for speed. The coil is centred over the landmark and secured so it does not move during the scan.
keypoints: A coil close to and sized for the anatomy gives the best signal to noise.
Phased array coils keep small coil signal over a larger area.
The coil is centred on the landmark and enables parallel imaging.

body.title: How do multiple sclerosis plaques appear on MRI?
body.html:
Multiple sclerosis plaques are bright on T2 and FLAIR. They are typically ovoid and sit around the ventricles, oriented perpendicular to them along the deep veins, a pattern described as Dawson's fingers. The corpus callosum, brainstem, and spinal cord are also common sites.

An enhancing plaque on post contrast T1 indicates active inflammation with a broken blood brain barrier, while old plaques do not enhance. Seeing lesions of different ages supports the diagnosis of disease spread over time.
keypoints: Plaques are bright on T2 and FLAIR and often periventricular.
Dawson's fingers point perpendicular to the ventricles.
Enhancement on post contrast T1 marks an active plaque.

body.title: What does contrast enhancement tell you?
body.html:
Gadolinium enhancement means the blood brain barrier has broken down or that tissue is very vascular, because contrast that normally stays inside vessels leaks into the tissue and shortens its T1. Enhancing tissue is bright on post contrast T1 weighted images.

The pattern of enhancement is a clue: a smooth thin ring suggests an abscess, a thick irregular ring suggests a high grade tumour, and enhancement along the brain surface suggests infection or tumour spread. Comparing with the pre contrast T1 confirms that the brightness is truly new enhancement and not fat or blood.
keypoints: Enhancement reflects blood brain barrier breakdown or high vascularity.
The ring pattern helps separate abscess from tumour.
Compare with pre contrast T1 to confirm true enhancement.

body.title: How is a gadolinium contrast reaction managed?
body.html:
Most reactions to gadolinium are mild, such as nausea or hives, and need only observation or an antihistamine. The team watches for the rare severe reaction with wheezing, throat swelling, or a fall in blood pressure, which is treated as anaphylaxis with epinephrine, oxygen, and emergency support.

Preparation matters: a screening interview identifies prior reactions and asthma, emergency equipment is kept ready, and staff know the escalation path. A patient with a documented prior reaction may be premedicated or imaged without contrast.
keypoints: Most gadolinium reactions are mild and need only observation or an antihistamine.
A severe reaction is treated as anaphylaxis with epinephrine and support.
Screening and ready emergency equipment prepare for the rare severe case.

body.title: How is a sedated or anxious patient monitored?
body.html:
A claustrophobic or paediatric patient may need sedation, and a sedated patient must be monitored throughout with MRI safe equipment. Pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and where needed capnography use non ferromagnetic monitors rated for the magnet, because ordinary equipment is a projectile hazard and its readings are corrupted by the field.

Simpler measures help many anxious patients avoid sedation: a clear explanation, a prone or feet first position, mirrors, and a squeeze ball for communication. A responsible escort and a recovery period are arranged whenever sedation is used.
keypoints: Sedated patients need continuous monitoring with MRI safe equipment.
Monitors must be non ferromagnetic and rated for the magnet.
Explanation, positioning, and a call device help avoid sedation.

body.title: What are transmit and receive coils?
body.html:
The radiofrequency system has two jobs. A transmit coil, usually the large body coil built into the bore, sends the radiofrequency pulse that tips the magnetisation. A receive coil, placed close to the anatomy, picks up the faint returning signal.

Because signal to noise is best when the receiver is near the tissue, dedicated surface and phased array receive coils are used for each body part. Phased array coils combine many small elements to keep high signal over a large area and to allow parallel imaging for faster scans.
keypoints: A transmit coil sends the radiofrequency pulse, a receive coil detects the signal.
Receive coils sit close to the anatomy for the best signal to noise.
Phased array coils cover a large area and enable parallel imaging.

body.title: What is a maximum intensity projection?
body.html:
A maximum intensity projection, or MIP, is a way to view a three dimensional data set as a single image. A ray is cast through the volume for each pixel and only the brightest voxel along that ray is kept, so the bright vessels of an MRA stand out while darker background tissue is dropped.

MIP images are usually made from several angles so the vessels can be seen in the round and overlapping structures separated. Because only the brightest voxel is kept, a MIP can hide a small low signal clot, so the source images are always reviewed as well.
keypoints: A MIP keeps the brightest voxel along each ray through the volume.
It displays bright MRA vessels against suppressed background.
Source images are still reviewed because a MIP can hide low signal.

body.title: What is peripheral nerve stimulation and what causes it?
body.html:
Rapidly switching gradient fields induce electric currents in the body. When the rate of change of the gradient (dB/dt) is high enough, those currents can depolarise peripheral nerves and cause tingling or muscle twitching, usually where the body is widest inside the bore.

Scanners limit dB/dt to stay below the stimulation threshold, which is why very fast sequences such as echo planar imaging may slow their gradients or lengthen the echo spacing. The effect is uncomfortable but not dangerous at approved limits, and it resolves the moment the gradients stop.
keypoints: Fast gradient switching (high dB/dt) induces currents that can stimulate peripheral nerves.
It feels like tingling or twitching and appears first where the body is widest in the bore.
Scanners cap dB/dt below the stimulation threshold, sometimes limiting how fast a sequence can run.

body.title: What is SAR and how does the scanner control RF heating?
body.html:
Specific absorption rate is the radiofrequency power deposited per kilogram of tissue, and it is the main cause of patient heating during a scan. SAR climbs with field strength, flip angle, the number of refocusing pulses, and how tightly the slices are packed in time.

When a sequence would exceed the SAR limit the scanner lengthens the TR, reduces the flip angle, or drops refocusing pulses, which is why a dense fast spin echo train can force a longer scan at 3 tesla. Good coil placement, no unnecessary skin to skin contact, and adequate cooling all reduce the heating risk.
keypoints: SAR is RF power deposited per kilogram and is the main source of patient heating.
It rises with field strength, flip angle, and the number of refocusing pulses.
The scanner protects the patient by lengthening TR or lowering flip angle when SAR is too high.

body.title: What must be verified before scanning a patient with an implant?
body.html:
Every implant must be identified and checked against its MR labeling before the patient enters the room. A device is MR safe if it poses no hazard, MR conditional if it is safe only within stated limits, and MR unsafe if it must never enter the field.

For a conditional device the technologist confirms the exact conditions, such as the maximum field strength, the maximum SAR, and any scan time limit, and configures the scanner to stay inside them. If the implant cannot be identified or its labeling cannot be confirmed, the scan does not proceed until a definitive source clears it.
keypoints: Implants are classified MR safe, MR conditional, or MR unsafe by their labeling.
A conditional implant is only safe within stated limits such as field strength and SAR.
An unidentified or unverified implant is a contraindication until it is positively cleared.

body.title: What is proton density weighting?
body.html:
A proton density image is made with a long TR and a short TE. The long TR lets nearly all tissues recover their longitudinal magnetisation, which removes most of the T1 difference, and the short TE reads the signal before much T2 decay, which removes most of the T2 difference.

What is left mostly reflects how many mobile hydrogen protons each tissue holds, so tissues with more protons look brighter. Proton density images give high signal and are useful in the brain and especially in joints, where they show cartilage and menisci well.
keypoints: Proton density weighting uses a long TR and a short TE to suppress both T1 and T2 contrast.
Brightness then tracks the number of mobile protons in each tissue.
It is valued in musculoskeletal imaging for cartilage and meniscal detail.

body.title: How does gadolinium change tissue signal?
body.html:
Gadolinium contrast is paramagnetic and mainly shortens T1 in the tissue where it collects. On a T1 weighted image that shortened T1 recovers more signal between pulses, so enhancing tissue turns bright.

Gadolinium marks areas where it can leak from vessels or pool, such as tumours, active inflammation, and regions where the blood brain barrier has broken down. At high local concentration it also shortens T2 and can paradoxically darken tissue, which is why enhancement is read on T1 weighted sequences.
keypoints: Gadolinium is paramagnetic and chiefly shortens T1, brightening enhancing tissue on T1 images.
It highlights tumours, inflammation, and blood brain barrier breakdown.
Enhancement is assessed on T1 weighting because high concentrations can darken T2.

body.title: What is the difference between T2 and T2 star?
body.html:
T2 decay reflects the loss of phase coherence from random spin to spin interactions, and a spin echo uses a 180 degree refocusing pulse to reverse the fixed part of that dephasing. T2 star is the faster decay seen when nothing refocuses the spins, so it also includes dephasing from fixed magnetic field non uniformity.

T2 star is always shorter than T2 and is what a gradient echo measures. That sensitivity to field distortion makes T2 star weighted imaging good for finding blood products, calcium, and iron, which all disturb the local field.
keypoints: T2 is spin to spin decay; a spin echo refocuses the fixed field-related dephasing.
T2 star adds dephasing from field non-uniformity and is always shorter than T2.
Gradient echo measures T2 star, making it sensitive to blood, calcium, and iron.

body.title: What sets the spatial resolution of an MR image?
body.html:
Spatial resolution is the size of the smallest object the image can separate, and it is set by the voxel dimensions. In plane, the voxel shrinks with a smaller field of view or a larger acquisition matrix, and through plane it shrinks with a thinner slice.

Smaller voxels resolve finer detail but hold fewer protons, so each one gives less signal and the image gets noisier. Raising resolution therefore usually costs signal to noise or scan time, and the technologist chooses the voxel that just resolves the anatomy of interest.
keypoints: Resolution is set by voxel size: field of view and matrix in plane, slice thickness through plane.
Smaller voxels resolve more detail but contain fewer protons and give less signal.
Higher resolution is paid for in signal to noise or in scan time.

body.title: How do averages (NEX) affect the image?
body.html:
The number of averages, also called NEX or signal averages, is how many times each line of data is collected and combined. Signal adds coherently while noise adds randomly, so averaging raises signal to noise in proportion to the square root of the number of averages.

Because of that square root, doubling the averages doubles the scan time but only raises signal to noise by about forty percent. Averaging also smooths out random motion, so it is often used to reduce ghosting even when the base signal is already adequate.
keypoints: Averaging combines repeated measurements; SNR rises with the square root of NEX.
Doubling NEX doubles scan time for only about a 40 percent SNR gain.
Averaging also blurs random motion, reducing ghost artifacts.

body.title: What is the tradeoff between SNR, resolution, and scan time?
body.html:
Signal to noise, spatial resolution, and scan time form a triangle in which improving one usually worsens another. Bigger voxels and more averaging raise signal to noise but cost resolution or time, while smaller voxels raise resolution but lower signal, and covering more phase encoding steps raises resolution at the cost of scan time.

No single setting is best; the technologist picks the balance that answers the clinical question. A screening study may favour speed and signal over fine detail, while a small internal ear study accepts a longer scan for very high resolution.
keypoints: SNR, resolution, and scan time trade against each other; gaining one usually costs another.
Larger voxels and more averages help SNR but hurt resolution or time.
The right balance depends on the clinical question, not a fixed recipe.

body.title: What is fast (turbo) spin echo and why is it faster?
body.html:
A conventional spin echo collects one line of data per TR. A fast or turbo spin echo applies a train of 180 degree refocusing pulses after each excitation, producing several echoes that are each phase encoded differently, so many lines are filled per TR.

The number of echoes per TR is the echo train length, and it divides the scan time by roughly that factor. The tradeoff is some image blurring and, because of the many refocusing pulses, higher SAR and a tendency for fat to stay bright.
keypoints: Fast spin echo fills several k-space lines per TR using a train of 180 degree pulses.
Scan time falls by roughly the echo train length.
Costs are some blurring, higher SAR, and persistently bright fat.

body.title: What is an echo train and how does it affect the image?
body.html:
An echo train is the group of echoes collected after a single excitation in a fast spin echo or echo planar sequence. Each echo is read at a slightly different time, so the signals in the train have slightly different T2 weighting.

The echo that fills the centre of k-space sets the effective echo time and therefore the image contrast, while the later, weaker echoes at the edges contribute detail but also introduce blurring. A longer train is faster but blurs more, so the length is chosen to balance speed against sharpness.
keypoints: An echo train is the set of echoes read after one excitation.
The echo filling the centre of k-space sets the effective TE and the contrast.
Longer trains are faster but blur more because later echoes have decayed.

body.title: What is a single-shot sequence?
body.html:
A single-shot sequence fills an entire slice of k-space after just one excitation pulse, using a very long echo train. Because the whole slice is frozen in a fraction of a second, it is highly resistant to motion.

Single-shot fast spin echo gives heavily T2 weighted images and is used for uncooperative patients, fetal imaging, and fluid-bright studies such as MR cholangiopancreatography. The price of that speed is lower signal to noise and more blurring than a multi-shot acquisition.
keypoints: Single-shot sequences acquire a whole slice from one excitation with a long echo train.
They are very motion resistant and give heavy T2 weighting.
They are used for uncooperative or fetal patients and fluid-bright studies like MRCP, at the cost of SNR.

body.title: What is the difference between frequency and phase encoding?
body.html:
After slice selection, position within the slice is encoded in two directions. A frequency encoding gradient is on while the echo is read, so position along that axis is coded as signal frequency and the whole axis is captured in one readout.

The other axis uses phase encoding: before each readout a brief gradient gives spins a position dependent phase, and the step is repeated with a different gradient strength for every line of k-space. Because phase encoding needs one repetition per line, it is what drives scan time, while frequency encoding costs almost nothing.
keypoints: Frequency encoding codes one axis during readout and captures it in a single echo.
Phase encoding codes the other axis one k-space line at a time.
Scan time scales with the number of phase encoding steps, not frequency encoding.

body.title: What is partial Fourier imaging?
body.html:
K-space is nearly symmetric, so in principle one half predicts the other. Partial Fourier imaging acquires only somewhat more than half of the phase encoding lines and mathematically synthesises the missing lines from that symmetry.

Collecting fewer lines shortens the scan or the echo time, which is useful for motion sensitive or fluid-bright imaging. The cost is lower signal to noise, because real data has been replaced by estimated data, and greater sensitivity to any imperfection that breaks the assumed symmetry.
keypoints: Partial Fourier acquires just over half of k-space and reconstructs the rest from its symmetry.
It shortens scan time or echo time.
The tradeoff is reduced SNR and sensitivity to anything that breaks k-space symmetry.

body.title: What is parallel imaging and how does it speed acquisition?
body.html:
Parallel imaging uses a phased array coil whose several elements each see the anatomy from a different position. Because each element adds independent spatial information, the sequence can skip some phase encoding lines and still reconstruct a full image.

Skipping lines cuts scan time by an acceleration factor, or buys higher resolution in the same time. The cost is a signal to noise penalty that grows with the acceleration factor, and reconstruction artifacts if the coil calibration is imperfect.
keypoints: Parallel imaging exploits the distinct spatial views of phased array coil elements.
Skipping phase encoding lines shortens the scan by the acceleration factor.
It costs SNR that worsens with acceleration and can leave reconstruction artifacts.

body.title: What do the gradient coils do?
body.html:
Gradient coils add a small, controllable slope to the main magnetic field along each axis. That slope makes the field, and therefore the resonant frequency, vary with position, which is how the scanner selects a slice and encodes location within it.

Rapidly switching these coils is what produces the loud knocking of a scan, because the current pulses make the coil vibrate against its mounts. Stronger and faster gradients allow thinner slices, higher resolution, and faster sequences, but they also raise the risk of peripheral nerve stimulation.
keypoints: Gradient coils tilt the main field so frequency varies with position.
This enables slice selection and spatial encoding, and their switching causes the scan noise.
Stronger, faster gradients improve resolution and speed but can stimulate nerves.

body.title: What is a phased array coil and why does it help?
body.html:
A phased array is a receive coil built from several small elements, each with its own receiver channel. A small element sits close to the anatomy and has a high signal to noise ratio but only over a small region, and the array combines many of them to cover a large field of view without losing that local sensitivity.

Because each element also views the anatomy from a distinct position, a phased array is what makes parallel imaging possible. The result is better signal to noise over a large area and the option to accelerate the scan.
keypoints: A phased array combines many small receive elements, each with its own channel.
It keeps the high SNR of small coils while covering a large field of view.
Its multiple viewpoints enable parallel imaging acceleration.

body.title: How does field strength affect imaging?
body.html:
A higher field strength, such as 3 tesla compared with 1.5 tesla, gives more signal because a larger fraction of protons align with the field. That extra signal can be spent on higher resolution or faster scans.

Higher field also has costs: SAR rises roughly with the square of the field so heating is greater, chemical shift and susceptibility artifacts are larger, and some implants are only conditional at 1.5 tesla. The choice of field strength balances this signal gain against the added artifact and safety burden.
keypoints: Higher field strength yields more signal, which buys resolution or speed.
It also raises SAR steeply and enlarges chemical shift and susceptibility artifacts.
Some implants are conditional only at lower field, so field choice is a tradeoff.

body.title: What causes flow-related ghosting from vessels?
body.html:
Blood moving through the slice carries its phase with it, so from one phase encoding step to the next a vessel presents a different signal. Because phase encoding assumes the signal is steady between steps, that pulsatile change is mismapped and repeated copies of the vessel appear.

These ghosts smear along the phase encoding direction and can obscure nearby anatomy. They are reduced with flow compensation gradients, by placing saturation bands over incoming vessels, or by swapping the phase and frequency directions so the ghosts fall away from the region of interest.
keypoints: Pulsatile flow changes a vessel's signal between phase encoding steps, creating ghosts.
Ghosts repeat along the phase encoding direction and can cover anatomy.
Flow compensation, saturation bands, or swapping phase and frequency reduce them.

body.title: What is aliasing (wraparound) and how is it fixed?
body.html:
Aliasing, or wraparound, happens when anatomy extends beyond the field of view in the phase encoding direction. The part outside is under sampled, so it is misread and folds back onto the opposite side of the image.

It is removed by enlarging the field of view, by oversampling in the phase direction so the extra anatomy is properly sampled, or by placing saturation bands on the tissue that would fold in. Frequency direction wrap is usually handled automatically by digital oversampling of the readout.
keypoints: Aliasing folds anatomy outside the field of view back onto the image.
It occurs mainly in the phase encoding direction where sampling is limited.
Enlarging the field of view, phase oversampling, or saturation bands fix it.

body.title: What causes susceptibility artifact and where is it worst?
body.html:
Magnetic susceptibility artifact arises where tissues of very different magnetisability meet, such as air next to bone or metal next to soft tissue. The abrupt change distorts the local field, which dephases spins and shifts their apparent position, producing signal loss and geometric warping.

It is worst on gradient echo and echo planar sequences because they do not refocus fixed field non-uniformity, and it grows with field strength and echo time. A spin echo, a shorter echo time, and a smaller voxel all reduce it, while the same sensitivity is deliberately used to detect blood and metal.
keypoints: Susceptibility artifact comes from field distortion at air, bone, and metal interfaces.
It causes signal loss and geometric distortion, worst on gradient echo and EPI.
Spin echo, shorter TE, and smaller voxels reduce it; it is also exploited to find blood and metal.

body.title: Why does fat create chemical shift and a bright signal?
body.html:
Hydrogen in fat sits in a different chemical environment than hydrogen in water, so it resonates at a slightly lower frequency, about 3.5 parts per million below water. Because the scanner turns frequency into position, that frequency offset shifts fat a few pixels along the frequency encoding axis, the classic chemical shift artifact.

Fat also has a very short T1, so it recovers signal quickly and looks bright on T1 weighted and many fast spin echo images. That brightness can hide pathology, which is why fat suppression is often applied.
keypoints: Fat protons resonate about 3.5 ppm below water, causing a chemical shift along the frequency axis.
Fat's short T1 makes it bright on T1 and fast spin echo images.
Bright fat can obscure pathology, motivating fat suppression.

body.title: How does spectral fat saturation work and when does it fail?
body.html:
Spectral or chemical fat saturation sends a radiofrequency pulse tuned to the fat frequency just before the imaging pulse, tipping and then spoiling the fat signal so fat is dark while water is untouched. It gives clean, selective suppression when the field is uniform.

It fails where the field is inhomogeneous, such as near metal, at the edges of a large field of view, or off isocentre, because there the fat frequency drifts out from under the saturation pulse. In those situations an inversion method like STIR, which suppresses by T1 rather than frequency, is more reliable.
keypoints: Spectral fat saturation applies an RF pulse at the fat frequency to null fat selectively.
It needs a uniform field and fails near metal, off centre, or at large field of view edges.
STIR, which suppresses by T1, is the robust fallback in inhomogeneous fields.

body.title: Why should STIR be avoided after gadolinium?
body.html:
STIR suppresses fat by choosing an inversion time at which fat, which has a short T1, is passing through zero signal. The problem is that this nulling is based on T1, not on any property unique to fat.

Gadolinium shortens the T1 of enhancing tissue toward that of fat, so STIR can null the enhancement along with the fat and hide the very finding the contrast was given to show. After gadolinium, a spectral fat saturated T1 sequence is used instead, because it suppresses fat by frequency and leaves enhancement bright.
keypoints: STIR nulls tissue by T1, not by a fat-specific property.
Gadolinium shortens enhancing tissue toward fat's T1, so STIR can erase enhancement.
Post-contrast imaging uses spectral fat saturation to keep enhancement visible.

body.title: What is isotropic imaging and multiplanar reformation?
body.html:
An isotropic acquisition uses voxels that are equal in all three dimensions. Because the voxel is a cube, the data set can be reformatted into any plane without losing resolution.

This lets a single 3D acquisition be reviewed as axial, sagittal, coronal, or oblique images through multiplanar reformation, rather than acquiring each plane separately. It saves scan time overall and lets curved structures be followed, at the cost of a longer single acquisition and greater motion sensitivity.
keypoints: Isotropic voxels are equal in all three dimensions, so they reformat without losing resolution.
One 3D data set can be viewed in any plane by multiplanar reformation.
This replaces separate plane acquisitions but is longer and more motion sensitive.

body.title: What is a volumetric gradient echo sequence used for?
body.html:
A volumetric gradient echo excites a whole slab and phase encodes it in two directions to build a 3D data set of thin, contiguous slices. Using a gradient echo keeps the TR short so the large number of encoding steps stays feasible in time.

These sequences give high resolution isotropic T1 weighted volumes used for brain anatomy, contrast enhanced angiography, and any study that will be reformatted. Their weaknesses are sensitivity to susceptibility and to motion across the longer acquisition.
keypoints: Volumetric gradient echo encodes a slab in two directions for thin contiguous slices.
The short gradient echo TR keeps the many-step 3D acquisition feasible.
It yields high resolution T1 volumes for anatomy and angiography but is susceptibility and motion sensitive.

body.title: What are the tradeoffs of 3D imaging versus 2D?
body.html:
A 3D acquisition phase encodes through the slab as well as in plane, which gives thinner contiguous slices, higher signal to noise per voxel, and isotropic data for reformatting. It is the right choice when fine, arbitrary plane detail is needed.

The costs are a longer acquisition, more motion sensitivity because the whole slab is spoiled by movement, and higher SAR from the added pulses. A 2D acquisition, with its thicker gapped slices, remains faster and more robust for routine survey imaging.
keypoints: 3D gives thin contiguous slices, more SNR per voxel, and isotropic reformatting.
It costs scan time, motion robustness, and SAR compared with 2D.
2D stays faster and more robust for routine survey imaging.

body.title: Why is the region of interest centred at isocentre?
body.html:
The isocentre is the point where the main field is most uniform and the gradients are most linear. Placing the anatomy of interest there gives the best fat suppression, the least geometric distortion, and the highest signal.

Away from isocentre the field drifts and the gradients bend, so spectral fat saturation can fail and structures can appear warped. The technologist therefore lands the coil and table so the target anatomy, not the patient's overall centre, sits at isocentre.
keypoints: Isocentre has the most uniform field and the most linear gradients.
Centring anatomy there optimises fat suppression, geometry, and signal.
Off centre positioning causes distortion and failed spectral fat saturation.

body.title: How does coil-to-anatomy proximity affect the scan?
body.html:
A receive coil picks up the most signal from tissue close to its elements, and its sensitivity falls off quickly with distance. Placing the coil snugly against the region of interest therefore raises signal to noise and lets the technologist use higher resolution.

A coil that is too large or sits far from the anatomy wastes signal and may fold in distant tissue. The rule is to choose the smallest coil that still covers the target and to bring it as close as comfort and safety allow, keeping any conductive part off bare skin to avoid a heating loop.
keypoints: Coil sensitivity is highest near its elements and falls off rapidly with distance.
A snug, appropriately small coil maximises SNR and enables higher resolution.
Conductive coil parts must not touch bare skin, to avoid an RF heating loop.

body.title: What positioning steps reduce motion and improve comfort?
body.html:
Motion is the most common cause of a repeated sequence, and much of it is prevented at positioning. Supporting the part in a neutral, relaxed posture, padding pressure points, and immobilising with straps or cushions all reduce both voluntary and involuntary movement over a long scan.

Comfort measures double as safety and quality steps: hearing protection guards against the loud gradients, clear instructions and a squeeze ball reduce anxiety, and padding between the patient and the bore or coil prevents both pressure sores and conductive loops. A comfortable, well supported patient holds still, which protects image quality.
keypoints: Most repeats are from motion, much of which is prevented at positioning.
Neutral posture, padding, and immobilisation reduce movement over a long scan.
Hearing protection and padding between skin and hardware are safety and quality steps.

body.title: Patient positioning and coil setup: centering, comfort, and image quality
body.html:
Good images begin before the first pulse, at how the patient and coil are set up. The goal is to place the region of interest at the magnet isocenter, where the field is most uniform and the gradients most linear, because that is where fat suppression works best and geometry is truest. The technologist lands the coil and table on the target anatomy rather than on the patient's overall center.

The receive coil should be the smallest one that still covers the anatomy, brought as close as comfort allows, because coil sensitivity and therefore signal to noise fall off quickly with distance. Positioning is also the main defense against motion, the commonest cause of a repeated scan: a neutral relaxed posture, padding at pressure points, and immobilization all help the patient hold still. The same padding keeps conductive parts of the coil and cables off bare skin, which prevents an RF heating loop, and hearing protection guards against the loud gradient noise.
keypoints: Center the region of interest at isocenter for the best field uniformity, fat suppression, and geometry.
Use the smallest coil that covers the anatomy and place it close, because SNR falls off with distance.
Positioning is the main defense against motion, the commonest cause of repeats.
Padding and cable routing keep conductors off skin to prevent RF heating loops.
body.worked_example: A lumbar spine study is set up by landing the coil on the L3 region so the mid lumbar spine sits at isocenter, not by centring on the patient's waist.
