A spine array is chosen over the body coil for its higher local signal, foam pads are placed under the knees to flatten the lordosis and ease the back, and cushions immobilize the pelvis. Ear plugs go in, the cable is routed clear of the skin, and the patient is given a squeeze ball, which together cut both motion repeats and heating risk.
memory_hooks: Center the anatomy, not the patient, at isocenter.
Smallest covering coil, placed close, wins on signal to noise.
Pad for comfort, immobilization, and to keep conductors off skin.
exam_traps: Do not center on the patient's body midpoint; off-center anatomy loses fat suppression and distorts.
A larger coil or one held away from the part wastes signal and can fold in distant tissue.
STIR is not a substitute for correct centering; poor positioning still degrades every sequence.

body.title: Linear vs macrocyclic gadolinium agents
body.html:
Gadolinium is toxic as a free ion, so it is bound inside a chelate. The shape of that chelate sets how tightly the ion is held. Macrocyclic agents cage the ion in a closed ring and are the most stable. Linear agents hold it in an open chain and release more free gadolinium over time.

Free gadolinium can deposit in tissue, including brain, bone, and skin. Because of this, macrocyclic agents are now preferred, and several high risk linear agents have been restricted. Retention is usually seen without known symptoms, but the stability class is why one agent is chosen over another.
keypoints: Gadolinium is caged in a chelate because the free ion is toxic.
Macrocyclic agents are the most stable; linear agents release more free gadolinium.
Macrocyclic agents are preferred and reduce tissue retention risk.

body.title: Acute reactions to gadolinium contrast
body.html:
Gadolinium reactions are far less common than iodinated contrast reactions, but they still occur. Most are mild, such as nausea, hives, or a warm feeling. Severe reactions like bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, or anaphylaxis are rare but possible.

Screening asks about prior contrast reactions and severe allergies. The room should have emergency medication and monitoring ready before any injection. Mild reactions are watched and treated symptomatically; severe reactions need epinephrine, airway support, and rapid escalation.
keypoints: Gadolinium reactions are rarer than iodinated contrast reactions.
Most are mild; severe anaphylaxis is uncommon but possible.
Emergency drugs and monitoring must be ready before injection.

body.title: How gadolinium is given and timed
body.html:
Gadolinium is injected intravenously, usually weight based, and often followed by a saline flush to push the bolus into the central circulation. A power injector gives a reproducible rate when tight timing matters.

Timing is what turns a dose into a diagnostic study. Dynamic imaging captures arterial, then venous, then delayed phases as the agent washes in and out, which characterizes lesions by their enhancement pattern. A fixed delayed scan is used when late enhancement is the target, such as scar or slow uptake tissue.
keypoints: Dose is weight based and given intravenously, often with a saline flush.
Dynamic imaging captures arterial, venous, and delayed phases.
Delayed scans target late enhancement such as scar.

body.title: Why is FLAIR useful for brain lesions?
body.html:
FLAIR is a T2 weighted sequence with an inversion pulse timed to null the signal from cerebrospinal fluid. On a plain T2 image, bright CSF sits right next to bright lesions and hides them. FLAIR removes the CSF signal, so a bright lesion beside a ventricle or in the cortex stands out.

That is why FLAIR is the workhorse for white matter disease, multiple sclerosis plaques, and cortical or periventricular lesions. The tissue contrast is still T2 based; only the fluid has been darkened.
keypoints: FLAIR is T2 weighted with the CSF signal nulled.
Darkening CSF reveals lesions that sit next to fluid.
It is the workhorse for periventricular and cortical disease.

body.title: How does blood change appearance as it ages?
body.html:
Hemorrhage does not look the same over time because the iron in blood changes chemical form. Fresh oxyhemoglobin gives way to deoxyhemoglobin, then methemoglobin, and finally hemosiderin. Each form has different magnetic properties, so the signal on T1 and T2 shifts as the clot matures.

A useful anchor: subacute blood with methemoglobin is bright on T1, which is why a bright T1 focus can mean hemorrhage rather than fat or contrast. Old blood leaves hemosiderin that is dark on T2 and blooms on gradient echo and susceptibility images.
keypoints: Blood signal changes as iron shifts from oxy to deoxy to met to hemosiderin.
Subacute methemoglobin is bright on T1.
Old hemosiderin is dark on T2 and blooms on susceptibility imaging.

body.title: Which implants and devices are MRI concerns?
body.html:
Screening sorts devices into three labels. MR safe items have no metal and pose no risk. MR conditional items are safe only within stated limits, such as a field strength, a gradient rate, or an SAR ceiling. MR unsafe items must never enter the room.

Common concerns include cardiac pacemakers and defibrillators, cochlear implants, some aneurysm clips, and metallic foreign bodies in the eye. The safe answer is never to assume; the exact device is checked against its labeling before the patient goes near the magnet.
keypoints: Devices are labeled MR safe, MR conditional, or MR unsafe.
Conditional devices are safe only within stated scan limits.
Pacemakers, cochlear implants, clips, and orbital metal need verification.

body.title: How is comfort managed for a long scan?
body.html:
A diagnostic scan can take many minutes, and a patient who cannot hold still ruins the images. Comfort is therefore part of image quality, not a courtesy. Padding supports the joints, warmth and blankets reduce shivering, and clear explanation of the noise and duration lowers anxiety.

Hearing protection is required because the gradients are loud. A call squeeze ball lets the patient signal at any time, and regular contact through the intercom keeps them oriented. A calm, well positioned patient moves less, which directly improves the study.
keypoints: Comfort reduces motion, so it is part of image quality.
Padding, warmth, and clear explanation lower anxiety and shivering.
Hearing protection and a call ball are required for every scan.

body.title: What does a saturation band do for flow?
body.html:
A saturation band is a slab of tissue that receives an extra radiofrequency pulse to suppress its signal before the main acquisition. Blood flowing out of a saturated slab carries no signal, so it appears dark when it reaches the imaging volume.

In angiography this selects flow direction. Placing a saturation band above the slice removes venous inflow from one side, leaving only the arteries bright, or the reverse. It is also used to blank moving tissue that would otherwise ghost across the image.
keypoints: A saturation band pre-suppresses signal in a chosen slab.
Blood leaving that slab arrives dark in the imaging volume.
It selects artery or vein inflow and reduces ghosting.

body.title: MR safety: the static field, zones and projectiles
body.html:
The static magnetic field is always on, even when no scan is running, and it never turns off between patients. That single fact drives the biggest hazard in the suite: any ferromagnetic object brought too close becomes a projectile that accelerates toward the bore. Oxygen cylinders, mop buckets, scissors, and IV poles have all caused serious incidents.

Access is controlled by a four zone scheme. Zone I is public space, Zone II is the screening area, Zone III is the controlled area around the control room, and Zone IV is the magnet room itself. Only screened people and MR safe or verified conditional equipment cross into Zone IV. The field strength falls off with distance but does so steeply, so the dangerous region is close to the bore.

A quench is the sudden loss of superconductivity that boils off the cryogen and can vent helium into the room. It is rare, drops the field, and is an emergency because the room can lose oxygen. The quench button is a last resort, not a way to stop a scan.
keypoints: The static field is always on, including overnight and between patients.
Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles near the bore.
The four zone scheme controls who and what reaches the magnet.
A quench boils off cryogen and is an oxygen emergency.
body.worked_example: A porter wheels a standard steel oxygen cylinder toward a patient in Zone IV. As it passes the bore opening the field grips it and pulls it into the magnet at speed. The lesson is procedural, not physical: MR safe aluminum cylinders and screened equipment are the only gas supplies allowed past Zone III, and the fix is screening at the door, not reflexes at the bore.
memory_hooks: Always on means always dangerous: the field does not wait for a scan.
Four zones, one rule: nothing crosses into Zone IV unscreened.
exam_traps: Thinking the field is off when no scan runs; it is superconducting and permanent.
Confusing the quench button with a scan stop; a quench is an emergency, not a pause.

body.title: MR safety: acoustic noise, nerve stimulation and monitoring
body.html:
Beyond the static field, the changing gradients create their own hazards. Switching gradients push against the static field and vibrate the coil, which produces the loud knocking of a scan. Levels routinely exceed the threshold where hearing protection is required, so earplugs or headphones are mandatory for every patient, including the sedated and the very young.

Fast gradient switching can also cause peripheral nerve stimulation, felt as a twitch or tingle in the skin. Scanners limit the gradient slew rate to stay below this threshold, which is why very fast sequences are constrained. It is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, but it signals that the hardware is near its regulatory ceiling.

Because many patients cannot be watched directly inside the bore, monitoring matters. Sedated or unstable patients need MR conditional pulse oximetry and the means to communicate. A patient who can squeeze a call ball and hear the intercom is a patient who can report a problem before it becomes an incident.
keypoints: Gradient switching drives the acoustic noise of a scan.
Hearing protection is required for every patient, no exceptions.
Fast gradients can cause peripheral nerve stimulation, so slew rate is limited.
Sedated patients need MR conditional monitoring and a way to signal.
body.worked_example: A sequence is sped up by raising the gradient slew rate. The patient reports a tingling twitch across the abdomen. That is peripheral nerve stimulation, the body reaching the gradient limit before any imaging harm occurs. The operator backs off the slew rate; the scanner would otherwise cap it automatically to stay within the regulatory bound.
memory_hooks: Loud comes from the gradients, not the magnet.
A twitch means the gradients are at the edge; the fix is to slow the switching.
exam_traps: Blaming acoustic noise on the static field; it comes from gradient switching.
Assuming nerve stimulation is dangerous; it is a comfort limit that flags the gradient ceiling.

body.title: Motion and flow artifacts: ghosting, wrap and the fixes
body.html:
Most artifacts that streak an image trace back to something that moved or something that flowed. Both express themselves along the phase encoding direction, because phase is measured across many separate repetitions and any change between them is misread as position. Breathing, pulsing vessels, and swallowing all print faint copies, called ghosts, spread across that axis.

Flowing blood is a special case. Spins that move between excitation and readout can be mismapped, producing bright or dark ghosts that march across the image in step with the heartbeat. This is why a pulsing artery can smear a line right through the anatomy of interest.

The fixes follow the cause. Swapping the phase and frequency directions moves a ghost off the anatomy. Saturation bands blank the moving tissue. Flow compensation rephases moving spins, and cardiac or respiratory gating ties the acquisition to the cycle so each line is captured at the same moment. Wrap, or aliasing, is a related trap: anatomy outside a too small field of view folds back onto the image, fixed by enlarging the field or oversampling.
keypoints: Motion and flow artifacts appear along the phase encoding axis.
Pulsatile flow ghosts march across the image with the heartbeat.
Swapping phase and frequency moves a ghost off the anatomy.
Wrap folds outside anatomy back in and is fixed by a larger field or oversampling.
body.worked_example: A knee scan shows a pulsing artery ghosting a bright line across the meniscus. Two independent fixes help: swap phase and frequency so the ghost lands outside the joint, and add flow compensation so the moving blood is rephased. Either can rescue the study; combining them is common when the vessel sits right over the target.
memory_hooks: Ghosts always ride the phase axis.
If it moved or it flowed, look along phase encoding.
exam_traps: Expecting motion ghosts along the frequency direction; they follow phase encoding.
Confusing flow ghosting with wrap; wrap is field of view too small, not motion.

body.title: 3D acquisition: isotropic voxels and the sequences that make them
body.html:
A 3D acquisition encodes a whole slab at once with a second phase encoding along the slice direction, rather than exciting one thin slice at a time. The payoff is thin, contiguous partitions with high signal and, when the voxel is equal in all three dimensions, true isotropic data. Isotropic data can be reformatted into any plane after the fact without a loss of detail.

The named sequences reflect this. A spoiled gradient echo volume such as MPRAGE gives sharp T1 brain anatomy for surgical planning and reformats. A long echo train spin echo volume, called SPACE or CUBE depending on the vendor, delivers T2 or FLAIR contrast across a whole region in one scan that can be sliced any way the reader needs.

The cost is time and a sensitivity to motion, since the whole slab is spoiled by movement rather than a single slice. That is the tradeoff behind choosing 3D: pay in scan time and motion risk, receive isotropic data that reformats freely and reconstructs cleanly into MIP and curved views.
keypoints: 3D encodes a whole slab with a second phase encode along slice.
Isotropic voxels reformat into any plane without losing detail.
MPRAGE gives T1 volumes; SPACE or CUBE give T2 or FLAIR volumes.
The tradeoff is longer scans and greater motion sensitivity.
body.worked_example: A surgeon needs the same brain data viewed axially, sagittally, and coronally for planning. A single isotropic MPRAGE volume is acquired once, then reformatted into all three planes from one dataset. Acquiring three separate 2D stacks would cost more time and would not align voxel for voxel the way one isotropic volume does.
memory_hooks: Isotropic means slice it any way you like, later.
One 3D volume beats three 2D stacks when reformats are the goal.
exam_traps: Assuming 3D is always better; it costs time and punishes motion across the whole slab.
Forgetting that only isotropic voxels reformat without a loss of resolution.

body.title: Choosing a fat suppression method: strengths and pitfalls
body.html:
There is no single best way to suppress fat; each method trades robustness against precision. Spectral fat saturation targets the fat resonance directly and gives clean, selective suppression, but it depends on a uniform field. Off center and at low field it fails unevenly, leaving bright fat on one side of the image.

STIR suppresses fat by its short T1 using an inversion pulse, so it is robust where the field is imperfect, including large fields of view and the extremities. The catch is that it also suppresses anything with a fat like T1, such as some contrast enhancement, which is why STIR and gadolinium are a poor pair.

Dixon methods separate water and fat by their signal phase and produce both suppressed and combined images from one acquisition, which is robust and informative but needs the reconstruction. Water excitation only excites water in the first place. The exam relevant skill is matching the method to the situation: uniform small field favors spectral, difficult field favors STIR, and the need for reliable uniform suppression plus in and out of phase data favors Dixon.
keypoints: Spectral saturation is selective but needs a uniform field.
STIR is field robust but also nulls fat like T1, so avoid it with gadolinium.
Dixon separates water and fat and yields several image sets from one scan.
The skill is matching the method to field strength and uniformity.
body.worked_example: A large field of view ankle at the edge of the magnet shows patchy failed fat saturation with spectral suppression. Switching to STIR fixes it because STIR relies on T1, not on a uniform fat resonance. If the same study needed post contrast imaging, STIR would be wrong, since it would also suppress the enhancing tissue, and Dixon would be the better robust choice.
memory_hooks: Uniform field favors spectral; difficult field favors STIR.
STIR plus gadolinium is a trap: it nulls the enhancement too.
exam_traps: Using STIR after contrast; it suppresses enhancing tissue along with fat.
Expecting spectral saturation to work off center or at low field.

body.title: Diffusion in disease: stroke, abscess and cellular tumors
body.html:
Diffusion weighted imaging measures how freely water moves. Where movement is hindered, the DWI image stays bright and the ADC map goes dark, the pattern called restricted diffusion. Reading the pair together is essential, because bright DWI alone can be a T2 effect rather than true restriction. Confirming a low ADC is what proves the finding.

The clinical value is in what restricts. Acute ischemic stroke restricts within minutes as the sodium pump fails and cells swell, which makes DWI the earliest and most sensitive sign of infarct. A pus filled abscess restricts because its thick contents trap water, which helps separate it from a necrotic tumor whose center usually does not. Densely cellular tumors restrict because tightly packed cells leave little room for water to move.

The exam skill is to pair the sequences and know the differential. Restricted diffusion is a strong, early, specific sign, but only when DWI bright is matched by ADC dark. The trap, called T2 shine through, is bright DWI with a normal or high ADC, which is not restriction at all.
keypoints: Restricted diffusion is DWI bright with ADC dark, read as a pair.
Acute stroke restricts within minutes, so DWI is the earliest infarct sign.
Abscess and densely cellular tumor also restrict; necrotic tumor centers usually do not.
T2 shine through is bright DWI with normal ADC, which is not restriction.
body.worked_example: A ring enhancing brain lesion could be an abscess or a necrotic tumor. DWI shows a bright center; the ADC map confirms the center is dark. Restricted diffusion in the cavity favors abscess, because pus traps water, whereas a necrotic tumor center typically does not restrict. The ADC map is what settles it.
memory_hooks: Real restriction is bright DWI and dark ADC together.
Stroke lights up on DWI first, before T2 and FLAIR catch up.
exam_traps: Calling any bright DWI restriction; check the ADC to exclude T2 shine through.
Assuming a ring enhancing lesion is always tumor; a restricting center suggests abscess.

body.title: Perfusion by DSC: first-pass bolus tracking
body.html:
Dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) MRI tracks a rapid bolus of gadolinium as it first passes through brain tissue, using fast T2*-weighted (or T2-weighted) echo-planar imaging repeated every one to two seconds. Gadolinium is not being watched for its usual T1 brightening here; instead its local magnetic susceptibility disturbs the field around vessels and causes a transient, sharp drop in signal intensity as the bolus passes through the capillary bed, an effect that grows with tissue vascularity.

Plotting signal loss over time yields a concentration-time curve, whose shape drives the postprocessing. Integrating the curve gives relative cerebral blood volume (CBV), its height and timing feed cerebral blood flow (CBF), and dividing CBV by CBF gives mean transit time (MTT). A second, smaller signal dip often follows as contrast recirculates through the systemic circulation, and this recirculation must be modeled out or it will bias the curve. Because the whole technique depends on catching a sharp bolus, a fast, tight power-injector bolus and rapid whole-brain coverage are essential; a slow or spread-out injection blurs the curve and degrades the maps.
keypoints: DSC uses a fast gadolinium bolus and T2*-weighted EPI, imaged every 1 to 2 seconds.
Susceptibility from the bolus causes a transient signal drop, not enhancement.
Postprocessing yields CBV, CBF, and MTT maps from the concentration-time curve.
Recirculation produces a second, smaller signal dip that must be corrected for.
Requires a tight, fast power-injector bolus for reliable curves.
body.worked_example: A patient with a suspected high-grade glioma undergoes DSC perfusion as part of the brain tumor protocol. As the gadolinium bolus arrives, the tumor region shows a much deeper and faster signal drop than normal white matter, reflecting its dense, leaky neovasculature. The resulting relative CBV map shows a hot spot with values several times normal gray matter, a pattern that correlates with higher tumor grade and helps guide the biopsy target toward the most aggressive-appearing region.
memory_hooks: DSC: Drop in Signal, Contrast bolus, on T2*. Signal goes down as gadolinium passes.
CBV from the area under the curve, CBF from how fast and how high it rises, MTT equals CBV divided by CBF.
Think stroke and tumor grade: DSC is the fast bolus-chasing sequence.
exam_traps: DSC signal drops during the bolus (T2* susceptibility effect); do not confuse this with the signal rise seen on T1-weighted DCE enhancement curves.
CBV, CBF, and MTT are all derived from the same DSC acquisition; they are not three separate scans.
A slow or poorly timed injection ruins the first-pass curve; DSC is uniquely sensitive to bolus technique compared with DCE.

body.title: Perfusion by DCE: permeability and Ktrans
body.html:
Dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI uses repeated T1-weighted acquisitions before, during, and after a gadolinium injection to watch tissue enhance over several minutes, in contrast to the seconds-long bolus tracking of DSC. Because gadolinium shortens T1, tissue that takes up contrast brightens, and the shape of the resulting signal-time (enhancement) curve, how steeply it rises, how high it peaks, and whether it plateaus or washes out, characterizes the underlying tissue.

Pharmacokinetic modeling of this curve produces quantitative maps of capillary permeability. The key parameter is Ktrans, the transfer constant describing how quickly contrast leaks from plasma into the extravascular extracellular space; a related parameter, ve, describes the size of that extravascular extracellular space. Tumors with immature, leaky neovasculature typically show high Ktrans and rapid washout, so DCE is used for tumor characterization, distinguishing benign from malignant lesions, and for monitoring treatment response, since effective antiangiogenic therapy can lower Ktrans before a tumor visibly shrinks. Where DSC is a T2* bolus-tracking technique built around CBV, DCE is a T1 permeability technique built around Ktrans.
keypoints: DCE uses repeated T1-weighted imaging over minutes to track contrast uptake and washout.
The enhancement curve shape (rise, peak, washout) reflects tissue vascularity and permeability.
Ktrans is the transfer constant quantifying capillary permeability; ve is the extravascular extracellular space fraction.
High Ktrans and fast washout suggest aggressive, leaky tumor vasculature.
DCE (T1, permeability) is distinct from DSC (T2*, first-pass bolus).
body.worked_example: A patient with a suspicious prostate lesion undergoes multiparametric MRI including DCE. The lesion shows early, rapid enhancement followed by washout on the signal-time curve, a pattern with high Ktrans consistent with the leaky, disorganized vasculature of prostate cancer, whereas benign tissue nearby shows slow, progressive enhancement without washout. Combined with the anatomic and diffusion sequences, this DCE pattern raises suspicion and supports targeting that region for biopsy.
memory_hooks: DCE: Dynamic Contrast Enhancement, T1-weighted, minutes-long curve, tissue signal goes up.
Ktrans equals transfer constant equals how fast contrast leaks out of the vessel into tissue.
DSC drops on T2* in seconds; DCE rises on T1 over minutes.
exam_traps: Do not swap DCE and DSC: DCE is T1-weighted enhancement over minutes, DSC is T2*-weighted signal drop over seconds.
Ktrans measures permeability, not blood volume; CBV is a DSC parameter, not a DCE parameter.
Rapid washout on DCE suggests malignancy, but curve shape must be read alongside anatomic and diffusion findings, not in isolation.

body.title: Arterial spin labeling: perfusion without contrast
body.html:
Arterial spin labeling (ASL) measures brain perfusion without any injected contrast agent. Instead, an inversion pulse is applied to arterial blood water proximal to the imaging slab, magnetically labeling it as it flows toward the brain. After a delay that lets the labeled blood reach the tissue of interest, a label image is acquired; a second control image is acquired without labeling. Subtracting control from label removes static tissue signal and leaves a small residual signal proportional to blood delivered to tissue, the perfusion-weighted image, from which quantitative cerebral blood flow (CBF) maps are calculated.

Two main labeling schemes are used: pulsed ASL (PASL), which inverts a thick slab in a single short pulse, and pseudo-continuous ASL (pCASL), which labels for one to two seconds using a train of rapid pulses and generally gives higher SNR and is now the more widely recommended approach. The post-label delay (PLD), the time between labeling and image acquisition, must be long enough for labeled blood to reach the tissue but short enough that the label has not decayed; too short a PLD in a patient with slow or collateral flow can underestimate perfusion. Because the label and control difference is only a percent or two of brain signal, ASL is inherently low SNR and requires many repeated averages to build an adequate image. Its major advantages are that it needs no gadolinium, useful in renal impairment, pediatric patients, and anyone needing repeated serial follow-up, and that it is fully quantitative, yielding CBF in physical units directly rather than only relative maps.
keypoints: ASL labels arterial blood water with an inversion pulse instead of using injected contrast.
A control image is subtracted from the label image to isolate the small perfusion signal.
pCASL generally gives higher SNR than PASL and is the more widely recommended technique.
Post-label delay (PLD) must be tuned to transit time; too short a PLD underestimates flow in slow-flow states.
ASL is contrast-free and gives quantitative CBF, at the cost of inherently low SNR requiring many averages.
body.worked_example: A child needs a follow-up brain MRI for a known low-grade lesion and gadolinium is best avoided given the number of anticipated repeat scans over years. An ASL sequence is added instead of DSC perfusion. The label and control images are acquired and subtracted to generate a quantitative CBF map, showing no significant increase in perfusion within the lesion compared with the prior study, which is reassuring against transformation to a more aggressive, hypervascular tumor, all without any contrast injection.
memory_hooks: ASL: no injection, the blood itself is the contrast agent, magnetically tagged, then subtracted out.
Label minus control equals perfusion signal; pCASL beats PASL for SNR.
No gadolinium needed: think ASL for renal failure, kids, and repeat serial scans.
exam_traps: ASL uses no injected contrast at all; do not confuse it with DSC or DCE, both of which require gadolinium.
Too short a post-label delay underestimates perfusion in slow-flow or collateral-dependent territories, it is not simply a fixed universal setting.
ASL's low intrinsic SNR is compensated by averaging many repetitions, not by increasing labeling duration indefinitely.

body.title: Choosing a perfusion method: DSC, DCE, or ASL
body.html:
All three perfusion techniques answer different physiological questions, and picking the right one depends on what is being asked. DSC uses a fast gadolinium bolus imaged with T2*-weighted echo-planar sequences, tracking the first pass of contrast to generate CBV, CBF, and MTT maps; it is the workhorse for acute stroke (identifying the ischemic penumbra) and for tumor grading (high CBV correlating with higher-grade, more vascular tumors). DCE uses repeated T1-weighted imaging over several minutes to watch contrast slowly leak out of vessels, generating Ktrans and ve maps of capillary permeability; it is favored for tumor characterization and for monitoring treatment response to antiangiogenic or chemotherapy regimens.

ASL needs no contrast at all, magnetically labeling arterial blood and subtracting a control image to generate quantitative CBF maps directly; it is preferred whenever gadolinium should be minimized or avoided, such as renal impairment, pediatric patients, or serial follow-up imaging, and it is increasingly used in dementia and neurodegenerative disease workups, where regional hypoperfusion patterns (for example, parietotemporal hypoperfusion in Alzheimer disease) support the diagnosis without repeated contrast exposure. In practice, stroke and tumor-grading protocols often still favor bolus contrast techniques for their higher SNR, while ASL is the default when contrast is contraindicated, undesirable, or when only a quick, quantitative CBF check is needed.
keypoints: DSC (T2*, bolus, CBV/CBF/MTT) is the classic choice for stroke and tumor grading.
DCE (T1, Ktrans, ve) targets capillary permeability for tumor characterization and treatment response.
ASL needs no contrast and is preferred for renal impairment, pediatrics, and serial follow-up.
ASL is increasingly used in dementia and neurodegenerative disease workups for regional hypoperfusion patterns.
Choice depends on the clinical question: flow and volume (DSC), permeability (DCE), or contrast-free quantitative CBF (ASL).
body.worked_example: A patient with progressive memory loss is being evaluated for possible Alzheimer disease. Rather than adding a gadolinium-based perfusion sequence, the protocol includes ASL, which shows the classic pattern of reduced perfusion in the posterior cingulate and parietotemporal cortex with relative sparing of primary sensorimotor and occipital cortex, supporting the clinical diagnosis. Because ASL requires no injection, it can be repeated at a future visit to track disease progression without any added contrast burden.
memory_hooks: Volume and flow: DSC. Permeability: DCE. No contrast at all: ASL.
Stroke and grading lean DSC; characterization and treatment response lean DCE; renal failure, kids, and repeats lean ASL.
Three letters, three questions: DSC asks how much blood, DCE asks how leaky, ASL asks how much flow without any dye.
exam_traps: Higher tumor grade correlates with higher CBV on DSC, not with a specific Ktrans value; do not merge the DSC and DCE parameters.
ASL being contrast-free does not make it universally superior; its lower SNR means bolus techniques are still preferred when maximum spatial detail is needed.
Dementia perfusion patterns are regional (parietotemporal in Alzheimer disease), not just globally reduced flow; the distribution pattern is diagnostically relevant.

body.prompt: During the first pass of a gadolinium bolus in DSC perfusion imaging, which signal change is expected on the T2*-weighted images?
options: A transient signal drop as the bolus passes through the vascular bed
A transient signal rise as the bolus passes through the vascular bed
No signal change until the bolus recirculates
A steady rise in signal over several minutes
body.explain: DSC relies on the T2*/T2 susceptibility effect of gadolinium, which transiently lowers signal as concentrated contrast passes through capillaries; a rise in signal over minutes describes DCE, not DSC.

body.prompt: In DSC perfusion of a brain tumor, an elevated relative cerebral blood volume (CBV) most directly suggests:
options: Low tumor vascularity, suggestive of a lower tumor grade
Greater tumor vascularity, correlating with higher grade
Impaired capillary permeability with a low Ktrans value
Complete absence of any blood-brain barrier breakdown
body.explain: CBV reflects vascular density; high-grade, more vascular tumors typically show elevated relative CBV compared with lower-grade tumors and normal white matter.

body.prompt: In DSC perfusion, mean transit time (MTT) is calculated as:
options: CBV multiplied by CBF
CBV divided by CBF
CBF divided by CBV
The time from injection to peak signal drop only
body.explain: MTT equals CBV divided by CBF (the central volume principle), giving the average time blood takes to transit the vascular bed.

body.prompt: On a DSC signal-time curve, a second smaller dip in signal following the initial bolus passage is caused by:
options: Patient motion occurring during the DSC acquisition
Recirculation of contrast through the systemic circulation
T1 shortening effects overtaking the T2* signal drop
Failure or malfunction of the power injector device
body.explain: As contrast recirculates through the body and returns to the brain vasculature, it produces a smaller secondary signal dip that must be modeled out (for example with gamma-variate fitting) to avoid biasing the perfusion maps.

body.prompt: DCE perfusion imaging primarily relies on which image weighting and time scale?
options: T2*-weighted imaging over several seconds
T1-weighted imaging over several minutes
Proton-density weighted imaging over a single acquisition
Diffusion-weighted imaging over several minutes
body.explain: DCE uses repeated T1-weighted acquisitions over several minutes to capture the slower uptake and washout of gadolinium as it leaks into the extravascular extracellular space.

body.prompt: In DCE perfusion analysis, Ktrans specifically quantifies:
options: Cerebral blood volume held within the vascular bed
The rate of contrast transfer across the capillary wall
The total dose of gadolinium contrast administered
The time delay between injection and peak enhancement
body.explain: Ktrans is the volume transfer constant describing how quickly contrast leaks from the plasma space across the capillary endothelium into the extravascular extracellular space, a direct measure of permeability.

body.prompt: Arterial spin labeling (ASL) generates a perfusion-weighted image by:
options: Injecting a rapid bolus of gadolinium contrast and tracking its first pass
Applying an inversion pulse to label arterial blood, then subtracting the control image
Measuring the diffusion restriction of water across paired b-values
Acquiring T1-weighted images before and after a slow contrast infusion
body.explain: ASL magnetically labels inflowing arterial blood with an inversion pulse and subtracts a control acquisition (no labeling) from the label acquisition to isolate the small perfusion signal, without any injected contrast.

body.prompt: Compared with pulsed ASL (PASL), pseudo-continuous ASL (pCASL) is generally preferred because it:
options: Requires no post-label delay before imaging begins
Provides higher SNR through a longer labeling duration
Eliminates the need for a separate control image scan
Uses gadolinium contrast to boost the labeling signal
body.explain: pCASL labels blood for roughly one to two seconds using a train of rapid pulses, generally producing higher SNR than the single short inversion pulse used in PASL, which is why it is now the more widely recommended technique.

body.prompt: In ASL imaging, if the post-label delay (PLD) is set too short in a patient with slow or collateral arterial flow, the result is most likely:
options: Overestimation of the true cerebral blood flow value
Underestimation of flow, since labeled blood has not yet arrived
No effect, since PLD only changes contrast, not quantification
Complete loss of the paired control image acquisition
body.explain: If the PLD is too short, labeled blood may not have arrived in the tissue of interest by the time imaging occurs, leading to underestimated perfusion, particularly in territories with delayed or collateral flow.

body.prompt: A patient with stage 4 chronic kidney disease needs perfusion imaging to follow a known brain lesion over multiple future visits. Which technique best avoids added risk while still providing quantitative perfusion data?
options: DSC perfusion with a standard extracellular gadolinium agent
DCE perfusion with a linear gadolinium chelate
Arterial spin labeling (ASL)
Contrast-enhanced MRA of the circle of Willis
body.explain: ASL requires no injected gadolinium at all, avoiding NSF risk in impaired renal function, and still yields quantitative CBF maps, making it well suited for patients needing repeated follow-up imaging with reduced renal clearance.

body.title: Phase contrast MRA and velocity encoding (VENC)
body.html:
Phase contrast MRA works by applying a bipolar flow-encoding gradient along one axis. Stationary spins accrue no net phase because the two lobes cancel, but spins moving along that axis accrue a phase shift proportional to their velocity. The operator sets a single parameter, VENC (velocity encoding), the velocity that produces exactly 180 degrees of phase shift. This scales the phase-to-velocity relationship for the vessel being studied.

Choosing VENC is a trade-off. If true velocity exceeds VENC, the phase shift exceeds 180 degrees and wraps (aliases), displaying as an artifactually reversed or truncated velocity in the fastest part of the vessel, typically the center of a jet or stenosis. If VENC is set much higher than the expected peak velocity, aliasing is avoided but the true phase signal occupies only a small fraction of the encoding range, so the velocity measurement becomes noisy and less sensitive to slow flow. The correct VENC sits just above the expected peak velocity for the vessel and clinical question.

Because each spatial direction can be encoded independently, PC can measure velocity in a single through-plane direction or in all three directions for a full flow vector. Through-plane acquisitions with a region of interest drawn over the vessel allow flow quantification: multiplying mean velocity by cross-sectional area gives volumetric flow, used for shunt ratios, regurgitant fraction in valve disease, and CSF flow studies. A separate background phase correction step removes phase offsets from gradient nonlinearity and eddy currents that would otherwise bias the flow measurement.
keypoints: VENC is the velocity that produces 180 degrees of phase shift on the bipolar flow-encoding gradient.
Velocities above VENC wrap around and alias, appearing as reversed or truncated flow.
Setting VENC too high above true peak velocity reduces sensitivity to slow flow and adds noise.
Through-plane PC with an ROI over the vessel yields volumetric flow: mean velocity times cross-sectional area.
Background phase correction removes gradient and eddy-current offsets that would otherwise bias flow measurements.
body.worked_example: A patient with known aortic regurgitation is referred for phase-contrast quantification of regurgitant fraction. The technologist places a through-plane PC acquisition just above the aortic valve and sets VENC at 150 cm per second. Peak systolic velocity is about 120 cm per second, well under VENC, so forward flow is captured cleanly, and 150 also leaves enough range to resolve the lower-velocity diastolic reverse flow without wrapping the systolic peak or burying the reverse-flow signal in noise. Forward and reverse flow volumes are then integrated across the cardiac cycle to calculate the regurgitant fraction.
memory_hooks: VENC is a ceiling, not a target: set it just above the expected peak velocity to use most of the phase range without wrapping.
Aliasing in PC looks like a reversed sign or truncated value in the fastest part of the vessel, not signal dropout like TOF saturation.
exam_traps: Aliased PC flow can mimic a jet reversal or stenosis; the fix is repeating with a higher VENC, not reinterpreting the direction as real.
A single VENC must accommodate both the fastest and slowest velocities of interest in one acquisition; too narrow a range sacrifices one or the other.

body.title: Time-of-flight MRA: inflow, saturation, and pitfalls
body.html:
Time-of-flight MRA relies on flow-related enhancement: a short TR, high flip angle sequence rapidly saturates stationary tissue in the imaging slab, so it produces little signal by the time it is sampled again. Blood flowing into the slab from outside has not experienced the prior saturation pulses and enters fully magnetized, giving it much brighter signal than the saturated background, an effect strongest for blood entering perpendicular to the slab and moving quickly through it.

The same mechanism creates the main pitfall. Blood traveling in-plane, parallel to or within the imaging slab, or moving slowly, remains inside the excited volume long enough to receive repeated RF pulses and becomes saturated like stationary tissue, causing signal loss that can mimic stenosis or occlusion. Thin slabs and multiple overlapping thin-slab acquisition (MOTSA) reduce transit time through any one slab and limit this effect, though MOTSA introduces its own stair-step or venetian-blind artifact at the seams between slabs.

Because TOF depends on direction of entry rather than vessel identity, a spatial saturation band placed just outside the slab on one side nulls signal from blood entering from that direction: a band superior to the slab nulls venous inflow for an arterial-only study, while a band inferior to the slab nulls arterial inflow to isolate veins. Ramped RF excitation or TONE (tilted optimized nonsaturating excitation) pulses vary flip angle across the slab to compensate for progressive saturation as blood travels deeper into it. A separate pitfall is that any inherently T1-bright material, such as fat, subacute (methemoglobin) hemorrhage, or residual gadolinium, can mimic flow-related enhancement because the sequence cannot distinguish true inflow from any other source of T1 shortening.
keypoints: TOF signal comes from unsaturated inflowing blood entering a slab of saturated stationary tissue.
In-plane or slow flow becomes saturated like background tissue, causing pseudo-stenosis or pseudo-occlusion.
Thin slabs and MOTSA reduce saturation but MOTSA adds a stair-step artifact at slab overlaps.
A saturation band on one side of the slab nulls inflow from that direction, isolating arteries or veins.
T1-bright material (fat, subacute blood, residual gadolinium) can mimic flow on TOF.
body.worked_example: A 2D TOF venogram of the lower legs is planned to evaluate for deep vein thrombosis. Because venous flow runs roughly upward toward the heart, a superior saturation band is placed above each imaging slice to null arterial inflow, so only venous flow remains bright. If the band were mistakenly placed inferior to the slice instead, arterial signal would appear bright and venous signal would be nulled, producing a study that looks falsely occluded for the veins the exam was meant to assess.
memory_hooks: TOF signal is about direction of entry, not vessel type: the saturation band decides whether you see arteries or veins.
Slow or in-plane flow saturates like stationary tissue on TOF: it is stuck in the slab too long and loses its edge.
exam_traps: A TOF signal void from in-plane or slow flow can be mistaken for true stenosis or occlusion; correlate with another technique before calling a lesion.
Fat, subacute hemorrhage, or residual gadolinium can produce a T1-bright false positive on TOF that mimics a vessel.

body.title: Contrast-enhanced MRA: bolus timing and technique
body.html:
Contrast-enhanced MRA (CE-MRA) does not depend on inflow or velocity at all. Gadolinium shortens the T1 of blood dramatically, so a fast, heavily T1-weighted 3D gradient echo sequence makes contrast-filled vessels bright regardless of flow direction or velocity, eliminating the saturation and in-plane flow pitfalls that limit TOF. This makes the technique flow-independent, but it shifts the challenge to bolus timing.

Image contrast in a 3D acquisition is set almost entirely by which data fills the center of k-space, since that region carries overall contrast and signal while the periphery carries fine spatial detail. With centric k-space ordering, the center is acquired first, so timing needs only to get the leading edge of the bolus into the vessel at the start of the scan. With sequential (linear) ordering, the center of k-space is acquired partway through the scan, so the technologist must predict when peak arterial gadolinium concentration will coincide with that middle portion of acquisition.

Three common strategies fix the timing. A test bolus injects a small dose and times a single-slice dynamic series to measure the true transit time from injection to the artery of interest before the diagnostic bolus is given. Bolus tracking (commercially SmartPrep or CareBolus) monitors signal in the target vessel in real time and automatically triggers the diagnostic acquisition once a threshold is reached. Time-resolved techniques acquire many undersampled 3D volumes in rapid succession through the injection, trading spatial resolution for temporal resolution so at least one frame captures the pure arterial phase. If the acquisition is mistimed and the center of k-space is sampled too early, the study shows weak enhancement or ringing artifact from a still-rising bolus; if sampled too late, contrast has already reached the veins, producing venous contamination that obscures the arterial anatomy.
keypoints: CE-MRA is flow-independent: gadolinium T1-shortening makes vessels bright regardless of velocity or direction.
Whichever data fills the center of k-space sets overall image contrast; centric order front-loads it, sequential order places it mid-scan.
Test bolus and bolus tracking (SmartPrep or CareBolus) measure or detect true arrival time to trigger the diagnostic acquisition.
Time-resolved MRA trades spatial resolution for temporal resolution to guarantee a pure arterial-phase frame.
Mistimed acquisitions cause either ringing from a rising bolus or venous contamination from a late acquisition.
body.worked_example: A CE-MRA of the runoff vessels is ordered for a patient with peripheral arterial disease. Using a test bolus, the technologist measures a 14-second transit time from the antecubital injection site to the popliteal artery. The diagnostic sequence uses centric k-space ordering, so the scan starts roughly 14 seconds after the diagnostic bolus begins, ensuring the leading edge of gadolinium is in the artery right as the center of k-space, and therefore the image contrast, is being acquired. Had the scan instead started too late, the calf veins would already be enhancing by the time distal arterial images are acquired, contaminating the study with venous signal that can obscure arterial pathology.
memory_hooks: CE-MRA contrast is decided at the center of k-space: centric order means get there first, sequential means get there in the middle.
Test bolus measures transit time in advance; bolus tracking watches for arrival in real time; time-resolved just keeps shooting through the whole thing.
exam_traps: A CE-MRA acquired too early shows weak or ring-like arterial signal from a still-rising bolus, not true pathology; a repeat with adjusted delay is needed.
Venous contamination from delayed acquisition can obscure an arterial stenosis or mimic shunting; recognizing the timing error is a key registry skill.

body.title: MR venography and flow quantification
body.html:
MR venography adapts the same three angiographic techniques to the slower, lower-pressure venous system. 2D time-of-flight MRV is well suited to slow venous flow because each thin 2D slice is refreshed with a fresh RF excitation, limiting the in-plane saturation that would otherwise null slow-moving venous spins in a thick 3D slab; a saturation band placed on the arterial side of each slice nulls arterial inflow so only venous signal remains. Phase-contrast MRV uses a low VENC appropriate to venous velocities, typically well under arterial VENC settings, and additionally provides directional and quantitative flow data. Contrast-enhanced MRV times acquisition to the venous phase, later than an arterial CE-MRA, and is flow-independent, useful when slow or complex venous flow would otherwise degrade a non-contrast study.

Non-contrast venography has a well-known pitfall: pseudo-occlusion. On 2D TOF, in-plane flow within the plane of a slice, or flow parallel to a long vessel segment, can saturate and mimic thrombosis. Separately, a subacute clot containing methemoglobin is inherently T1-bright and can mimic patent, flowing blood, the reverse problem, a T1-bright false positive for patency. Correlating with PC or contrast-enhanced venography, or with the clinical picture, resolves these pitfalls.

Phase-contrast techniques are also the workhorse for flow quantification outside pure angiography, most notably CSF flow studies, for example at the cerebral aqueduct in suspected normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and vascular flow volume measurement. In both cases, a through-plane PC acquisition perpendicular to the vessel or CSF-filled space is obtained with a VENC scaled to the expected peak velocity, a region of interest is drawn over the structure on each cardiac phase, and volumetric flow is calculated as mean velocity multiplied by cross-sectional area, integrated across the cardiac cycle.
keypoints: 2D TOF MRV limits in-plane saturation of slow venous flow because each thin slice gets a fresh excitation.
A saturation band nulls arterial inflow so 2D TOF MRV isolates venous signal.
Pseudo-occlusion on TOF venography comes from in-plane saturation (false positive for clot) or T1-bright subacute clot (false positive for patency).
CE-MRV times acquisition to the venous phase and is flow-independent, useful when slow venous flow degrades non-contrast studies.
PC flow quantification (CSF or vascular) uses through-plane VENC and an ROI: flow equals mean velocity times cross-sectional area.
body.worked_example: A patient with suspected dural venous sinus thrombosis undergoes 2D TOF MRV. A segment of the superior sagittal sinus shows signal loss that raises concern for thrombosis, but that segment runs largely within the imaging plane over a long course. Because in-plane flow is prone to saturation on 2D TOF, the technologist adds a phase-contrast or contrast-enhanced venogram for correlation. The follow-up study shows normal flow through the segment, confirming the TOF finding was pseudo-occlusion from in-plane saturation rather than true thrombosis.
memory_hooks: TOF venography pseudo-occlusion has two opposite causes: in-plane saturation looks falsely clotted, T1-bright clot looks falsely patent.
Flow quantification is just geometry: velocity from phase times area from the ROI equals volume per time.
exam_traps: A TOF venography signal void is not diagnostic of thrombosis by itself given the in-plane saturation pitfall; a second technique is expected.
PC flow quantification needs the imaging plane truly perpendicular to the vessel; an oblique plane underestimates velocity and biases the flow calculation.

body.prompt: On a phase-contrast MRA, the true peak velocity in a vessel exceeds the VENC. What artifact results in the vessel signal?
options: Phase aliasing, seen as reversed or truncated flow
Complete signal void through the vessel lumen
Chemical shift misregistration at the vessel wall
Zipper artifact along the phase-encode axis
body.explain: When true velocity exceeds VENC, the phase shift exceeds 180 degrees and wraps, appearing as reversed or truncated flow, usually in the fastest part of the vessel.

body.prompt: A phase-contrast sequence is set with a VENC far above the true peak velocity of the vessel being studied. What is the main consequence?
options: Reduced sensitivity and increased noise in velocity data
Immediate wraparound aliasing of the peak velocity
Complete and permanent loss of the magnitude image
Full elimination of background phase correction error
body.explain: A VENC set far above true velocity wastes most of the encoding range on unused signal, making the actual velocity measurement noisier and less sensitive to slow flow.

body.prompt: A carotid TOF MRA shows apparent signal loss in a segment where the vessel courses within the imaging plane for a long distance. This most likely represents:
options: Saturation of in-plane flow, not true stenosis
A true high-grade stenosis at that level
Gadolinium-related T1 shortening of the vessel
Aliasing from an undersized VENC setting
body.explain: Blood traveling in-plane stays within the excited slab long enough to become saturated like stationary tissue, mimicking stenosis; this is a known TOF pitfall, not necessarily true disease.

body.prompt: On a 2D TOF neck MRA where arterial flow is caudocranial, placing the spatial saturation band inferior to each imaging slice will:
options: Null arterial inflow and isolate venous signal
Null venous inflow and isolate arterial signal
Suppress fat signal throughout the field of view
Increase the VENC value for the acquisition
body.explain: A band placed inferior to the slice saturates blood before it flows upward into the slice, nulling the caudocranial arterial inflow and leaving venous flow visible.

body.prompt: Multiple overlapping thin-slab acquisition (MOTSA) reduces flow saturation in 3D TOF MRA but is known to introduce which artifact?
options: A stair-step or venetian-blind artifact at slab overlaps
Chemical shift artifact along the frequency axis
Motion-related ghosting across the phase axis
Aliasing from wraparound of the field of view
body.explain: Slight signal differences at the boundary between adjacent overlapping slabs create a periodic banding pattern, known as stair-step or venetian-blind artifact, on MOTSA acquisitions.

body.prompt: On a brain TOF MRA, an area of bright signal is later shown to be subacute hemorrhage rather than a vessel. Why did it appear bright on TOF?
options: Its intrinsic T1 shortening mimics flow enhancement
It flowed into the slab from outside the volume
It exceeded the VENC and aliased on the sequence
It was suppressed by the spatial saturation band
body.explain: TOF cannot distinguish true inflow enhancement from any other source of T1 shortening; methemoglobin in subacute blood, like fat or residual gadolinium, is intrinsically T1-bright and can mimic a vessel.

body.prompt: In a centric-ordered 3D contrast-enhanced MRA, the center of k-space is acquired:
options: First, so the bolus must arrive at the scan start
Last, so the bolus must arrive at the scan end
At a fixed point regardless of bolus timing
Only during the second half of acquisition
body.explain: Centric ordering samples the center of k-space, which sets overall image contrast, first, so the contrast bolus needs to reach the target vessel right as the scan begins.

body.prompt: A CE-MRA of the renal arteries is acquired several seconds later than intended. The most likely resulting artifact is:
options: Venous contamination obscuring the arterial anatomy
Complete absence of any vessel signal at all
Saturation of in-plane arterial flow in the slab
Phase aliasing of the arterial velocity signal
body.explain: A delayed acquisition allows gadolinium to reach and enhance the veins before or during the scan, producing venous contamination that can obscure or mimic arterial pathology.

body.prompt: A bolus-tracking technique monitors real-time signal in the target vessel and automatically triggers the diagnostic CE-MRA once a threshold is reached. This is best described as:
options: An automated triggering method, such as SmartPrep or CareBolus
A fixed empiric delay based on body weight
A test bolus requiring a separate preliminary injection
A time-resolved acquisition of multiple volumes
body.explain: Automated bolus-tracking techniques, commercially SmartPrep or CareBolus, watch signal in the target vessel in real time and trigger the scan once it crosses a threshold, unlike a separate test bolus or time-resolved approach.

body.prompt: Quantitative phase-contrast flow measurement, for example CSF flow at the cerebral aqueduct, calculates volumetric flow as:
options: Mean velocity multiplied by cross-sectional area
Peak velocity divided by the VENC value
Signal intensity multiplied by the echo time
Repetition time divided by the flip angle
body.explain: Volumetric flow through a vessel or CSF space equals the mean velocity within the region of interest multiplied by its cross-sectional area, integrated across the cardiac cycle.

body.title: The diffusion tensor and fractional anisotropy (FA)
body.html:
Basic DWI treats diffusion as if it were the same in every direction. In white matter that assumption breaks down. Water inside and around myelinated axons moves easily along the fiber but is hindered across it, a property called anisotropic diffusion. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) captures this by measuring diffusion along at least six non-collinear directions, plus a b0 image with no diffusion weighting, and fitting the results to a 3x3 diffusion tensor for every voxel.

The tensor can be decomposed into three eigenvectors and three eigenvalues. The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue points along the dominant diffusion direction, which in a coherent white matter tract lines up with the axons themselves. From the eigenvalues, two summary numbers drive most clinical and research use. Mean diffusivity (MD) is the average diffusion magnitude, independent of direction. Fractional anisotropy (FA) is a unitless ratio from 0 to 1 that describes how directional the diffusion is.

An FA of 0 means diffusion is equal in all directions, isotropic, as in CSF. An FA near 1 means diffusion is strongly restricted to one axis, as in a dense, coherently organized tract like the corpus callosum. FA maps are commonly color coded by direction: red for left-right, green for anterior-posterior, blue for superior-inferior, with brightness scaled to the FA value itself.
keypoints: White matter diffusion is anisotropic: faster along axons, hindered across them.
DTI requires at least 6 non-collinear diffusion directions plus a b0 image to solve the tensor.
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the tensor give the principal diffusion direction and its magnitude.
FA ranges 0 (isotropic, e.g. CSF) to 1 (highly anisotropic, dense coherent tracts).
Color FA maps use a standard convention: red left-right, green anterior-posterior, blue superior-inferior.
body.worked_example: A color FA map through the centrum semiovale shows a bright red band running side to side. This is the corpus callosum, whose fibers cross the midline, so their principal diffusion direction is left-right. Immediately superior to it, a green band marks the cingulum bundle running front to back. The color tells the direction; the brightness within that color tells how strongly organized the tract is.
memory_hooks: Six directions plus a b0 is the minimum recipe to solve a tensor.
FA colors follow RGB axes: red left-right, green front-back, blue up-down.
exam_traps: Confusing FA (directionality of diffusion) with MD (average magnitude of diffusion); they answer different questions.
Assuming any single diffusion direction acquisition is DTI; true DTI needs the multi-direction tensor fit.

body.title: DTI tractography: mapping white matter tracts
body.html:
Tractography uses the voxel-by-voxel principal diffusion direction from DTI to reconstruct the paths of white matter tracts as streamlines. The algorithm starts at a seed voxel and steps outward, following the principal eigenvector from one voxel into the next, building a line that approximates an underlying fiber bundle.

Deterministic tractography follows a single best direction at each step, producing one streamline per seed. Probabilistic tractography instead models a distribution of possible directions at each voxel and samples repeatedly, producing many streamlines that express confidence as streamline density rather than a single fixed path. Tracking is stopped, or a streamline discarded, when FA drops below a set threshold or when the path bends more sharply than an allowed turning angle, since both suggest the voxel no longer represents a single coherent fiber population.

The clinical payoff is presurgical mapping of eloquent white matter, such as the corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus, and optic radiations, so a neurosurgeon can plan an approach that avoids them. The major limitation is crossing and kissing fiber populations within a single voxel. A standard single tensor model cannot separate two fiber populations crossing at an angle, and partial volume averaging can make tracking stop early, drift onto the wrong tract, or fail to continue through the crossing region.
keypoints: Streamlines are built by following the principal eigenvector from voxel to voxel.
Deterministic tractography gives one path per seed; probabilistic tractography gives a distribution of likely paths.
FA threshold and maximum turning angle are the standard stopping criteria for a streamline.
Presurgical use includes mapping the corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus, and optic radiations.
Crossing and kissing fibers, plus partial volume averaging, are the main limitation of single tensor tracking.
body.worked_example: Before resecting a lesion near the motor cortex, tractography is run to outline the corticospinal tract. The reconstructed tract is displayed alongside the tumor on the surgical navigation system, showing the tract is displaced but not invaded. The surgeon plans a corridor that stays lateral to the tracked fibers, reducing the risk of a postoperative motor deficit.
memory_hooks: Streamlines just chase the biggest eigenvector, voxel after voxel.
Crossing fibers are the single tensor model's blind spot.
exam_traps: Treating a tractography reconstruction as a direct anatomic photograph rather than a model built on assumptions that can fail.
Forgetting that a low FA region, such as a crossing fiber zone, can prematurely terminate a real tract on the reconstruction.

body.title: Diffusion pitfalls: T2 shine-through, ADC, and b-value
body.html:
The classic diffusion pitfall is T2 shine-through. Diffusion weighted images carry inherent T2 weighting, so a lesion with a very long T2, like a chronic cyst or an old infarct, can appear bright on high b-value DWI purely from that T2 signal, with no true restriction present. This mimics acute restricted diffusion and can mislead an unwary reader.

The fix is always to check the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map, which is calculated from at least two b-values and removes the T2 contribution, leaving a purely quantitative map of diffusivity. True restriction is bright DWI paired with a low, dark ADC. Shine-through is bright DWI paired with an ADC that is bright or unremarkable, because diffusion there is not actually hindered.

The b-value itself sets how strongly the sequence is weighted toward diffusion. A higher b-value increases diffusion contrast and lesion conspicuity but comes at the cost of lower signal to noise and more geometric distortion, and it also reduces the residual T2 contribution, which is why very high b-value images are less prone to shine-through than low b-value images. Reading DWI and ADC together, rather than DWI alone, is the standard of practice for this reason.
keypoints: T2 shine-through is bright high-b DWI from a long T2 lesion, not true diffusion restriction.
The ADC map removes T2 weighting and gives a quantitative diffusivity value per voxel.
True restriction: bright DWI with low, dark ADC. Shine-through: bright DWI with bright or normal ADC.
Higher b-value increases diffusion weighting and conspicuity but lowers SNR and increases distortion.
DWI should never be interpreted without its matched ADC map.
body.worked_example: A chronic lacunar infarct from years earlier appears bright on the high b-value DWI image, raising concern for a new acute stroke. The ADC map is reviewed and shows the same region is bright, not dark, confirming T2 shine-through from the old, gliotic, long T2 tissue rather than a new restricting lesion. No acute intervention is warranted based on this finding alone.
memory_hooks: Bright DWI is a question; the ADC map is the answer.
Shine-through shines on both DWI and ADC; true restriction only shines on DWI.
exam_traps: Calling a chronic lesion an acute infarct because it is bright on DWI without checking ADC.
Assuming a higher b-value is always better; it trades SNR and adds distortion for stronger weighting.

body.title: Advanced diffusion applications: DWI beyond stroke
body.html:
Diffusion imaging extends well past acute stroke into everyday problem solving across the body. In the brain, restricted diffusion helps separate a pyogenic abscess, which restricts because its thick, viscous pus hinders water motion, from a necrotic or cystic tumor, whose fluid center is typically less viscous and does not restrict. Epidermoid cysts also restrict, unlike a simple arachnoid cyst, which follows CSF signal and diffusivity on every sequence, a distinction that is otherwise easy to miss on conventional imaging alone.

Densely cellular tumors, such as lymphoma and some high-grade or small round blue cell tumors, restrict diffusion because their tightly packed cells leave little extracellular space for water to move through. This makes DWI a useful adjunct for grading and for distinguishing cellular tumor from surrounding vasogenic edema, which does not restrict.

Outside the brain, whole-body diffusion weighted imaging with background suppression (DWIBS) is used in oncology for lesion detection and staging and for monitoring treatment response, since a successfully treated tumor typically loses restriction as cellularity falls and ADC values rise. This makes diffusion one of the few unenhanced, radiation free tools for tracking tumor response over time.
keypoints: Abscess restricts (viscous pus); necrotic or cystic tumor center typically does not restrict.
Epidermoid cyst restricts diffusion; arachnoid cyst follows CSF and does not.
Densely cellular tumors like lymphoma restrict because of tightly packed cells and little extracellular space.
Whole-body DWI (DWIBS) supports oncologic lesion detection, staging, and treatment response monitoring.
A rising ADC after treatment generally signals falling tumor cellularity, a favorable response.
body.worked_example: A suprasellar cystic mass is worked up with DWI to decide between epidermoid and arachnoid cyst before surgical planning. The mass restricts diffusion, bright on DWI with a low ADC, confirming epidermoid rather than arachnoid cyst, which would have followed CSF signal throughout. This diffusion finding directly changes the surgical approach, since epidermoid tumors require more meticulous capsule dissection.
memory_hooks: Pus is thick, so an abscess restricts; necrotic tumor fluid usually does not.
Epidermoid acts like a solid on DWI; arachnoid cyst just acts like CSF.
exam_traps: Assuming every ring enhancing lesion with a restricting center is an abscess without considering cellular tumor.
Mixing up epidermoid and arachnoid cyst on conventional T1/T2 alone; DWI is what separates them.

body.prompt: The minimum diffusion acquisition needed to solve a full diffusion tensor requires:
options: A b0 image plus at least 6 non-collinear diffusion directions
A single diffusion direction acquired at two b-values
A b0 image plus exactly 3 orthogonal diffusion directions
Any two diffusion weighted images at different TEs
body.explain: The diffusion tensor is a symmetric 3x3 matrix with 6 independent elements, so at least 6 non-collinear diffusion directions plus a non-diffusion-weighted b0 image are needed to solve it at each voxel.

body.prompt: A fractional anisotropy (FA) value close to 0 is most consistent with which tissue?
options: CSF, where diffusion is essentially equal in all directions
The corpus callosum, a densely packed coherent tract
The corticospinal tract at the level of the internal capsule
The optic radiations, a well organized fiber bundle
body.explain: FA near 0 means diffusion is isotropic, equal in every direction, which describes free fluid like CSF. Dense, coherently organized white matter tracts have FA values closer to 1.

body.prompt: On a standard color coded FA map, a tract colored green is oriented mainly along which axis?
options: Anterior-posterior
Left-right
Superior-inferior
Oblique, at roughly 45 degrees to all axes
body.explain: The standard color convention codes red for left-right, green for anterior-posterior, and blue for superior-inferior, with brightness scaled to the FA magnitude.

body.prompt: In DTI tractography, a streamline is typically stopped or discarded when:
options: FA drops below threshold or turning angle exceeds its limit
The b-value used for acquisition exceeds 1000 s/mm2
The voxel size becomes smaller than 2 mm isotropic
The seed point lies outside the brain parenchyma
body.explain: Tracking algorithms stop a streamline when FA falls below a set threshold or the path bends more sharply than an allowed turning angle, both signs the voxel no longer represents one coherent fiber population.

body.prompt: The major limitation of single tensor DTI tractography through a region where two fiber bundles cross is that it:
options: Cannot resolve two distinct fiber directions within one voxel
Requires contrast injection to visualize the crossing region
Only works when the crossing angle is less than 10 degrees
Cannot be performed on scanners below 3 Tesla field strength
body.explain: A single tensor model produces one principal direction per voxel, so it cannot separate two genuinely distinct fiber populations crossing within that voxel, which can cause tracking to stop, drift, or misroute.

body.prompt: A chronic infarct appears bright on high b-value DWI. What confirms this is T2 shine-through rather than true restriction?
options: The ADC map at the same location is bright, not dark
The lesion also enhances after gadolinium injection
The lesion is hyperintense on the T1 weighted image
The lesion shows blooming on a susceptibility sequence
body.explain: T2 shine-through is bright DWI paired with a bright or normal ADC, since diffusion in the tissue is not actually hindered. True restriction requires a low, dark ADC at the same location.

body.prompt: Increasing the b-value of a diffusion sequence generally has which effect?
options: Stronger diffusion contrast, but lower signal to noise ratio
Weaker diffusion contrast, but improved signal to noise ratio
No change in diffusion contrast or image signal to noise
Elimination of the need to acquire a matching ADC map
body.explain: A higher b-value increases diffusion weighting and lesion conspicuity but reduces signal to noise ratio and increases susceptibility to geometric distortion, a standard tradeoff in DWI protocol design.

body.prompt: A ring enhancing brain lesion has a center that restricts diffusion, bright DWI with low ADC. This favors:
options: Pyogenic abscess over necrotic tumor
Necrotic tumor over pyogenic abscess
Simple arachnoid cyst over any tumor
Chronic gliosis over any infectious process
body.explain: Thick, viscous pus in an abscess hinders water motion and restricts diffusion, while a necrotic or cystic tumor center is typically less viscous and does not restrict, making this a key differentiating sign.

body.prompt: Which suprasellar cystic lesion characteristically restricts diffusion, unlike a simple arachnoid cyst?
options: Epidermoid cyst
Rathke cleft cyst with simple fluid content
Simple pineal cyst
Choroid plexus cyst
body.explain: Epidermoid cysts restrict diffusion, bright on DWI with low ADC, because of their keratin debris content, which distinguishes them from an arachnoid cyst that simply follows CSF signal on every sequence.

body.prompt: Whole-body diffusion weighted imaging with background suppression (DWIBS) is primarily used in clinical oncology for:
options: Lesion detection, staging, and monitoring treatment response
Real time guidance during percutaneous tumor biopsy
Replacing contrast enhanced CT for lung nodule characterization
Measuring cardiac ejection fraction in cancer patients
body.explain: DWIBS provides an unenhanced, radiation free way to detect and stage tumors and to monitor treatment response, since successfully treated tumors typically lose restriction and show rising ADC values.

body.title: Cardiac gating and triggering: ECG, VCG, and the R-wave
body.html:
Cardiac MRI requires synchronizing data acquisition with the heartbeat, since cardiac motion during a single TR would blur the image beyond usefulness. The scanner uses ECG gating, most commonly a vectorcardiogram (VCG) lead set, to detect the R-wave and mark the start of each cardiac cycle. VCG algorithms combine multiple lead vectors to reliably identify the R-wave peak even though the static magnetic field and pulsatile blood flow distort the surface ECG signal inside the bore.

Blood is a conductive fluid moving through the strong static field, and this motion induces a voltage across the aorta that is superimposed on the ECG trace, most pronounced during systole and worsening at higher field strength. This magnetohydrodynamic effect elevates and distorts the T-wave, sometimes mimicking or obscuring the R-wave, which is why VCG-based detection algorithms rather than simple amplitude thresholds are required for reliable triggering.

Prospective triggering waits for the R-wave, then acquires a fixed set of k-space lines for a predetermined portion of the cardiac cycle, leaving a gap near end-diastole before the next trigger to allow for heart rate variability. Retrospective gating instead acquires data continuously throughout the entire R-R interval, tagging each line with its timing relative to the ECG trace, then sorts and reconstructs images spanning the full cardiac cycle, including end-diastole. Retrospective gating is generally preferred for cine function studies because it does not truncate late diastole and tolerates mild arrhythmia better, since outlier beats can be rejected during reconstruction.

Because a single heartbeat does not contain enough time to fill k-space for a full set of cine frames, data are collected in segments across many consecutive heartbeats, with each segment assigned to a specific phase of the cardiac cycle. An arrhythmia rejection window discards data from beats whose R-R interval falls outside an accepted range around the patient's average heart rate, preventing ectopic or premature beats from corrupting the reconstructed cine series.
keypoints: VCG lead placement improves R-wave detection over conventional ECG inside the magnet.
The magnetohydrodynamic effect distorts the T-wave from pulsatile aortic flow in the static field, worst during systole.
Prospective triggering acquires a fixed window after each R-wave and skips end-diastole.
Retrospective gating covers the full R-R interval and is preferred for accurate function studies.
Arrhythmia rejection windows exclude beats with abnormal R-R intervals from cine reconstruction.
body.worked_example: A patient's heart rate varies between 58 and 74 bpm during a short-axis cine acquisition. The technologist sets a moderate arrhythmia rejection window so an occasional premature ventricular contraction does not corrupt the diastolic frames, and chooses retrospective gating so end-diastolic volume is fully captured for ejection fraction calculation.
memory_hooks: Prospective triggers after the beat and misses the finish line at end-diastole.
Retrospective records the whole race, then sorts the photos afterward.
exam_traps: Assuming prospective triggering is always preferable because it is simpler; it actually truncates end-diastole and suits function assessment poorly.
Forgetting that the magnetohydrodynamic effect worsens with higher field strength and faster flow rather than being fixed by better electrode contact.

body.title: Cine imaging and ventricular function
body.html:
Cardiac cine imaging is built on a balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) sequence, valued for its inherently bright blood pool signal that comes from the ratio of T2 to T1 rather than flow-related enhancement, giving high and reliable contrast between the blood pool and myocardium regardless of flow velocity or direction. bSSFP also delivers excellent temporal resolution and signal-to-noise per unit time, both essential for capturing wall motion accurately across the cardiac cycle.

Each cine frame is built from a small segment of k-space lines acquired during a limited window of the cardiac cycle, repeated across roughly 8 to 16 consecutive heartbeats within a single breath-hold to assemble a full set of temporal phases, typically 20 to 30 frames per R-R interval. Patients hold their breath at end-expiration for each slice to suppress respiratory motion, since diaphragmatic movement between beats would otherwise misregister the heart from one segment to the next.

A short-axis stack of contiguous cine slices from the mitral valve plane to the apex allows the end-diastolic and end-systolic myocardial contours to be traced on every slice, and volumes are summed using the method of discs, or Simpson's method, to calculate end-diastolic volume, end-systolic volume, stroke volume, and ejection fraction. This slice-by-slice contouring approach avoids the geometric assumptions that limit echocardiographic ejection fraction estimates.

Regional wall motion is graded qualitatively across the cine frames using a standardized segmentation model, describing each myocardial segment as normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, or dyskinetic, which helps localize the territory affected by prior infarction or ischemia before tissue characterization sequences are even reviewed.
keypoints: bSSFP contrast comes from the T2/T1 ratio, giving bright blood without needing flow-related enhancement.
Cine frames are assembled from k-space segments acquired across many heartbeats within one breath-hold.
A short-axis stack from mitral valve to apex enables volumetric ejection fraction by Simpson's method.
About 20 to 30 cardiac phases per R-R interval are typical for smooth cine playback.
Regional wall motion is graded as normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, or dyskinetic.
body.worked_example: A technologist prescribes a short-axis stack of ten contiguous 8 mm slices covering the left ventricle from base to apex, has the patient hold their breath for each slice, and the software auto-contours the endocardial and epicardial borders at end-diastole and end-systole to calculate an ejection fraction of 52 percent, within normal range.
memory_hooks: bSSFP for cine: balanced sequence, bright blood, because of T2/T1, not flow.
