Short-axis stack, Simpson stacks the discs, no geometry guessing needed.
exam_traps: Confusing bSSFP bright-blood contrast with time-of-flight inflow enhancement; bSSFP brightness is intrinsic to the T2/T1 ratio and holds even with slow flow.
Assuming a single mid-ventricular slice can estimate ejection fraction; accurate volumetric EF requires the full short-axis stack, not one representative slice.

body.title: Myocardial tissue characterization: LGE and parametric mapping
body.html:
Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging is acquired roughly 10 to 15 minutes after contrast injection, once gadolinium has washed out of normal myocardium but remains trapped in areas of scar or fibrosis due to expanded extracellular space and slower washout kinetics. An inversion-recovery prepared gradient-echo sequence is used, with the inversion time (TI) selected to null the signal from normal myocardium, so that any tissue retaining more gadolinium appears bright against a dark, suppressed normal myocardial background.

TI is not fixed; it must be adjusted for each patient and rechecked over the course of the exam because gadolinium continues to wash out during acquisition. Most protocols include a TI scout sequence displaying several inversion times, letting the operator pick the one that makes normal myocardium appear darkest just before the LGE images are acquired.

The distribution of enhancement carries diagnostic meaning. Subendocardial enhancement that extends toward the epicardium and follows a coronary artery territory is the hallmark of ischemic infarction, since the subendocardium is the last tissue layer perfused and the first to suffer irreversible injury; enhancement can remain confined to the inner third of the wall or progress to full transmural involvement depending on infarct size. Enhancement confined to the mid-wall or epicardium, sparing the subendocardium and not respecting a coronary territory, instead suggests a non-ischemic process such as myocarditis or non-ischemic cardiomyopathy.

Parametric mapping extends tissue characterization beyond LGE by measuring absolute T1 and T2 relaxation times pixel by pixel rather than relying on a nulled reference. Native, pre-contrast, T1 mapping and extracellular volume calculation detect diffuse interstitial fibrosis that LGE can miss because it has no normal region to null against, while T2 mapping identifies myocardial edema in acute processes such as myocarditis or recent infarction, since free water content raises T2 independent of contrast administration.
keypoints: LGE images are acquired 10 to 15 minutes post-contrast, once gadolinium has washed out of normal myocardium but remains in scar.
TI is chosen to null normal myocardium so retained gadolinium in scar appears bright.
Subendocardial to transmural enhancement following a coronary territory indicates ischemic infarction.
Mid-wall or epicardial enhancement sparing the subendocardium suggests non-ischemic disease.
T2 mapping detects edema; native T1 mapping and extracellular volume detect diffuse fibrosis.
body.worked_example: A patient with prior anterior chest pain undergoes LGE imaging showing bright signal spanning the full thickness of the anteroseptal wall in the left anterior descending territory, consistent with transmural infarction and predicting poor recovery of contractile function in that segment even after revascularization.
memory_hooks: LGE nulls the normal, so scar stands out; if it touches the endocardium, think ischemia.
T2 for wet tissue from edema, T1 mapping for the diffuse fibrosis LGE cannot null.
exam_traps: Picking a TI that nulls blood or fat instead of myocardium; the null point is specific to normal myocardial signal and shifts throughout the exam.
Calling mid-wall enhancement ischemic; enhancement that spares the subendocardium and ignores coronary territories points to a non-ischemic cause, not infarction.

body.title: Cardiac sequences and artifacts: black-blood, phase contrast, and banding
body.html:
Black-blood imaging uses a double inversion-recovery, or double IR, preparation: a nonselective inversion pulse followed immediately by a slice-selective reinversion pulse restores longitudinal magnetization only within the imaging slice, while blood outside the slice remains inverted and flows into the slice by the time of imaging, nulled near the null point of blood. The result is dark, suppressed blood pool signal that sharply defines the myocardial and vessel wall borders, useful for anatomic evaluation of wall thickness, pericardium, and masses where bright intraluminal signal would otherwise obscure the border.

Phase-contrast imaging encodes flow velocity into the phase of the MR signal using bipolar gradients, producing both a magnitude image and a velocity, or phase, map that can quantify peak velocity and flow volume across a heart valve or great vessel. The operator sets a velocity encoding value (venc) close to the expected peak velocity in the region of interest; a venc set too low causes velocity aliasing that wraps the phase signal, while a venc set too high sacrifices velocity-to-noise sensitivity, so venc should be chosen based on the clinical question, such as a high venc for a stenotic aortic valve jet.

bSSFP cine sequences are vulnerable to dark banding artifact from off-resonance effects, since the balanced gradient waveform requires a very uniform magnetic field and any local field inhomogeneity shifts the frequency response enough to create bands of signal loss. These bands commonly arise near the lungs, at tissue interfaces, or from imperfect shimming, and can mimic or obscure pathology if they cross the myocardium.

Banding is minimized by performing a careful local shim over the heart and running a frequency scout to adjust the center frequency so the resulting band is pushed away from the region of interest, ideally out into the lung or chest wall rather than across the ventricle. For free-breathing acquisitions such as coronary MRA, navigator echoes placed over the right hemidiaphragm track its position in real time, accepting data only when the diaphragm falls within a narrow gating window near end-expiration, suppressing respiratory motion without requiring a breath-hold.
keypoints: Double inversion recovery nulls blood signal for black-blood anatomic imaging of the myocardium and vessel walls.
Phase-contrast imaging quantifies flow velocity through bipolar gradient encoding; venc should approximate expected peak velocity.
Venc set too low causes velocity aliasing; venc set too high reduces velocity sensitivity.
bSSFP banding artifact comes from off-resonance field inhomogeneity and is corrected with local shimming and frequency adjustment.
Navigator echoes track diaphragm position to gate free-breathing acquisitions such as coronary MRA.
body.worked_example: For a patient with suspected aortic stenosis, the technologist prescribes a phase-contrast sequence through the aortic valve with venc set to 400 cm/s based on the expected high-velocity jet, and separately notices a dark band crossing the inferior wall on the bSSFP cine, which resolves after rerunning the local shim and frequency scout centered on the heart.
memory_hooks: Black-blood inverts twice, once for the whole body and once to save the slice, so blood washes out dark.
Banding lives where the field is bumpy; shim it, then scout the frequency to push it into the lung.
exam_traps: Setting venc too low to improve resolution; that causes aliasing that wraps and misrepresents high-velocity jets as falsely lower or reversed.
Blaming banding artifact on patient motion; it is an off-resonance shimming problem specific to bSSFP, corrected with shim and frequency adjustment, not breath-holding.

body.prompt: Which statement best describes the trade-off between prospective triggering and retrospective gating in cardiac MRI?
options: Prospective triggering samples the entire R-R interval, while retrospective gating stops short before end-diastole.
Prospective triggering misses end-diastole with its fixed post-R-wave window; retrospective gating spans the full cycle instead.
Retrospective gating requires a fixed radiofrequency duty cycle and cannot reconstruct any end-systolic frames.
Prospective triggering is always preferred for ejection fraction since it captures more cardiac phases overall.
body.explain: Prospective triggering waits for the R-wave and stops before end-diastole, whereas retrospective gating samples the whole R-R interval and can reject outlier beats during reconstruction.

body.prompt: Why is balanced steady-state free precession (bSSFP) the standard sequence for cardiac cine imaging?
options: It suppresses the blood pool signal to sharpen the endocardial border on every frame.
It nulls normal myocardium signal so that infarcted tissue appears bright on every phase.
It produces bright blood contrast from the T2/T1 ratio with fast temporal sampling.
It requires a gadolinium contrast injection to generate any blood pool signal at all.
body.explain: bSSFP contrast depends on the T2/T1 ratio of tissue rather than inflow or contrast, giving reliable bright blood and the fast temporal sampling cine requires.

body.prompt: In late gadolinium enhancement imaging, how is the inversion time (TI) selected?
options: TI is fixed at 180 milliseconds for every patient regardless of contrast timing.
TI is chosen to null normal myocardium so gadolinium retained in scar appears bright.
TI is chosen to null blood pool signal so the endocardial border is sharply defined.
TI is chosen to maximize fat signal to help identify pericardial disease clearly.
body.explain: Nulling normal myocardium makes it dark, so areas retaining gadolinium such as scar or fibrosis stand out as bright signal.

body.prompt: A patient's LGE images show enhancement confined to the subendocardium of the anterior wall, following the left anterior descending territory. What does this pattern most likely represent?
options: Non-ischemic cardiomyopathy from a prior episode of active myocarditis.
Ischemic infarction, following the vulnerable subendocardial perfusion territory.
A normal variant of contrast enhancement seen in healthy myocardium.
Amyloid infiltration presenting with diffuse mid-wall enhancement pattern.
body.explain: Subendocardial to transmural enhancement following a coronary territory is the classic ischemic pattern, since the subendocardium is the last layer perfused and first injured.

body.prompt: Elevated myocardial T2 relaxation times on parametric mapping most directly indicate which process?
options: Diffuse interstitial fibrosis from long-standing chronic remodeling.
Chronic scar tissue with reduced extracellular water content.
Myocardial edema from an acute process such as myocarditis or recent infarction.
Fatty infiltration typical of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.
body.explain: T2 rises with free water content, so elevated T2 mapping values reflect acute edema rather than chronic fibrosis or fat.

body.prompt: Which magnetization preparation produces the dark blood pool seen on black-blood cardiac imaging?
options: A single slice-selective inversion pulse timed precisely to the null point of fat.
A double inversion recovery, pairing a nonselective pulse with a slice-selective reinversion.
A pair of saturation bands placed superior and inferior to the imaging slice plane.
A T2 preparation pulse applied immediately before the image readout begins.
body.explain: The nonselective pulse inverts all spins, then the slice-selective reinversion restores the imaging slice, leaving inflowing blood from outside the slice nulled at imaging time.

body.prompt: When prescribing a phase-contrast sequence across a stenotic aortic valve, how should the velocity encoding value (venc) be set?
options: As low as possible, to maximize velocity-to-noise sensitivity in the image.
Close to the expected peak jet velocity, to avoid aliasing while preserving sensitivity.
Equal to the venc used for a normal mitral valve regardless of the clinical question.
At the scanner default value, since venc has no effect on image quality.
body.explain: A venc near the expected peak velocity avoids wraparound aliasing from too low a value while preserving the sensitivity a too-high value would sacrifice.

body.prompt: A dark band crosses the inferior myocardial wall on a bSSFP cine sequence. What is the appropriate remedy?
options: Increase the receiver bandwidth to eliminate chemical shift artifact.
Switch to a spin-echo sequence to remove the flow-related signal void.
Improve the local shim and adjust the center frequency to push the band away from the heart.
Add a saturation band over the chest wall to suppress the off-resonance signal.
body.explain: Banding comes from off-resonance field inhomogeneity in bSSFP, so improving the local shim and adjusting frequency shifts the band out of the region of interest.

body.prompt: What is the purpose of a navigator echo in a free-breathing coronary MRA acquisition?
options: To detect the R-wave when surface ECG leads fail to trigger inside the bore.
To track diaphragm position and gate data collection to a consistent respiratory phase.
To measure blood flow velocity through the coronary ostia before contrast injection.
To null myocardial signal in place of an inversion recovery pulse.
body.explain: A navigator echo, usually placed over the right hemidiaphragm, monitors its position so data are accepted only near end-expiration, suppressing respiratory motion without breath-holding.

body.prompt: How is left ventricular ejection fraction most accurately calculated from a cardiac MRI exam?
options: Measuring the left ventricular cavity diameter on a single four-chamber cine view.
Tracing endocardial contours on each short-axis slice at end-diastole and end-systole, using Simpson's method.
Estimating chamber volume from the mitral valve annulus diameter using a fixed geometric formula.
Averaging myocardial wall thickness measurements across three mid-ventricular short-axis slices.
body.explain: Tracing contours on the full short-axis stack and summing discs by Simpson's method avoids the geometric assumptions that limit single-view or formula-based estimates.

body.title: MR spectroscopy basics: chemical shift and the spectrum
body.html:
Every proton in the body resonates at a frequency set by the main magnetic field, but the cloud of electrons surrounding each proton shields it slightly from that field. Protons bound in different molecular environments, such as a proton on a fat chain versus a proton on a metabolite, experience different degrees of electron shielding and therefore precess at slightly different frequencies. This small frequency separation is called chemical shift, and it is the entire physical basis of magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

Because chemical shift is proportional to field strength, it is expressed as a ratio in parts per million (ppm) rather than in hertz, which keeps the scale consistent whether the study is acquired at 1.5T or 3T. A proton spectrum plots signal amplitude on the vertical axis against this ppm frequency axis, running conventionally from high ppm on the left to low ppm on the right. Each peak on that axis corresponds to a specific metabolite or group of chemically similar protons, and the area under a peak reflects the relative concentration of that metabolite within the sampled tissue.

Single-voxel spectroscopy collects one spectrum from a single, operator-placed cubic region of interest, giving a fast, high signal-to-noise measurement of that one location. Chemical-shift imaging, also called MRSI or multi-voxel spectroscopy, instead samples a grid of voxels across a slab or slice, producing a spectrum for every voxel and allowing metabolite maps to be generated across a lesion and its margins, at the cost of longer scan time and lower SNR per voxel.

Metabolite signals are roughly 10,000 times weaker than the signal from tissue water, so without suppression the water peak would completely dominate the spectrum and bury every metabolite peak beneath it. Robust water suppression, typically a chemical-shift selective saturation pulse applied before acquisition, is therefore mandatory. Fat also produces a signal orders of magnitude stronger than most metabolites, so lipid suppression or careful voxel placement away from fat is equally important for a diagnostic-quality spectrum.
keypoints: Chemical shift, from differing electron shielding around protons, is the physical basis of the MR spectrum.
The ppm scale is field-independent, so ppm positions are the same at 1.5T and 3T.
A spectrum plots signal amplitude versus ppm; peak area reflects relative metabolite concentration.
Single-voxel spectroscopy samples one region fast; MRSI/chemical-shift imaging samples a voxel grid for mapping.
Water and lipid suppression are mandatory because metabolites are about 10,000 times weaker than water.
body.worked_example: A 45-year-old with a new enhancing frontal lobe lesion is sent for single-voxel MRS to help distinguish tumor from an infectious or demyelinating process; the technologist places the voxel centered on the enhancing portion of the lesion, confirms the water suppression pulse is properly tuned on the pre-scan, and reviews the resulting spectrum with the ppm axis running from about 4 ppm down to 0 ppm before the peaks are labeled.
memory_hooks: Chemical shift is like an echo in different rooms: same shout, different room shapes the frequency you hear back.
ppm is the universal ruler: it reads the same no matter which scanner, 1.5T or 3T, is holding it.
exam_traps: Candidates sometimes assume ppm values change with field strength; they do not, because ppm is a ratio that cancels out field dependence.
Forgetting that fat, not just water, needs suppression leads to voxel placement errors near marrow or scalp fat.

body.title: Metabolites and clinical interpretation
body.html:
N-acetylaspartate (NAA) produces the dominant peak on a normal brain spectrum at about 2.0 ppm and is considered a marker of neuronal integrity and density. NAA falls in almost any process that damages or destroys neurons, including tumor, infarct, and demyelinating disease, so a reduced NAA peak is a nonspecific but reliable sign that normal neuronal tissue has been replaced or injured.

Creatine (Cr) appears at about 3.0 ppm and reflects cellular energy metabolism. Because its concentration is relatively stable across many pathologic conditions, Cr is commonly used as an internal reference peak, with other metabolites reported as ratios to creatine, such as Cho/Cr or NAA/Cr, rather than as absolute concentrations.

Choline (Cho) resonates at about 3.2 ppm and reflects cell membrane turnover, since it is a precursor and breakdown product of membrane phospholipids. Rapidly dividing cells build and break down membrane at a high rate, so an elevated choline peak, and a raised Cho/NAA or Cho/Cr ratio, is a classic spectroscopic sign of neoplasm.

Lactate appears as a characteristic doublet at about 1.3 ppm and signals anaerobic glycolysis, seen in ischemia, necrosis, and high-grade or rapidly growing tumors where blood supply cannot keep pace with metabolic demand. Lipid peaks cluster in the same 0.9 to 1.3 ppm region and indicate tissue breakdown or necrosis. Myo-inositol, at about 3.5 ppm, is a glial marker that can be elevated in low-grade glial proliferation and in early Alzheimer disease. Put together, a spectrum showing elevated choline, decreased NAA, and a raised Cho/NAA ratio suggests neoplasm, while the additional presence of lactate or lipid points toward necrosis or a higher-grade, more aggressive tumor.
keypoints: NAA (~2.0 ppm) is a marker of neuronal integrity; it falls with neuronal injury from tumor, infarct, or demyelination.
Creatine (~3.0 ppm) is relatively stable and serves as the internal reference for metabolite ratios.
Choline (~3.2 ppm) reflects membrane turnover; elevated choline and a raised Cho/NAA ratio suggest neoplasm.
Lactate (~1.3 ppm doublet) signals anaerobic metabolism, seen in ischemia, necrosis, and aggressive tumor.
Lipids (~0.9-1.3 ppm) indicate necrosis; myo-inositol (~3.5 ppm) is a glial marker.
body.worked_example: A spectrum obtained from a high-grade glioma shows a markedly elevated choline peak, a suppressed NAA peak, an elevated Cho/NAA ratio, and a prominent inverted lactate doublet at 1.3 ppm, a pattern the radiologist correlates with tumor necrosis and uses to help guide the biopsy target toward the region of highest choline rather than the necrotic center.
memory_hooks: NAA for Neurons Alive and Active; when it drops, neurons are in trouble.
Cho goes up when cells are dividing and chowing down on membrane, the signature of tumor.
exam_traps: Candidates confuse creatine's role: it is the reference peak, not the marker being measured for pathology.
A rising Cho/NAA ratio can be mistaken for infection; without clinical context it is a nonspecific sign of increased cell turnover, most classically neoplasm.

body.title: Acquisition techniques: STEAM, PRESS, and echo time
body.html:
Localized single-voxel spectroscopy relies on one of two pulse sequence families to select signal from a single volume while suppressing signal from everywhere else. STEAM (stimulated echo acquisition mode) uses three 90 degree pulses, one along each gradient axis, to generate a stimulated echo from the intersection of the three slices. Because a stimulated echo carries only half the available signal compared with a spin echo, STEAM delivers roughly half the SNR of PRESS, but its use of only 90 degree pulses allows a shorter minimum echo time, useful when the goal is to detect short-T2 metabolites or J-coupled compounds close to the water and lipid signal.

PRESS (point-resolved spectroscopy) uses one 90 degree pulse followed by two 180 degree refocusing pulses along the three orthogonal planes. Because it produces a true spin echo rather than a stimulated echo, PRESS delivers roughly twice the SNR of STEAM at a matched voxel size and TE, which is why PRESS is the more commonly used sequence in clinical practice, particularly for smaller voxels or lower field strength studies where SNR is already limited.

Echo time has a strong effect on the appearance of the spectrum. A short TE (around 30 to 35 ms) shows more metabolite peaks, including myo-inositol, glutamate, and glutamine, because these compounds have short T2 values and would otherwise decay before a longer echo time could capture them, but the tradeoff is a rolling, less flat baseline that can make quantification harder. A long TE (commonly 135 to 144 ms, or sometimes 288 ms) produces a cleaner, flatter baseline that more clearly displays NAA, creatine, choline, and lactate, at the cost of losing the shorter-T2 metabolite signals.

Long TE acquisitions have one additional diagnostic advantage: because of J-coupling between the two methyl protons in the lactate molecule, the lactate doublet at 1.3 ppm characteristically inverts below the baseline at TE values around 135 to 144 ms, then returns above the baseline at very long TE such as 288 ms. This predictable inversion is a useful confirmation that a peak at 1.3 ppm is truly lactate and not overlapping lipid, which does not invert. Regardless of technique, careful voxel placement away from bone, fat, and air, combined with high-order shimming to achieve a narrow linewidth, is essential for a spectrum that can be reliably interpreted.
keypoints: STEAM uses three 90 degree pulses (stimulated echo), giving shorter minimum TE but about half the SNR of PRESS.
PRESS uses 90-180-180 (spin echo) pulses, giving higher SNR, and is the more commonly used clinical sequence.
Short TE shows more metabolites, including myo-inositol, but has a rolling, harder-to-quantify baseline.
Long TE (commonly 135-144 ms) gives a cleaner, flatter baseline highlighting NAA, Cr, Cho, and lactate.
The lactate doublet characteristically inverts below baseline at TE around 135-144 ms, confirming its identity.
body.worked_example: For a suspected pediatric posterior fossa tumor, the protocol includes both a short-TE acquisition to screen for myo-inositol and other short-T2 metabolites, and a long-TE (144 ms) PRESS acquisition; the long-TE spectrum shows an inverted doublet at 1.3 ppm, confirming lactate rather than overlapping lipid contamination and supporting a diagnosis of a metabolically active, possibly necrotic mass.
memory_hooks: STEAM has three 90s and half the signal; PRESS has 90-180-180 and packs twice the punch.
Lactate flips upside down around TE 135 to 144, like it is doing a handstand to prove its identity.
exam_traps: Candidates often assume higher TE always means better quality; long TE actually loses short-T2 metabolites even as the baseline flattens.
An inverted peak at 1.3 ppm at short TE is sometimes misread as an artifact; the inversion is only expected at the intermediate TE range, not at short TE.

body.title: Pitfalls and spectral quality
body.html:
The single greatest determinant of spectral quality is magnetic field homogeneity within the voxel. A good higher-order shim narrows the linewidth of every peak, keeping adjacent metabolite peaks distinct and allowing accurate measurement of peak height and area. A poor shim broadens each peak, and when linewidths broaden enough, closely spaced peaks, such as glutamate and glutamine near creatine, merge into an unresolvable hump, making the spectrum difficult or impossible to interpret reliably.

Incomplete water suppression leaves a residual water signal that can swamp the baseline and distort the shape and apparent height of nearby metabolite peaks, especially choline and creatine, which sit close to the water resonance. If the suppression pulse is mistuned or the shim is poor, the residual water hump can be mistaken for baseline drift or can obscure a genuine metabolite abnormality.

Voxel contamination from tissue outside the intended region of interest is one of the most common technologist-controllable pitfalls. A voxel placed too close to the skull, scalp, or facial fat picks up an intense lipid signal that bleeds into the 0.9 to 1.3 ppm region, obscuring or mimicking the lactate doublet. A voxel that includes bone, air, or a portion of CSF or ventricle introduces additional susceptibility effects, dilutes the metabolite signal with fluid or air that contains essentially no measurable metabolites, and further degrades the local shim.

Finally, patient motion during a spectroscopy acquisition, which typically takes several minutes, shifts the voxel relative to the anatomy mid-scan and can smear or duplicate peaks, while a voxel that is made too small to avoid these contaminants sacrifices signal-to-noise to the point that peaks are lost in noise. Careful voxel placement well away from bone, fat, and air interfaces, patient immobilization, and attention to shim quality before acquisition begins are the practical keys to a diagnostic spectrum.
keypoints: Good higher-order shim gives narrow, well-resolved peaks; poor shim broadens and merges adjacent peaks.
Incomplete water suppression leaves residual signal that can swamp the baseline near choline and creatine.
Voxel contamination from adjacent fat, such as skull or scalp, can mimic or obscure the lactate doublet.
Including CSF or ventricle in the voxel dilutes metabolite signal and worsens local shim quality.
Patient motion and undersized voxels both degrade spectral quality, the former by misregistration and the latter by low SNR.
body.worked_example: A spectrum obtained near the skull base shows an unexpected broad hump under 1.3 ppm and poorly resolved NAA and creatine peaks; on review, the voxel was placed too close to the temporal bone and adjacent fat, and the shim report shows a wider than expected linewidth, prompting the technologist to reposition the voxel further from bone and fat and reshim before repeating the acquisition.
memory_hooks: Shim narrow, peaks stand tall and separate; shim wide, peaks slump together.
Fat next door drowns out the lactate signal, so keep the voxel away from the skull and scalp.
exam_traps: A broad hump around 1.3 ppm from adjacent lipid contamination is easily mistaken for a true lactate doublet unless a long-TE inversion check is performed.
Candidates sometimes shrink the voxel to avoid contamination without recognizing that this trades contamination risk for a significant loss of SNR.

body.prompt: What physical property gives rise to the different ppm positions of metabolite peaks in an MR spectrum?
options: Magnetic susceptibility differences at borders
Flow-related signal loss in vessels
Chemical shift from electron shielding
T1 relaxation differences between tissues
body.explain: Electrons around a proton shield it from the main field to different degrees depending on its molecular environment, producing the small frequency shifts that create the ppm axis.

body.prompt: Why is water suppression essential in proton MR spectroscopy?
options: Water causes excessive tissue heating artifacts
Metabolites are far weaker than water
Water contains no hydrogen protons detected
Suppression shortens the total scan time
body.explain: Metabolite concentrations are roughly 10,000 times lower than tissue water, so without suppression the water peak would obscure every metabolite peak.

body.prompt: The NAA peak at approximately 2.0 ppm on a proton spectrum is primarily a marker of what?
options: Cell membrane turnover rate
Anaerobic glycolytic metabolism level
Glial cell proliferation marker
Neuronal integrity and density
body.explain: NAA is produced in neurons and falls with any process that damages or destroys neuronal tissue, making it a marker of neuronal integrity.

body.prompt: An elevated choline peak with a raised Cho/NAA ratio on brain MRS is most suggestive of which process?
options: Simple CSF filled cyst
Neoplasm with membrane turnover
Acute ischemic infarction
Chronic demyelinating disease
body.explain: Choline reflects membrane phospholipid turnover, and rapidly dividing tumor cells build and break down membrane at a high rate, raising the Cho/NAA ratio.

body.prompt: At what echo time range does the lactate doublet characteristically invert below the spectral baseline?
options: About 500 to 600 ms
About 1500 to 2000 ms
About 135 to 144 ms
About 20 to 30 ms
body.explain: J-coupling between the two methyl protons in lactate causes its 1.3 ppm doublet to invert below baseline at intermediate echo times around 135 to 144 ms.

body.prompt: Compared with STEAM, why is PRESS the more commonly used single-voxel localization technique?
options: PRESS allows a shorter echo time
PRESS requires only one RF pulse
PRESS avoids the need for shimming
PRESS gives higher signal to noise
body.explain: PRESS uses a true spin echo, 90-180-180, rather than a stimulated echo, giving about twice the SNR of STEAM at a matched TE and voxel size.

body.prompt: What is the main advantage of chemical-shift imaging, or MRSI, over single-voxel spectroscopy?
options: It samples a grid of voxels
It gives higher SNR per voxel
It needs no shim adjustment at all
It removes the need for water suppression
body.explain: MRSI samples a grid of voxels across a slice, producing metabolite maps across a lesion, whereas single-voxel spectroscopy samples only one region.

body.prompt: Why is creatine commonly used as the internal reference peak in MRS interpretation?
options: It only appears in tumor tissue
It has no chemical shift value
Its concentration stays relatively stable
It produces the tallest peak always
body.explain: Creatine reflects cellular energy metabolism and remains relatively stable across many pathologic conditions, so other metabolites are commonly reported as ratios to it.

body.prompt: What effect does poor magnetic field homogeneity, or shim, have on a proton spectrum?
options: It doubles the total scan time
It broadens and merges adjacent peaks
It sharpens and separates adjacent peaks
It shifts all peaks to zero ppm
body.explain: Poor shim widens the linewidth of every peak, and when linewidths broaden enough, closely spaced peaks merge into an unresolvable hump.

body.prompt: Placing a spectroscopy voxel too close to the skull most commonly causes what problem?
options: Complete loss of the water peak
An artificially elevated NAA peak
A falsely narrow spectral linewidth
Lipid contamination mimicking lactate
body.explain: Fat from the skull, scalp, or marrow produces an intense signal in the 0.9 to 1.3 ppm region that can obscure or mimic the lactate doublet.

body.title: BOLD contrast: neurovascular coupling
body.html:
Functional MRI localizes brain activity using the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) effect, an indirect marker of neuronal activity based on local blood chemistry rather than the electrical signal itself. When a region of cortex becomes active, its metabolic demand rises, and the vascular system responds with an overcompensating increase in local cerebral blood flow that exceeds the actual oxygen consumed. The result is a paradoxical local rise in the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated hemoglobin within and around the active tissue.

Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and creates local field inhomogeneities that dephase spins, shortening T2* and, to a lesser extent, T2. Oxyhemoglobin is diamagnetic and has little effect on the surrounding field. Because active tissue ends up with relatively less deoxyhemoglobin, there is less dephasing, T2* lengthens slightly, and the T2*-weighted signal rises by a few percent in that region. This small signal increase, not a decrease, is what fMRI detects as activation.

Because the effect depends on T2* changes, fMRI is acquired with T2*-weighted gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (GRE-EPI), which is fast enough to sample the whole brain repeatedly and sensitive to the susceptibility differences the BOLD effect produces. The vascular response is sluggish compared to the neuronal event that triggers it: the hemodynamic response function typically peaks about 4 to 6 seconds after a brief stimulus and then returns toward baseline over several more seconds. BOLD is therefore an indirect, delayed, low-amplitude surrogate for neuronal activity, not a direct measurement of it.
keypoints: BOLD signal reflects local blood oxygenation, not neuronal firing directly.
Active cortex shows increased blood flow that outpaces oxygen extraction, raising the oxy to deoxy hemoglobin ratio.
Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and dephases spins; oxyhemoglobin is diamagnetic.
Less deoxyhemoglobin means less T2* dephasing, so active regions show a signal increase.
BOLD is acquired with T2*-weighted GRE-EPI; the hemodynamic response peaks 4 to 6 seconds after the stimulus.
body.worked_example: A technologist runs a finger-tapping fMRI paradigm and shows the radiologist a color activation map over the precentral gyrus. The radiologist asks why the activated voxels appear brighter rather than darker on the T2*-weighted images, and the technologist explains that increased flow to the tapping-related motor cortex washes out deoxyhemoglobin faster than it is produced, so the paramagnetic dephasing effect drops and the local signal rises.
memory_hooks: More flow, less deoxy, more signal: activation lights up on BOLD.
Deoxyhemoglobin is the villain of T2*; oxyhemoglobin is harmless.
exam_traps: Do not assume active brain regions show a signal drop; the overcompensating blood flow makes them brighter, not darker, on T2*-weighted images.
BOLD reflects hemodynamics with a several-second lag, not the instant of neuronal firing, so it cannot resolve activity on a millisecond timescale.

body.title: Task-based fMRI: paradigms and analysis
body.html:
Task-based fMRI compares brain activity during a controlled task against a baseline or control condition to identify regions engaged by that task. The two common paradigm designs are block design and event-related design. In a block design, the task and rest conditions alternate in extended epochs, for example 20 to 30 seconds of finger tapping followed by 20 to 30 seconds of rest, repeated several times. This produces a large, sustained hemodynamic response with high signal-to-noise ratio and is the more robust and common approach for clinical presurgical mapping.

In an event-related design, brief individual stimuli are presented, and the hemodynamic response to each discrete event is modeled separately, often with randomized or jittered timing. This design offers more flexibility, such as sorting trials after the fact by correct versus incorrect responses, but each individual response has lower amplitude and statistical power than a sustained block, so more repetitions and longer scan times are typically needed.

Analysis is usually performed with a general linear model (GLM), which correlates the measured time course of each voxel against a predicted hemodynamic response derived from the task timing. Voxels whose signal fluctuations match the predicted response are flagged as statistically active. Because thousands of voxels are tested simultaneously, a correction for multiple comparisons is applied before the resulting statistical map is thresholded and overlaid on a high-resolution anatomic image. The single largest source of spurious or lost activation in task fMRI is patient head motion, since even small movements between the task and rest epochs generate signal changes that can swamp the true BOLD effect.
keypoints: Block design alternates extended task and rest epochs, giving a strong, robust signal favored clinically.
Event-related design models responses to brief individual stimuli, offering flexibility but lower power.
The general linear model (GLM) correlates each voxel time course with a predicted hemodynamic response.
Statistical activation maps require correction for multiple comparisons before thresholding.
Head motion is the dominant confounder in task-based fMRI.
body.worked_example: For presurgical language mapping in a patient with a frontal glioma, the neuroradiology team chooses a block design alternating word-generation and rest blocks rather than a single-word event-related task, because the sustained block produces a stronger, more reliable activation map over Broca's area despite the patient's limited attention span.
memory_hooks: Block design: long and strong. Event-related: short and flexible.
GLM: the model predicts the wiggle, the voxel either matches it or does not.
exam_traps: Event-related designs are not simply better because they are more flexible; they trade signal strength and statistical power for that flexibility.
A statistically active voxel on an uncorrected map may just be noise; multiple-comparisons correction is required before a map is clinically meaningful.

body.title: Resting-state fMRI and functional connectivity
body.html:
Resting-state fMRI is acquired while the patient lies quietly without performing any task, typically simply told to relax with eyes open or closed and stay awake. Rather than looking for signal changes tied to a stimulus, this technique measures spontaneous, low-frequency BOLD fluctuations, generally in the range of about 0.01 to 0.1 Hz, that occur continuously across the brain even at rest.

The key finding is that distant brain regions whose spontaneous fluctuations rise and fall together over time are considered functionally connected, meaning they are part of the same working network even though they may be anatomically far apart. One well known example is the default mode network, a set of regions including the posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex that are more active at rest than during an external task. Other established networks include sensorimotor, visual, and executive control networks.

Two common analysis approaches are seed-based correlation, in which the time course of a chosen reference region is correlated against every other voxel in the brain, and independent component analysis (ICA), which decomposes the whole data set into separate spatial patterns of correlated activity without requiring a predefined seed. Resting-state fMRI is especially useful in patients who cannot reliably perform a task, such as young children, sedated patients, or patients with cognitive impairment, since no active cooperation is required beyond staying still.
keypoints: Resting-state fMRI requires no task; the patient simply rests while spontaneous BOLD fluctuations are recorded.
Relevant fluctuations occur at low frequency, roughly 0.01 to 0.1 Hz.
Regions with correlated time courses are termed functionally connected, forming networks.
The default mode network is the classic example, more active at rest than during task engagement.
Analysis uses seed-based correlation or independent component analysis (ICA).
body.worked_example: A pediatric patient who is sedated for a separate reason has resting-state fMRI added to the protocol so the team can still map sensorimotor and language networks for surgical planning, since a task-based paradigm would be impossible under sedation.
memory_hooks: Resting-state: no task, no problem; the brain still talks to itself.
Fire together, wire together: correlated time courses define a network.
exam_traps: Resting-state fMRI does not eliminate motion sensitivity; the patient still must stay still even though no task is performed.
The default mode network is more active at rest, not during task performance; do not reverse this relationship.

body.title: fMRI acquisition and pitfalls
body.html:
Functional MRI acquisition demands speed, since the whole brain must be sampled repeatedly, typically every 1 to 3 seconds (the TR), to track the slow hemodynamic response over the course of a run. This is achieved with fast gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (GRE-EPI), which fills an entire slice of k-space after a single excitation and provides strong T2* weighting to make the sequence sensitive to the small susceptibility changes that underlie the BOLD effect.

The same susceptibility sensitivity that makes EPI useful for BOLD also makes it vulnerable to artifact. At air-tissue interfaces, especially near the orbitofrontal and anterior temporal lobes close to the sinuses and skull base, local field distortion causes geometric warping and regions of signal dropout, sometimes obscuring true activation in those areas entirely.

Patient motion is a critical technical concern because the true BOLD signal change is only a few percent; even sub-voxel head motion between frames can generate apparent signal changes of similar or greater magnitude, either mimicking activation that is not real or masking activation that is real. Motion correction (realignment) and censoring of severely corrupted frames are standard preprocessing steps. Physiological noise from cardiac pulsation and respiration also contaminates the BOLD time course and is typically modeled or filtered out.

Clinically, the leading application of task-based fMRI is presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex, such as primary motor and language areas, so the surgical team can plan a resection of a tumor or epileptic focus while minimizing damage to critical function.
keypoints: fMRI uses fast T2*-weighted GRE-EPI with a TR of about 1 to 3 seconds to sample the whole brain repeatedly.
EPI's susceptibility sensitivity causes distortion and signal dropout near air-tissue interfaces.
Orbitofrontal and anterior temporal regions are classic sites of EPI dropout.
Head motion is critical because true BOLD changes are only a few percent of signal.
Presurgical eloquent-cortex mapping (motor, language) is a major clinical application.
body.worked_example: A presurgical fMRI for a left temporal lobe tumor shows unexpectedly poor activation in the anterior temporal lobe near the task region; the technologist recognizes this may reflect EPI susceptibility dropout near the skull base and temporal bone rather than a true absence of language function, and flags it for correlation with other mapping methods.
memory_hooks: EPI is fast but touchy: great for BOLD, bad near air.
A few percent signal, a few pixels of motion: fMRI has almost no room for error.
exam_traps: Signal dropout near the orbitofrontal or temporal lobes on fMRI is often mistaken for absent function; it may simply be a susceptibility artifact of EPI.
Do not assume a single motion-corrupted frame is harmless; because true BOLD changes are only a few percent, small motion can fully mimic or erase activation.

body.prompt: Which hemoglobin species is responsible for the local field inhomogeneity that underlies the BOLD signal?
options: Oxyhemoglobin, because it is paramagnetic
Deoxyhemoglobin, because it is paramagnetic
Oxyhemoglobin, because it is diamagnetic
Methemoglobin, because it is ferromagnetic
body.explain: Deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic and creates local field inhomogeneities that dephase spins and shorten T2*. Oxyhemoglobin is diamagnetic and has little magnetic effect.

body.prompt: During neuronal activation, cerebral blood flow to the active region increases more than oxygen consumption does. What effect does this have on the T2*-weighted BOLD signal?
options: Signal decreases because more oxygen is being consumed
Signal stays the same because flow and consumption balance out
Signal increases because there is relatively less deoxyhemoglobin
Signal increases because there is relatively more deoxyhemoglobin
body.explain: The overcompensating flow washes out deoxyhemoglobin faster than it accumulates, so less paramagnetic dephasing occurs and the T2*-weighted signal rises in the active region.

body.prompt: Which pulse sequence is standard for acquiring BOLD fMRI data?
options: T2*-weighted gradient-echo echo-planar imaging
T1-weighted spin-echo imaging
Proton-density-weighted fast spin-echo imaging
T2-weighted turbo spin-echo imaging
body.explain: BOLD contrast depends on T2* changes from local susceptibility, so fMRI uses fast T2*-weighted GRE-EPI to capture the whole brain repeatedly with the needed sensitivity.

body.prompt: Approximately how long after a brief neuronal event does the hemodynamic response function typically peak?
options: 100 to 300 milliseconds
About 1 second
About 10 to 15 seconds
About 4 to 6 seconds
body.explain: The vascular response lags the neuronal event, with the hemodynamic response function typically peaking around 4 to 6 seconds before returning toward baseline.

body.prompt: Which paradigm design alternates extended epochs of task and rest and generally produces the most robust signal for clinical mapping?
options: Event-related design
Block design
Resting-state design
Sparse-sampling design
body.explain: Block design uses sustained task and rest epochs, producing a large, robust hemodynamic response favored for clinical presurgical mapping.

body.prompt: What statistical method correlates each voxel's time course with a predicted hemodynamic response to generate an fMRI activation map?
options: Independent component analysis
Seed-based correlation analysis
General linear model analysis
Fourier spectral analysis
body.explain: The general linear model (GLM) correlates each voxel's measured signal with the predicted hemodynamic response from the task timing to identify statistically active voxels.

body.prompt: What is the single most significant confounding factor that degrades task-based fMRI activation maps?
options: Patient head motion
Scanner gradient nonlinearity
Radiofrequency coil loading
Static magnetic field drift
body.explain: Because true BOLD changes are only a few percent, even small head motion between task and rest frames can mimic or obscure real activation, making motion the dominant confounder.

body.prompt: Resting-state fMRI identifies functional networks, such as the default mode network, by analyzing what kind of signal?
options: High-frequency BOLD changes tied to the cardiac and respiratory cycle
Signal changes precisely time-locked to a specific behavioral task
Static differences in T1-weighted anatomic signal intensity
Spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations, roughly 0.01 to 0.1 Hz
body.explain: Resting-state fMRI measures spontaneous low-frequency BOLD fluctuations, generally around 0.01 to 0.1 Hz; regions whose fluctuations correlate over time define functional networks such as the default mode network.

body.prompt: EPI-based fMRI is most prone to susceptibility-related signal dropout and distortion near which of the following regions?
options: Superior frontal and parietal cortex
Orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex
Posterior cingulate and precuneus cortex
Occipital and cerebellar cortex
body.explain: Air-tissue interfaces near the sinuses and skull base cause local field distortion, producing geometric warping and signal dropout in the orbitofrontal and anterior temporal lobes on EPI.

body.prompt: What is the leading clinical application of task-based fMRI in a patient with a brain tumor?
options: Measuring tumor perfusion for grading
Detecting hemorrhage within the tumor
Presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex
Confirming tumor cellularity before biopsy
body.explain: Task-based fMRI is widely used before surgery to map eloquent cortex, such as primary motor and language areas, so the surgical team can plan resection while sparing critical function.
